tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

8826	+# Feedback channel: suggested insertions for the evaluation design calculus
8827	+
8828	+Draft 0.1 — 2026-10-11. Suggestions only.
8829	+
8830	+This file changes nothing in `evaluation_design_calculus.md` or
8831	+`evaluation_game_testbed.md`. Each block names a location in those documents,
8832	+offers text for it, and states what supports the text. Where a block is adopted,
8833	+its wording should be made the author's own. Where it is not, the executable
8834	+fixtures still stand by themselves.
8835	+
8836	+The gap being addressed: the calculus already says that a judgment "shown during
8837	+play or used for learning ... also enters observations or controller updates"
8838	+(§2), and that frozen-controller sensitivity differs from sensitivity "after
8839	+retraining, selecting another controller" (§7). It has no operator for that
8840	+channel, no estimand for what the channel does to a score, and no record of how
8841	+often it was used. A self-improvement loop is that channel applied once per
8842	+generation.
8843	+

8888	+## D. §5, three laws and one observation
8889	+
8890	+**Coarsening law.**
8891	+
8892	+> The access classes are ordered: sealed is a deterministic function of the
8893	+> score, and the score is a deterministic function of the per-item outcomes.
8894	+> Total-variation distance between two controllers' feedback therefore cannot
8895	+> increase from item-level to score-only to sealed. Two controllers that fail
8896	+> different items with equal totals are separated completely by item-level
8897	+> feedback and not at all by a score.
8898	+
8899	+Support: `access_order_fixture`; the ordering is checked for every pair of
8900	+distributions on a rational grid over two-item outcomes.
8901	+
8902	+**Selection law.**
8903	+
8904	+> Keeping the best of \(K\) candidates by score on \(s\), then reporting that
8905	+> score, overstates: \(\mathbb E[\max_k\hat S_k]\ge\max_k\mathbb E[\hat S_k]\).
8906	+> This is the same convexity as the mixture law, with the candidate index in
8907	+> place of the mixture component. For candidates of equal true value
8908	+> one half, two candidates and one item give a reported value of three quarters.
8909	+
8910	+Support: `selection_inflation`, checked against independent enumeration of
8911	+every outcome matrix in seven small cells. Exact gaps for two candidates at
8912	+\(p=\tfrac12\) are \(\tfrac14\), \(\tfrac{35}{256}\), about 0.0700 and about
8913	+0.0352 at 1, 4, 16 and 64 items; multiplied by \(\sqrt n\) these are 0.250,
8914	+0.273, 0.280 and 0.282. The value \(1/(2\sqrt\pi)\approx0.2821\) is the
8915	+standard Gaussian figure for the larger of two draws. The fixture verifies the
8916	+listed cells and no limit.
8917	+
8918	+Boundary: one generation, equal candidates, independent items. Accumulation
8919	+across generations is a simulation result, not an exact one.
8920	+
8921	+**Ceiling law.**
8922	+
8923	+> With labels flipped independently at rate \(\varepsilon<\tfrac12\), no
8924	+> predictor blind to the flips exceeds \(1-\varepsilon\) on observed labels.
8925	+> A controller that has memorized a share \(m/n\) of \(s\), and scores \(v\)
8926	+> elsewhere, scores \(m/n+(1-m/n)v\) on \(s\). It crosses the ceiling only when
8927	+> \(m/n>(1-\varepsilon-v)/(1-v)\). Below that share a ceiling check is silent.
8928	+
8929	+Support: `ceiling_detection_threshold`. With clean accuracy \(\tfrac45\) and
8930	+\(\varepsilon=\tfrac1{10}\): \(v=\tfrac{37}{50}\), threshold \(\tfrac8{13}\).
8931	+The formula assumes a memorized item has no effect on any other item, which the
8932	+nearest-neighbour learner in the simulations did not satisfy.
8933	+
8934	+**Observation on what item-level feedback selects.**
8935	+
8936	+> An item the controller fails is more likely than an average item to carry a
8937	+> wrong label, whenever the controller is better than chance:
8938	+> \(\Pr[\text{flipped}\mid\text{failed}]=\varepsilon a/(\varepsilon a+(1-\varepsilon)(1-a))\),
8939	+> which exceeds \(\varepsilon\) exactly when \(a>\tfrac12\). Feeding failures
8940	+> back concentrates label noise in what the next controller is built from.
8941	+
8942	+Support: `failed_item_noise_share`; \(\tfrac4{13}\) against a base rate of
8943	+\(\tfrac1{10}\) in the fixture. In the second simulation the measured share
8944	+among patched items was 20–29% against the same 10% base rate. This is the
8945	+reason the unchecked answer in the Proposer–Solver recipe (atlas §11) matters
8946	+once its output is fed back.

8951	+> the simulations, score-only selection of fresh training batches raised it.

9044	+## 1. The question put to each case
9045	+
9046	+A forecast of compounding needs one estimand: the gain from one generation of
9047	+controllers to the next, repeated, on a readout the improvement process did not
9048	+touch. In the notation of the insertions, that is a series of \(V^{r}_{\pi_g}\)
9049	+with \(r\) sealed, together with a ledger showing that it stayed sealed.
9050	+
9051	+| Card field | What to look for in a takeoff claim |
9052	+|---|---|
9053	+| \(\Pi\) | What improves: weights, harness, test-time budget, or the mix of who does the work |
9054	+| \(D\) | How scored items were chosen, and whether the choice followed a look at results |
9055	+| \(Z\) | Whether what was kept depends on how it scored |
9056	+| \(J\) | Who or what judges, and whether the judge shares errors with the judged |
9057	+| Feedback | Whether scores or items from the scored set reached the improvement process |
9058	+| Readout | Whether any reported number comes from a set declared sealed |
9059	+| \(C\) | Which estimand the evidence supports, as against the one the headline implies |

9075	+## 3. OpenAI's internal model: an amplification curve read as a trajectory
9076	+

9078	+10 September, states: "Since August 28 we have been training a new internal
9079	+model," and "This model's training is ongoing and its performance continues to
9080	+improve." It describes the model as built through large-scale reinforcement
9081	+learning on a pretrained model. That result involved on the order of 10,000
9082	+concurrent agents, about 88 hours, about 2.7 million messages and roughly 130
9083	+billion output tokens, with Lean formalization taking a further 17 hours.

9085	+
9086	+A chart titled "Performance of GPT-6 Astra and our Internal Model on a curated
9087	+set of open math problems" plots pass rate against test-time compute on a log
9088	+scale, with error bars. Read by eye from a screenshot, the internal model runs
9089	+from about 0.26 to about 0.48 over six points and GPT-6 Astra from about 0.09 to
9090	+about 0.17 over five. The chart could not be retrieved from the page text.
9091	+[Screenshot](https://x.com/AndrewCurran_/status/2108609708441657531)
9092	+
9093	+The 6 October release reports 722 manuscripts in 372 result families, about
9094	+4,000 problems posed, 162 main results formalized in Lean, ten reasoning
9095	+summaries, and an average result using "the equivalent compute of roughly three
9096	+hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking." Its README says: "We expanded these evaluations
9097	+after performance on our existing mathematical evaluations saturated."
9098	+[Primary, summarized](https://openai.com/index/sharing-ai-progress-in-mathematics/);
9099	+counts from a [secondary reading of the repository](https://cellcog.ai/blog/openai-math-results/).

9102	+compares two controllers at several inference budgets at one moment. It is not
9103	+a series over training time, and the sentence that performance "continues to
9104	+improve" has no plotted support in what was read.

9106	+Four declarations are absent:
9107	+
9108	+- \(D\): the rule by which the set was "curated", and whether curation followed

9110	+  items, and is also a decision taken on results.
9111	+- \(Z\): results were kept when judged significant. What is published is
9112	+  conditioned on the judgment.

9115	+  addresses a different contamination question and is silent on this one.

9118	+problems to manuscripts was not in what was read):
9119	+
9120	+\[
9121	+\frac{722}{4000}=\frac{361}{2000},\qquad
9122	+\frac{372}{4000}=\frac{93}{1000},\qquad
9123	+\frac{162}{722}=\frac{81}{361}\approx0.224 .
9124	+\]

9127	+failed attempt cost what a kept one did, compute per kept family would be

9129	+whether failures are in its average.

9140	+## 4. Anthropic's Automation Index: a judge measuring a mix
9141	+
9142	+**Observed.** A prototype index catalogues about 15,000 granular tasks into a
9143	+frozen tree of 542 nodes, 378 of them leaves, each rated on Epoch AI's
9144	+automation scale. "Leads" (AL4) means the model completes most of a task
9145	+end-to-end from a high-level prompt while a human supervises. Aggregation is
9146	+weighted by person-time. A Claude agent gathers evidence per node and an
9147	+independent Claude judge assigns the level. Staff rated their own areas as a
9148	+check: model–human exact agreement 59%, human–human 35%, within one level 97%.
9149	+As of August 2026 the "leads" share is 26% and the share at or above
9150	+"collaborates" exceeds 90%; no measured subset is fully autonomous. The basket
9151	+is frozen at July 2026. Stated caveats include dependence on the judge,
9152	+contestable AL3/AL4 cases, crude weighting, and a judge that may share errors
9153	+with the models it rates.
9154	+[Primary, summarized](https://www.anthropic.com/institute/measuring-pace-of-ai-development)
9155	+
9156	+**Interpretation.** This is the atlas's Rubric Discovery case at institutional
9157	+scale: the produced artifact is a judge, and it needs its own evaluation. Three
9158	+points follow from the card.
9159	+
9160	+1. The headline is a threshold count at one boundary of a six-level scale.
9161	+   Agreement "within one level" does not protect a count taken exactly at a
9162	+   one-level boundary. Exact agreement between judge and human, 59%, is the
9163	+   relevant figure, and it is higher than agreement between humans.
9164	+2. Weights are person-time measured after automation. A task that became fast
9165	+   takes less time and so weighs less. The direction of that bias is to
9166	+   understate the automated share of the original work.
9167	+3. It is a measurement of who does the work. It is the \(p\) of an Amdahl
9168	+   bound, not a gain per generation.
9169	+
9170	+**Derived arithmetic** (illustrative, and conditional on reading 26% as a
9171	+pre-automation time share, which point 2 says it is not):
9172	+
9173	+\[
9174	+\frac{1}{1-\tfrac{13}{50}}=\frac{50}{37}\approx1.35 .
9175	+\]
9176	+
9177	+That is the ceiling on overall speedup if the "leads" share became free and
9178	+nothing else changed.
9179	+
9180	+**Proposed variation.** Blind human re-rating of a stratified sample of nodes
9181	+near the AL3/AL4 boundary, with the headline reported as an interval under a
9182	+one-level perturbation of the judge. Separately, weights taken from a
9183	+pre-automation time survey.
9184	+
9185	+**Claim boundary.** There is no scored item set here, so feedback and readout
9186	+do not apply. The index supports a statement about task mix under a declared
9187	+judge. It does not measure whether each generation improves the next by more.

9189	+## 5. METR's time horizon: a suite that hides by saturating
9190	+
9191	+**Observed.** Time Horizon 1.1 fits a logistic curve of success against human
9192	+task duration over "over a hundred diverse software tasks" from RE-Bench, HCAST
9193	+and shorter novel tasks, and reads off the 50% point. The page states:
9194	+"Measurements above 16 hrs are unreliable with our current task suite." It
9195	+carries a notice dated 8 September 2026 that it is no longer actively updated.
9196	+It mentions private tasks without giving the public/private split.
9197	+[Primary, summarized](https://metr.org/time-horizons/)
9198	+
9199	+Values come from secondary readings of METR's data: Claude Mythos Preview
9200	+(early) at 1044.78 minutes
9201	+([DataLearner](https://www.datalearner.com/en/benchmarks/metr-time-horizons-v1-1));
9202	+doubling times of 131 days for the post-2023 fit and 89 days for the since-2024
9203	+fit ([Manifold market text](https://manifold.markets/Bayesian/claude-sonnet-5-metr-50-time-horizo)).
9204	+
9205	+**Interpretation.** In the testbed's terms a saturated suite is an
9206	+observation-only Hide. Once a controller's ability exceeds the hardest items,
9207	+distinct controllers push forward to the same record, and the discrimination
9208	+gap between them goes to zero. No change in the game is involved.
9209	+
9210	+The suite is fixed and reused across model generations, by every developer. At
9211	+the level of the field that is at least score-only feedback over years. Nothing
9212	+read asserts that any developer trained against it.
9213	+
9214	+**Derived arithmetic.**
9215	+
9216	+\[
9217	+\frac{1044.78}{60}\approx17.41\ \text{hours}>16 .
9218	+\]
9219	+
9220	+The highest frontier point lies above the bound the instrument's owner calls
9221	+reliable. The 131-day and 89-day figures are fits over nested windows, so their
9222	+difference is not the ratio of two successive doubling intervals.
9223	+
9224	+**Proposed variation.** Report, per model, the count of items above its
9225	+estimated ability. Extend the suite with long tasks held sealed. Declare the
9226	+freeze date as part of the instrument.
9227	+
9228	+**Claim boundary.** Below the ceiling the horizon supports a statement about
9229	+released models on this task family. Above it, neither a plateau nor an
9230	+acceleration is identified.

9235	+scored on a selection suite of ML engineering, heuristic algorithm engineering
9236	+and harness engineering tasks; scoring uses private data averaged into a grade.
9237	+Inner agents see only a public signal. The outer agent "reads the previously
9238	+proposed agents and their grades", and its reviewer "explores the evaluation
9239	+artifacts". The main run lasted eight days: one initial agent and 99 proposals,
9240	+seven accepted at steps 2, 6, 28, 39, 47, 63 and 85, raising the incumbent grade
9241	+from 0.703 to 0.778. The outer loop ran on Claude Opus 4.7 and the inner agents
9242	+on Gemini 3 Flash. Two further runs accepted two and four rewrites.

9244	+Held-out reporting uses ALE-Bench (10 tasks, 10 seeds), MLE-Bench (22 tasks, 3
9245	+seeds), FML-Bench (18 tasks, 3 seeds) and WeatherBench 2 (1 task, 3 seeds).
9246	+Gains there are described as "positive throughout but not monotone"; the step-47
9247	+agent is best on two of the four. Reward hacking on 38 held-out KernelBench
9248	+pairs fell from 55% to 39% to 32%. The authors state that the selection trace
9249	+cannot show generalization because candidates were selected on the grade, and
9250	+that the outer loop's role "cannot be decisively distinguished" from a strong

9285	+and the contrast is about 1.90 of them, below 1.96. The reward-hacking
9286	+percentages are consistent with 21, 15 and 12 of 38; those counts are inferred
9287	+from rounding.
9288	+
9289	+**Proposed variation.** Fix the readout checkpoints before the run and publish
9290	+the ledger. Hold a second private split of the selection suite sealed, and read
9291	+it once at the end: the difference from the grade is a direct measurement of
9292	+the readout gap on the suite the loop worked against.
9293	+
9294	+**Claim boundary.** One trajectory supports the existence of held-out gains
9295	+from harness self-modification, with acceptances thinning over the run. It does
9296	+not support a rate.
9297	+
9298	+## 7. Princeton shadow evaluation: sealed against contamination, open at the judge
9299	+
9300	+**Observed.** Agents were given the central question of two unpublished NeurIPS
9301	+2026 submissions. Main runs used Claude Opus 4.8 with extra-high reasoning on
9302	+OpenClaw; a robustness run used GPT-5.6 Sol on Codex for one question. Each run
9303	+had six days, $3,000 in API credits and GPU credits. The papers' own authors
9304	+graded on a 1–6 scale, knowing the work was AI-generated: 2/6 and 1/6. Stated
9305	+limitations are five runs on two papers, non-blind grading by the original
9306	+authors, researcher degrees of freedom in question selection, possible
9307	+under-elicitation including a scaffold bug, and evaluation awareness. The
9308	+authors found no significant reward hacking, and report five instances of
9309	+subagents misrepresenting results that the orchestrator caught.
9310	+[Primary, summarized](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27191)
9311	+
9312	+**Interpretation.** Using unpublished questions seals the item set against
9313	+pretraining, a choice none of the other four makes for its items. The opening
9314	+is at \(J\): the judge knows the condition and wrote the reference answer. In
9315	+the terms of the v3 protocol's provenance block, `scorer_blinded` would be
9316	+false, and there is no negative control. A human-written submission graded
9317	+under the same label would say how much of the score belongs to the label.
9318	+
9319	+The models tested predate the internal model of §3. The result is silent on
9320	+that model.
9321	+
9322	+**Proposed variation.** Blind grading with human-written decoys mixed in, on
9323	+more questions, with the authors of each question grading only the others'.
9324	+
9325	+**Claim boundary.** Failure on two questions under an unblinded judge supports
9326	+"not demonstrated here". It does not bound what a later controller does.
9327	+
9328	+## 8. What these examples add to the calculus
9329	+
9330	+1. **Feedback class and ledger.** Only one case of five declares whether scores
9331	+   from a scored set reached the process being measured. The card should ask.
9332	+2. **Saturation as Hide.** A fixed suite outgrown by its subjects loses
9333	+   discrimination without any change to the game. The ceiling belongs on the
9334	+   card as a property of \(Z\).
9335	+3. **Acquisition conditioned on judgment.** Publishing what scored well makes
9336	+   \(Z\) depend on \(J\). Counts of what was attempted are then part of the
9337	+   evidence, not a courtesy.
9338	+4. **A judge that shares errors with the judged.** Agreement statistics must be
9339	+   reported at the boundary the headline is counted at.
9340	+5. **Estimand named against headline.** Amplification slope, task share,
9341	+   horizon, harness gain and open-ended failure are five different quantities.
9342	+   A statement about compounding needs a sixth, which none supplies.
9343	+
9344	+The machine-readable companion is `configs/rsi_claim_cards.json`.
9345	+`scripts/verify_rsi_claims_atlas.py` verifies manifest structure and the
9346	+derived arithmetic only; its receipt is under `output/rsi_claims_atlas/`.

+# Feedback channel: suggested insertions for the evaluation design calculus
+
+Draft 0.1 — 2026-10-11. Suggestions only.
+
+This file changes nothing in `evaluation_design_calculus.md` or
+`evaluation_game_testbed.md`. Each block names a location in those documents,
+offers text for it, and states what supports the text. Where a block is adopted,
+its wording should be made the author's own. Where it is not, the executable
+fixtures still stand by themselves.
+
+The gap being addressed: the calculus already says that a judgment "shown during
+play or used for learning ... also enters observations or controller updates"
+(§2), and that frozen-controller sensitivity differs from sensitivity "after
+retraining, selecting another controller" (§7). It has no operator for that
+channel, no estimand for what the channel does to a score, and no record of how
+often it was used. A self-improvement loop is that channel applied once per
+generation.
+
+## Evidence behind the suggestions
+
+| Level | Source | What it supplies |
+|---|---|---|
+| Finite verified example | `src/spiral_ln/evaluation_game_feedback.py`, 29 tests, receipt under `output/evaluation_game_feedback/` | Access-class ordering, one-generation selection gap, noise-ceiling threshold, failed-item enrichment, ledger enforcement |
+| Synthetic mechanism result | `output/eval_reuse_toys/` (two seeded simulations, predictions hashed before each run) | Multi-generation behaviour of the gap under score-only and item-level feedback |
+| Not available | — | Any language-model loop, any observed controller |
+
+The simulations are JavaScript, seeded, and not exact. Their prediction record
+is 5 of 6 in the first run and 3 of 6 in the second, and both overpredicted the
+size of the gap. One arm of the second run was added after its sealed results
+were seen and is marked exploratory in its own files.
+
+## A. §2, after "Maintain three distinctions"
+
+Suggested fourth distinction:
+
+> 4. A judgment that reaches whatever produces the next controller is a channel.
+> Its source set, its access class, and the number of times it was used belong
+> in the experiment record. A score measured on a set that fed this channel is a
+> selection score. A capability claim needs a set that did not.
+
+## B. §3, operator table
+
+Suggested row:
+
+| Proposed operator | Primary effect | Required detail |
+|---|---|---|
+| \(\operatorname{Feedback}_{s,q}\) | Controller roster/protocol of a later generation | Source set \(s\); access class \(q\in\{\text{sealed},\text{score-only},\text{item-level}\}\); whether the consumer selects among candidates or supplies a training input; generation scope. |
+
+Suggested sentence beneath the table:
+
+> Feedback is not \(\operatorname{Rescore}\), which is offline, and not
+> \(\operatorname{Observe}\), which changes what the evaluator records. It reads
+> \(J\) restricted to \(s\) and writes \(\Pi\) for the next generation. Declaring
+> a set sealed while a score from it reaches the loop is ill-typed.
+
+## C. §4, after the sentence on `Repeat` and reset/carry maps
+
+> Generations joined by Feedback are not independent blocks. The carry map
+> carries the controller, and with it whatever of \(s\) the channel transmitted.
+> Aggregating a per-generation score across such generations as if each were a
+> fresh draw of the same experiment mistakes the unit.
+
+## D. §5, three laws and one observation
+
+**Coarsening law.**
+
+> The access classes are ordered: sealed is a deterministic function of the
+> score, and the score is a deterministic function of the per-item outcomes.
+> Total-variation distance between two controllers' feedback therefore cannot
+> increase from item-level to score-only to sealed. Two controllers that fail
+> different items with equal totals are separated completely by item-level
+> feedback and not at all by a score.
+
+Support: `access_order_fixture`; the ordering is checked for every pair of
+distributions on a rational grid over two-item outcomes.
+
+**Selection law.**
+
+> Keeping the best of \(K\) candidates by score on \(s\), then reporting that
+> score, overstates: \(\mathbb E[\max_k\hat S_k]\ge\max_k\mathbb E[\hat S_k]\).
+> This is the same convexity as the mixture law, with the candidate index in
+> place of the mixture component. For candidates of equal true value
+> one half, two candidates and one item give a reported value of three quarters.
+
+Support: `selection_inflation`, checked against independent enumeration of
+every outcome matrix in seven small cells. Exact gaps for two candidates at
+\(p=\tfrac12\) are \(\tfrac14\), \(\tfrac{35}{256}\), about 0.0700 and about
+0.0352 at 1, 4, 16 and 64 items; multiplied by \(\sqrt n\) these are 0.250,
+0.273, 0.280 and 0.282. The value \(1/(2\sqrt\pi)\approx0.2821\) is the
+standard Gaussian figure for the larger of two draws. The fixture verifies the
+listed cells and no limit.
+
+Boundary: one generation, equal candidates, independent items. Accumulation
+across generations is a simulation result, not an exact one.
+
+**Ceiling law.**
+
+> With labels flipped independently at rate \(\varepsilon<\tfrac12\), no
+> predictor blind to the flips exceeds \(1-\varepsilon\) on observed labels.
+> A controller that has memorized a share \(m/n\) of \(s\), and scores \(v\)
+> elsewhere, scores \(m/n+(1-m/n)v\) on \(s\). It crosses the ceiling only when
+> \(m/n>(1-\varepsilon-v)/(1-v)\). Below that share a ceiling check is silent.
+
+Support: `ceiling_detection_threshold`. With clean accuracy \(\tfrac45\) and
+\(\varepsilon=\tfrac1{10}\): \(v=\tfrac{37}{50}\), threshold \(\tfrac8{13}\).
+The formula assumes a memorized item has no effect on any other item, which the
+nearest-neighbour learner in the simulations did not satisfy.
+
+**Observation on what item-level feedback selects.**
+
+> An item the controller fails is more likely than an average item to carry a
+> wrong label, whenever the controller is better than chance:
+> \(\Pr[\text{flipped}\mid\text{failed}]=\varepsilon a/(\varepsilon a+(1-\varepsilon)(1-a))\),
+> which exceeds \(\varepsilon\) exactly when \(a>\tfrac12\). Feeding failures
+> back concentrates label noise in what the next controller is built from.
+
+Support: `failed_item_noise_share`; \(\tfrac4{13}\) against a base rate of
+\(\tfrac1{10}\) in the fixture. In the second simulation the measured share
+among patched items was 20–29% against the same 10% base rate. This is the
+reason the unchecked answer in the Proposer–Solver recipe (atlas §11) matters
+once its output is fed back.
+
+Suggested closing sentence, matching the section's existing last line:
+
+> No unconditional claim is made that feedback lowers readout performance. In
+> the simulations, score-only selection of fresh training batches raised it.
+
+## E. §7, after the definition of the order effect
+
+> For a controller \(\pi_g\) produced with feedback from \(s\), and a sealed set
+> \(r\) from the same sampling law, define the readout gap
+> \(\rho_g=V^{s}_{\pi_g}-V^{r}_{\pi_g}\). It compares two measurements of one
+> controller, not two designs, so it is not a design difference. A gain series
+> computed on \(s\) estimates the change in value plus the change in \(\rho\).
+
+## F. §11, the evaluation card
+
+Suggested amendment to item 6:
+
+> ... and whether any score feeds back into play *or into the production of a
+> later controller*.
+
+Suggested additional item:
+
+> 10. **Feedback ledger:** for each evaluation set, its role (selection or
+> readout), declared access class, score queries, items fed back, number and
+> generation of readouts, and the rule that retires it.
+
+## G. `evaluation_game_testbed.md`, estimand table
+
+Suggested fifth row:
+
+| Estimand | Definition | It is not |
+|---|---|---|
+| Readout gap | \(\rho=V^{s}_\pi-V^{r}_\pi\), with \(s\) having fed judgment to the loop and \(r\) sealed | A baseline gain, or evidence that capability changed |
+
+Suggested section, placed after "Executable confirmation and adversarial
+checks":
+
+> ### Feedback channel and multi-generation ledger
+>
+> `evaluation_game_feedback.py` extends the single split enforced by `confirm()`
+> to a sequence of generations. Sets are declared with a role and an access
+> class. Events record a score reaching the loop, items reaching the loop, or an
+> experimenter reading a sealed set. Malformed declarations raise, including a
+> readout set not declared sealed and identifiers shared across sets. Breaches
+> of a well-formed declaration are recorded instead, and move the readout
+> endpoint to `not_evaluated`: a breach is a finding about the run. Reads of the
+> sealed set are budgeted, since a stop-or-continue decision taken on a readout
+> is itself adaptive. Identifiers detect recorded overlap. They do not certify
+> independence.
+>
+> ```powershell
+> $env:PYTHONPATH = "src"
+> python scripts/verify_evaluation_game_feedback.py --output output/evaluation_game_feedback/feedback_v0_1.json
+> python -m pytest tests/test_evaluation_game_feedback.py -q
+> ```
+
+## H. What is not delivered
+
+- `Feedback` is not implemented against `hive_lab` adapters or any external
+  policy. The module checks declarations and arithmetic.
+- No loop with a language model has been run. The first observed-controller
+  study would pair a small model with a declared selection set and a sealed
+  readout, and report the ledger.
+- Partial leakage, where the loop learns failure categories and not items, has
+  no fixture.
+- The simulations fix one parameter set each. No sweep over candidate count,
+  decay rate, or label-noise rate was run.

+# Takeoff-evidence examples for the evaluation design calculus
+
+Draft 0.1 — inspected 2026-10-11.
+
+This atlas applies [the calculus](evaluation_design_calculus.md) and the
+[suggested feedback insertions](evaluation_feedback_insertions.md) to five
+published claims that bear on AI-driven AI research and development. These are
+design analyses and proposed studies. No model was called and no published
+result was reproduced.
+
+Each case distinguishes **observed**, **interpretation**, and **proposed
+variation**, as the [Prime Intellect atlas](prime_intellect_eval_atlas.md) does.
+
+**Reading caveat.** Every source below was read on the inspection date through
+a fetch tool that returns a summary of the page, not its bytes. One chart was
+read from a screenshot in a third-party post. Figures are as that tool returned
+them. A line-level check against the originals is outstanding and should
+precede any circulation. Source levels are marked per case:
+
+- *primary, summarized*: the publisher's own page or paper, through the tool.
+- *secondary*: a report about the source.
+- *screenshot*: an image of the source reproduced by a third party.
+
+## 1. The question put to each case
+
+A forecast of compounding needs one estimand: the gain from one generation of
+controllers to the next, repeated, on a readout the improvement process did not
+touch. In the notation of the insertions, that is a series of \(V^{r}_{\pi_g}\)
+with \(r\) sealed, together with a ledger showing that it stayed sealed.
+
+| Card field | What to look for in a takeoff claim |
+|---|---|
+| \(\Pi\) | What improves: weights, harness, test-time budget, or the mix of who does the work |
+| \(D\) | How scored items were chosen, and whether the choice followed a look at results |
+| \(Z\) | Whether what was kept depends on how it scored |
+| \(J\) | Who or what judges, and whether the judge shares errors with the judged |
+| Feedback | Whether scores or items from the scored set reached the improvement process |
+| Readout | Whether any reported number comes from a set declared sealed |
+| \(C\) | Which estimand the evidence supports, as against the one the headline implies |
+
+## 2. The example set
+
+| Case | Source level | What improves | Scored set fed back? | Sealed readout declared? | Estimand supported |
+|---|---|---|---|---|---|
+| OpenAI internal model, mathematics | primary summarized; chart by screenshot | Test-time compute at one checkpoint | Not stated | No | Amplification slope |
+| Anthropic R&D Automation Index | primary summarized | Share of work led by the model | Not applicable | Not applicable | Task-share under a learned judge |
+| METR time horizon | primary summarized; values secondary | Released models over years | Not stated; suite reused | No | Horizon on a fixed suite, below its ceiling |
+| AIDE² harness self-improvement | primary summarized | Agent harness, model frozen | Yes, by design | Yes, four external benchmarks | Held-out gain across harness generations |
+| Princeton shadow evaluation | primary summarized | Nothing; a single-generation test | No loop | Yes, against pretraining | Failure on two open-ended questions under one judge |
+
+None of the five supplies a generation-over-generation gain ratio for model
+weights on a sealed readout. The fourth comes closest, at the level of the
+harness.
+
+## 3. OpenAI's internal model: an amplification curve read as a trajectory
+
+**Observed.** The Navier–Stokes post, dated 8 September 2026 with an update on
+10 September, states: "Since August 28 we have been training a new internal
+model," and "This model's training is ongoing and its performance continues to
+improve." It describes the model as built through large-scale reinforcement
+learning on a pretrained model. That result involved on the order of 10,000
+concurrent agents, about 88 hours, about 2.7 million messages and roughly 130
+billion output tokens, with Lean formalization taking a further 17 hours.
+[Primary, summarized](https://openai.com/index/navier-stokes-solution/)
+
+A chart titled "Performance of GPT-6 Astra and our Internal Model on a curated
+set of open math problems" plots pass rate against test-time compute on a log
+scale, with error bars. Read by eye from a screenshot, the internal model runs
+from about 0.26 to about 0.48 over six points and GPT-6 Astra from about 0.09 to
+about 0.17 over five. The chart could not be retrieved from the page text.
+[Screenshot](https://x.com/AndrewCurran_/status/2108609708441657531)
+
+The 6 October release reports 722 manuscripts in 372 result families, about
+4,000 problems posed, 162 main results formalized in Lean, ten reasoning
+summaries, and an average result using "the equivalent compute of roughly three
+hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking." Its README says: "We expanded these evaluations
+after performance on our existing mathematical evaluations saturated."
+[Primary, summarized](https://openai.com/index/sharing-ai-progress-in-mathematics/);
+counts from a [secondary reading of the repository](https://cellcog.ai/blog/openai-math-results/).
+
+**Interpretation.** The chart's horizontal axis is test-time compute. It
+compares two controllers at several inference budgets at one moment. It is not
+a series over training time, and the sentence that performance "continues to
+improve" has no plotted support in what was read.
+
+Four declarations are absent:
+
+- \(D\): the rule by which the set was "curated", and whether curation followed
+  a look at outcomes. Expanding an evaluation after saturation supplies fresh
+  items, and is also a decision taken on results.
+- \(Z\): results were kept when judged significant. What is published is
+  conditioned on the judgment.
+- \(J\) for the chart: what counts as a pass, and who decides.
+- Feedback: whether these problems or their outcomes reached training. The page
+  addresses a different contamination question and is silent on this one.
+
+**Derived arithmetic** (conditional on the reported counts; the mapping from
+problems to manuscripts was not in what was read):
+
+\[
+\frac{722}{4000}=\frac{361}{2000},\qquad
+\frac{372}{4000}=\frac{93}{1000},\qquad
+\frac{162}{722}=\frac{81}{361}\approx0.224 .
+\]
+
+These are ratios of kept output to problems posed, not success rates. If a
+failed attempt cost what a kept one did, compute per kept family would be
+\(4000/372\approx10.8\) times the per-result figure; the release does not say
+whether failures are in its average.
+
+**Proposed variation.** The same pass-rate curve at two training checkpoints, on
+a problem set declared sealed before the first, with the selection rule and all
+failures published. That yields the training-time gain at fixed inference
+budget, which is the quantity the caption asserts.
+
+**Claim boundary.** A steeper curve for the newer model is evidence that more
+inference buys more from it than from its predecessor, in mathematics, on this
+set. It is silent on whether that margin is being trained back in.
+
+## 4. Anthropic's Automation Index: a judge measuring a mix
+
+**Observed.** A prototype index catalogues about 15,000 granular tasks into a
+frozen tree of 542 nodes, 378 of them leaves, each rated on Epoch AI's
+automation scale. "Leads" (AL4) means the model completes most of a task
+end-to-end from a high-level prompt while a human supervises. Aggregation is
+weighted by person-time. A Claude agent gathers evidence per node and an
+independent Claude judge assigns the level. Staff rated their own areas as a
+check: model–human exact agreement 59%, human–human 35%, within one level 97%.
+As of August 2026 the "leads" share is 26% and the share at or above
+"collaborates" exceeds 90%; no measured subset is fully autonomous. The basket
+is frozen at July 2026. Stated caveats include dependence on the judge,
+contestable AL3/AL4 cases, crude weighting, and a judge that may share errors
+with the models it rates.
+[Primary, summarized](https://www.anthropic.com/institute/measuring-pace-of-ai-development)
+
+**Interpretation.** This is the atlas's Rubric Discovery case at institutional
+scale: the produced artifact is a judge, and it needs its own evaluation. Three
+points follow from the card.
+
+1. The headline is a threshold count at one boundary of a six-level scale.
+   Agreement "within one level" does not protect a count taken exactly at a
+   one-level boundary. Exact agreement between judge and human, 59%, is the
+   relevant figure, and it is higher than agreement between humans.
+2. Weights are person-time measured after automation. A task that became fast
+   takes less time and so weighs less. The direction of that bias is to
+   understate the automated share of the original work.
+3. It is a measurement of who does the work. It is the \(p\) of an Amdahl
+   bound, not a gain per generation.
+
+**Derived arithmetic** (illustrative, and conditional on reading 26% as a
+pre-automation time share, which point 2 says it is not):
+
+\[
+\frac{1}{1-\tfrac{13}{50}}=\frac{50}{37}\approx1.35 .
+\]
+
+That is the ceiling on overall speedup if the "leads" share became free and
+nothing else changed.
+
+**Proposed variation.** Blind human re-rating of a stratified sample of nodes
+near the AL3/AL4 boundary, with the headline reported as an interval under a
+one-level perturbation of the judge. Separately, weights taken from a
+pre-automation time survey.
+
+**Claim boundary.** There is no scored item set here, so feedback and readout
+do not apply. The index supports a statement about task mix under a declared
+judge. It does not measure whether each generation improves the next by more.
+
+## 5. METR's time horizon: a suite that hides by saturating
+
+**Observed.** Time Horizon 1.1 fits a logistic curve of success against human
+task duration over "over a hundred diverse software tasks" from RE-Bench, HCAST
+and shorter novel tasks, and reads off the 50% point. The page states:
+"Measurements above 16 hrs are unreliable with our current task suite." It
+carries a notice dated 8 September 2026 that it is no longer actively updated.
+It mentions private tasks without giving the public/private split.
+[Primary, summarized](https://metr.org/time-horizons/)
+
+Values come from secondary readings of METR's data: Claude Mythos Preview
+(early) at 1044.78 minutes
+([DataLearner](https://www.datalearner.com/en/benchmarks/metr-time-horizons-v1-1));
+doubling times of 131 days for the post-2023 fit and 89 days for the since-2024
+fit ([Manifold market text](https://manifold.markets/Bayesian/claude-sonnet-5-metr-50-time-horizo)).
+
+**Interpretation.** In the testbed's terms a saturated suite is an
+observation-only Hide. Once a controller's ability exceeds the hardest items,
+distinct controllers push forward to the same record, and the discrimination
+gap between them goes to zero. No change in the game is involved.
+
+The suite is fixed and reused across model generations, by every developer. At
+the level of the field that is at least score-only feedback over years. Nothing
+read asserts that any developer trained against it.
+
+**Derived arithmetic.**
+
+\[
+\frac{1044.78}{60}\approx17.41\ \text{hours}>16 .
+\]
+
+The highest frontier point lies above the bound the instrument's owner calls
+reliable. The 131-day and 89-day figures are fits over nested windows, so their
+difference is not the ratio of two successive doubling intervals.
+
+**Proposed variation.** Report, per model, the count of items above its
+estimated ability. Extend the suite with long tasks held sealed. Declare the
+freeze date as part of the instrument.
+
+**Claim boundary.** Below the ceiling the horizon supports a statement about
+released models on this task family. Above it, neither a plateau nor an
+acceleration is identified.
+
+## 6. AIDE²: the case with a declared readout
+
+**Observed.** An agent proposes rewrites of its own harness; candidates are
+scored on a selection suite of ML engineering, heuristic algorithm engineering
+and harness engineering tasks; scoring uses private data averaged into a grade.
+Inner agents see only a public signal. The outer agent "reads the previously
+proposed agents and their grades", and its reviewer "explores the evaluation
+artifacts". The main run lasted eight days: one initial agent and 99 proposals,
+seven accepted at steps 2, 6, 28, 39, 47, 63 and 85, raising the incumbent grade
+from 0.703 to 0.778. The outer loop ran on Claude Opus 4.7 and the inner agents
+on Gemini 3 Flash. Two further runs accepted two and four rewrites.
+
+Held-out reporting uses ALE-Bench (10 tasks, 10 seeds), MLE-Bench (22 tasks, 3
+seeds), FML-Bench (18 tasks, 3 seeds) and WeatherBench 2 (1 task, 3 seeds).
+Gains there are described as "positive throughout but not monotone"; the step-47
+agent is best on two of the four. Reward hacking on 38 held-out KernelBench
+pairs fell from 55% to 39% to 32%. The authors state that the selection trace
+cannot show generalization because candidates were selected on the grade, and
+that the outer loop's role "cannot be decisively distinguished" from a strong
+baseline.
+[Primary, summarized](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26457)
+
+From a search excerpt of the paper's PDF, not the summarized page: on ALE-Bench,
+Gemini 3 Flash with the step-85 harness reaches \(1858\pm22\) against Fable 5
+with the initial harness at \(1796\pm24\); on MLE-Bench the step-85 harness
+with Fable 5 "stays within one standard error" of its initial score. What the
+\(\pm\) denotes was not in the excerpt.
+
+**Interpretation.** This is the only case of the five that separates a
+selection set from a readout and says which numbers came from which. In ledger
+terms:
+
+- Selection set: one fixed suite, 99 score queries. Declared access is at least
+  score-only; the reviewer's reading of evaluation artifacts may make it
+  item-level. The rise from 0.703 to 0.778 is a selection score.
+- Readout: four external benchmarks, read at several checkpoints. How many
+  checkpoints were read, and whether they were fixed in advance, was not in
+  what was read. Reporting the best checkpoint per benchmark would be selection
+  on the readout.

9745	+def audit_ledger(sets, events, readout_budget, exhaustion_bound):
9746	+    """Check a multi-generation feedback ledger against its declarations.
9747	+
9748	+    Malformed declarations raise.  Breaches of a well-formed declaration are
9749	+    recorded, and move the affected endpoint to ``not_evaluated``, because a
9750	+    breach is a finding about the run and should survive into its report.
9751	+
9752	+    A ``score_query`` or ``item_feedback`` event means the result reached the
9753	+    loop.  A ``readout`` event means the experimenter read a sealed set; if a
9754	+    loop-affecting decision followed, that reading is itself adaptive, so the
9755	+    number of readouts is budgeted.  Identifiers detect recorded overlap only.
9756	+    They cannot certify that two differently named items are independent.
9757	+    """
9758	+
9759	+    if not sets:
9760	+        raise ValueError("at least one evaluation set must be declared")
9761	+    if type(readout_budget) is not int or readout_budget < 1:
9762	+        raise ValueError("readout budget must be a positive integer")
9763	+    if not exhaustion_bound > 0:
9764	+        raise ValueError("exhaustion bound must be positive")
9765	+    declared, owner = {}, {}
9766	+    for item in sets:
9767	+        if (not item.set_id or item.role not in ROLES or item.access not in ACCESS_CLASSES
9768	+                or not item.item_ids or len(set(item.item_ids)) != len(item.item_ids)):
9769	+            raise ValueError("invalid evaluation set declaration")
9770	+        if item.set_id in declared:
9771	+            raise ValueError("duplicate set identifier")
9772	+        if item.role == "readout" and item.access != "sealed":
9773	+            raise ValueError("a readout set must be declared sealed")
9774	+        for identifier in item.item_ids:
9775	+            if identifier in owner:
9776	+                raise ValueError("selection/readout identifiers overlap")
9777	+            owner[identifier] = item.set_id
9778	+        declared[item.set_id] = item
9779	+    if not any(item.role == "readout" for item in sets):
9780	+        raise ValueError("no readout set declared")
9781	+
9782	+    state = {
9783	+        set_id: {"role": item.role, "declared_access": item.access,
9784	+                 "size": len(item.item_ids), "score_queries": 0, "patches": 0,
9785	+                 "distinct_patched": set(), "readouts": [], "retired_at": None,
9786	+                 "breaches": []}
9787	+        for set_id, item in declared.items()
9788	+    }
9789	+    previous = None
9790	+    for event in events:
9791	+        if (type(event.generation) is not int or event.generation < 0
9792	+                or event.kind not in EVENT_KINDS or event.set_id not in declared):
9793	+            raise ValueError("invalid loop event")
9794	+        if previous is not None and event.generation < previous:
9795	+            raise ValueError("events must be ordered by generation")
9796	+        previous = event.generation
9797	+        target, record = declared[event.set_id], state[event.set_id]
9798	+        if event.kind == "readout":
9799	+            if target.role != "readout":
9800	+                raise ValueError("readout events apply to readout sets only")
9801	+            record["readouts"].append(event.generation)
9802	+            if len(record["readouts"]) > readout_budget:
9803	+                record["breaches"].append(f"readout budget exceeded at generation {event.generation}")
9804	+            continue
9805	+        if event.kind == "item_feedback":
9806	+            if not event.item_ids or not set(event.item_ids) <= set(target.item_ids):
9807	+                raise ValueError("item feedback must name items of its own set")
9808	+        if target.role == "readout":
9809	+            record["breaches"].append(
9810	+                f"{event.kind} exposed the readout set at generation {event.generation}")
9811	+            continue
9812	+        if record["retired_at"] is not None:
9813	+            record["breaches"].append(f"used after retirement at generation {event.generation}")
9814	+        allowed = ACCESS_CLASSES.index(target.access)
9815	+        needed = ACCESS_CLASSES.index("item_level" if event.kind == "item_feedback" else "score_only")
9816	+        if needed > allowed:
9817	+            record["breaches"].append(
9818	+                f"{event.kind} exceeds declared {target.access} access at generation {event.generation}")
9819	+        if event.kind == "score_query":
9820	+            record["score_queries"] += 1
9821	+        else:
9822	+            record["patches"] += len(event.item_ids)
9823	+            record["distinct_patched"].update(event.item_ids)
9824	+            if (record["retired_at"] is None
9825	+                    and Q(record["patches"], record["size"]) > exhaustion_bound):
9826	+                record["retired_at"] = event.generation

9834	+                "score_queries": record["score_queries"], "patches": record["patches"],
9835	+                "distinct_patched": len(record["distinct_patched"]),
9836	+                "patch_share": Q(record["patches"], record["size"]),
9837	+                "retired_at_generation": record["retired_at"],

9850	+        for entry in report[group].values())

9854	+def divergence_flags(points, margin):
9855	+    """Compare selection-set and readout-set gains between permitted readouts.
9856	+
9857	+    ``points`` are ``(generation, selection_score, readout_score)`` at strictly
9858	+    increasing generations.  A flag voids claims resting on the selection set.
9859	+    It does not void the sealed readout.
9860	+    """
9861	+
9862	+    points = list(points)
9863	+    if len(points) < 2:
9864	+        raise ValueError("at least two readout points required")
9865	+    if not margin >= 0:
9866	+        raise ValueError("margin must be nonnegative")
9867	+    rows = []
9868	+    for (g0, s0, r0), (g1, s1, r1) in zip(points, points[1:]):
9869	+        if type(g0) is not int or type(g1) is not int or g1 <= g0:
9870	+            raise ValueError("generations must be strictly increasing integers")
9871	+        if not all(0 <= value <= 1 for value in (s0, r0, s1, r1)):
9872	+            raise ValueError("scores must lie in [0, 1]")
9873	+        divergence = (s1 - s0) - (r1 - r0)
9874	+        rows.append({"from_generation": g0, "to_generation": g1,
9875	+                     "selection_gain": s1 - s0, "readout_gain": r1 - r0,
9876	+                     "divergence": divergence, "readout_gap_at_end": s1 - r1,
9877	+                     "flagged": divergence > margin})
9878	+    return rows

+"""Run exact synthetic feedback-channel checks; no models or agents are contacted."""
+
+from __future__ import annotations
+
+import argparse
+import json
+from datetime import datetime, timezone
+from hashlib import sha256
+from pathlib import Path
+
+from spiral_ln.evaluation_game_feedback import verify
+
+
+def _encode(value):
+    if hasattr(value, "numerator") and hasattr(value, "denominator"):
+        return str(value)
+    if isinstance(value, (tuple, set, frozenset)):
+        return list(value)
+    raise TypeError(f"cannot encode {type(value)!r}")
+
+
+def main() -> int:
+    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
+    parser.add_argument("--output", type=Path)
+    args = parser.parse_args()
+    report = {"schema_version": "0.1",
+              "generated_at_utc": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(), **verify()}
+    root = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
+    sources = ("scripts/verify_evaluation_game_feedback.py",
+               "src/spiral_ln/evaluation_game_feedback.py",
+               "src/spiral_ln/evaluation_game_testbed.py")
+    report["source_sha256"] = {name: sha256((root/name).read_bytes()).hexdigest() for name in sources}
+    report = json.loads(json.dumps(report, default=_encode))
+    rendered = json.dumps(report, indent=2) + "\n"
+    if args.output:
+        args.output.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
+        with args.output.open("x", encoding="utf-8") as stream:
+            stream.write(rendered)
+    else:
+        print(rendered, end="")
+    return 0 if report["all_passed"] else 1
+
+
+if __name__ == "__main__":
+    raise SystemExit(main())

+"""Check takeoff-claims atlas structure and derived arithmetic; no models are run."""
+
+from __future__ import annotations
+
+import argparse
+from datetime import datetime, timezone
+from fractions import Fraction as Q
+from hashlib import sha256
+import json
+from pathlib import Path
+
+
+ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
+SOURCE_KINDS = {"primary_summarized", "secondary", "screenshot", "search_excerpt"}
+REQUIRED = ("observed_contract", "what_improves", "estimand_supported", "headline_estimand",
+            "missing_declarations", "proposed_axes", "independent_unit", "claim_boundary")
+
+
+def verify(manifest):
+    checks = []
+
+    def check(name, passed, **evidence):
+        checks.append({"name": name, "passed": bool(passed), "evidence": evidence})
+
+    cards = manifest["cards"]
+    check("five_distinct_cards",
+          len(cards) == manifest["cases"] == 5 and len({c["id"] for c in cards}) == 5)
+    check("every_source_has_a_declared_reading_level",
+          all(c["sources"] and all(s["kind"] in SOURCE_KINDS and s["url"].startswith("https://")
+                                   and s["read_on"] == manifest["inspected_date"]
+                                   for s in c["sources"]) for c in cards))
+    check("no_card_rests_on_secondary_reading_alone",
+          all(any(s["kind"] == "primary_summarized" for s in c["sources"]) for c in cards))
+    check("all_studies_explicitly_proposed",
+          manifest["model_evaluations_run"] == 0
+          and all(c["study_status"] == "proposed_not_executed" for c in cards))
+    check("cards_carry_estimand_boundary_and_missing_declarations",
+          all(all(c[key] for key in REQUIRED) for c in cards))
+    check("headline_and_supported_estimands_differ_on_every_card",
+          all(c["estimand_supported"] != c["headline_estimand"] for c in cards))
+    declared = [c["id"] for c in cards
+                if c["loop_present"] == "yes" and c["feedback_access_declared"]
+                and c["sealed_readout_declared"] is True]
+    check("one_case_declares_feedback_and_a_sealed_readout",
+          len(declared) == manifest["cases_with_declared_feedback_and_sealed_readout"] == 1,
+          case=declared)
+    check("no_case_supplies_the_compounding_estimand",
+          manifest["cases_supplying_weight_level_gain_ratio_on_sealed_readout"] == 0
+          and not any(c["what_improves"].startswith("model_weights") for c in cards))
+
+    f = manifest["derived_fixtures"]
+    m = f["openai_math"]
+    check("openai_ratios",
+          Q(m["manuscripts"], m["problems_posed_approx"]) == Q(m["manuscripts_per_problem"])
+          and Q(m["families"], m["problems_posed_approx"]) == Q(m["families_per_problem"])
+          and Q(m["lean_main_results"], m["manuscripts"]) == Q(m["lean_share_of_manuscripts"])
+          and Q(m["problems_posed_approx"], m["families"]) == Q(m["problems_per_family"]),
+          scope="Ratios of reported counts; the problem count is approximate in the source")
+    check("openai_swarm_scale",
+          m["swarm_agents"] * m["swarm_hours"] == m["swarm_agent_hours_upper_bound"]
+          and Q(m["output_tokens"], m["messages"]) == Q(m["tokens_per_message"]),
+          tokens_per_message=float(Q(m["tokens_per_message"])))
+
+    a = f["anthropic_index"]
+    check("amdahl_ceiling_for_leads_share",
+          1 / (1 - Q(a["leads_share"])) == Q(a["amdahl_ceiling_if_leads_share_free"]),
+          scope="Illustrative; post-automation person-time is not a pre-automation time share")
+    check("judge_agrees_with_humans_more_than_humans_agree",
+          Q(a["exact_agreement_model_human"]) > Q(a["exact_agreement_human_human"])
+          and a["leaves"] < a["nodes"])
+
+    t = f["metr"]
+    hours = Q(t["top_frontier_minutes"]) / 60
+    check("top_frontier_point_above_stated_ceiling",
+          hours == Q(t["top_frontier_hours"]) and hours > t["stated_reliable_ceiling_hours"]
+          and t["exceeds_ceiling"], hours=float(hours))
+
+    d = f["aide2"]
+    steps = d["accepted_steps"]
+    check("aide2_acceptance_arithmetic",
+          Q(len(steps), d["proposals"]) == Q(d["acceptance_rate"])
+          and (Q(d["grade_end"]) - Q(d["grade_start"])) / len(steps)
+          == Q(d["mean_grade_gain_per_acceptance"])
+          and [b - a_ for a_, b in zip(steps, steps[1:])] == d["acceptance_intervals"]
+          and sum(s <= 49 for s in steps) == d["accepted_first_half"]
+          and sum(s >= 50 for s in steps) == d["accepted_second_half"]
+          and d["proposals"] - steps[-1] == d["proposals_after_last_acceptance"])
+    variance = sum(v * v for v in d["ale_pm"])
+    z_squared = Q(d["ale_contrast"] ** 2, variance)
+    check("ale_contrast_below_conventional_threshold_if_independent_standard_errors",
+          variance == d["ale_combined_variance"] and z_squared == Q(d["ale_z_squared"])
+          and (z_squared < Q(196, 100) ** 2) == d["ale_below_1_96_if_independent_standard_errors"],
+          z_squared=float(z_squared), scope="Conditional on what the plus-or-minus figures denote")
+    check("reward_hacking_counts_consistent_with_rounded_percentages",
+          all(round(100 * Q(count, d["reward_hacking_pairs"])) == pct
+              for count, pct in zip(d["reward_hacking_counts_inferred"],
+                                    d["reward_hacking_percentages"])),
+          scope="Counts are inferred from rounding, not reported")
+
+    p = f["princeton"]
+    check("princeton_sample_is_two_questions",
+          p["questions"] == len(p["scores"]) == 2 and p["runs"] == 5
+          and all(1 <= s <= p["scale_max"] for s in p["scores"]))
+    return checks
+
+
+def main():
+    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
+    parser.add_argument("--manifest", type=Path, default=ROOT / "configs/rsi_claim_cards.json")
+    parser.add_argument("--output", type=Path)
+    args = parser.parse_args()
+    manifest_bytes = args.manifest.read_bytes()
+    checks = verify(json.loads(manifest_bytes))
+    report = {
+        "schema_version": "0.1",
+        "generated_at_utc": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
+        "evidence_status": "manifest_structure_and_exact_derived_arithmetic_only",
+        "model_evaluations_run": 0,
+        "sources_verified_line_by_line": False,
+        "manifest_sha256": sha256(manifest_bytes).hexdigest(),
+        "verifier_sha256": sha256(Path(__file__).read_bytes()).hexdigest(),
+        "check_count": len(checks),
+        "all_passed": all(c["passed"] for c in checks),
+        "checks": checks,
+    }
+    serialized = json.dumps(report, indent=2) + "\n"
+    if args.output:
+        args.output.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
+        with args.output.open("x", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
+            handle.write(serialized)
+        print(json.dumps({"all_passed": report["all_passed"], "checks": len(checks),
+                          "output": str(args.output.resolve())}))
+    else:
+        print(serialized)
+    return 0 if report["all_passed"] else 1
+
+
+if __name__ == "__main__":
+    raise SystemExit(main())
