The problem

We’re sharing a solution to the Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem, one of the Millennium Prize Problems. This proof, produced by an internal OpenAI system, shows that the dynamics of the Navier-Stokes equations for fluid motion can develop a singularity in finite time. We’re sharing both a writeup of the proof and a formalization in Lean.

The Millennium Prize Problems⁠
(opens in a new window)
 represent some of the deepest questions at the frontier of mathematics. The question of whether smooth three-dimensional fluid motion can break down has remained unresolved for roughly 90 years.

A major goal of our work is to empower scientists to advance research and technology that benefits all of humanity. To solve the Navier–Stokes problem, we used an internal model that is significantly more capable than GPT‑6 Astra. We believe it is important to inform the world about the pace of AI progress and what to expect from upcoming models.

The problem

The Navier–Stokes equations use Newton’s second law of motion (“F=ma”) to describe how fluids move. Importantly, they treat a fluid as a continuous medium rather than tracking individual molecules. These equations are used for aircraft design, weather forecasting, and the study of blood flow.

A fundamental open question for these dynamical equations has been whether the continuum approximation of the fluid can break down. Specifically, can the Navier–Stokes equations for a three-dimensional incompressible fluid with constant density develop a “singularity,” even when the motion starts smoothly? Here, a singularity means the dynamics lead to speeds in the fluid growing without bound within a finite amount of time. The development of a singularity would have to happen despite the presence of viscosity, which tends to smooth out motion. Because a real fluid cannot move infinitely fast, this would mark a breakdown in how the equations model the fluid. To continue modeling the system, one would then need to track the behaviour of each particle individually.

The equations date to the nineteenth-century work of Claude-Louis Navier and George Gabriel Stokes. In 1934, Jean Leray proved that solutions exist in a generalized sense, but whether they always remain smooth became a central unanswered question. In 2000, the Clay Mathematics Institute named the Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem one of seven Millennium Prize Problems.

The result

Our system produced an analytical proof and a Lean formalization that an initially smooth fluid at rest can develop a singularity in a finite time. The fluid has a smooth force applied to it, and its energy remains finite through the entire dynamics, from rest to the formation of the singularity. This resolves the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize problem by establishing statement “C” (and also “D”) in the official Millennium Prize formulation⁠
(opens in a new window)
.

The solution is a vortex, a spinning swirl of fluid, that spirals inward and gets increasingly elongated, like spaghetti. This central region shrinks while it speeds up in such a way that its energy still stays finite, as required by the laws of physics. The technical challenge is for the equations to develop the breakdown through the motion of the fluid itself, rather than, for example, us putting in an infinite force by hand. More mathematically, the terms in the Navier–Stokes equations that describe the motion—acceleration, pressure gradients, momentum transfer, viscosity—must both become big yet cancel in a precise way. This detailed balance leaves a smooth external force even as the velocity of the fluid grows without bound.

A snapshot of local incompressible motion. Orange marks faster angular rotation; teal marks slower rotation. Circulating speed also depends on radius. The trajectories show inward spiraling and axial stretching.

How we found the proof

Since August 28 we have been training a new internal model that has exhibited unprecedented performance in our benchmarks, including mathematics. This model’s training is ongoing and its performance continues to improve.

On Tuesday, September 1, we heard rumors that two Millennium Prize problems had been resolved. Inspired by these rumors and by the step change in performance of our internal model, we launched an effort to evaluate it on all open Millennium Prize problems and a few other high-impact problems.

We used a system of coordinating agents powered by our internal model. The agents had access to tools such as the ability to read from a cached version of the internet and the ability to run code. Agents were subdivided into groups with the ability to communicate within the group. The groups varied in size, and the group that produced the Navier–Stokes resolution involved on the order of 10,000 concurrent agents. At all times we maintained the same strict safeguards that we apply to all our frontier model evaluations, including monitoring and isolation.

For each problem, we prompted different groups of agents with different variants of the problem statement, covering all variants of the problem. For the Navier–Stokes problem, we suggested versions “A” and “B” (particular forms of the Navier–Stokes problem which would result in a proof) and versions “C” and “D” (which would result in a disproof) to separate groups of agents.

In addition to the full Millennium Prize problems, we asked our multiagent system to try a set of “easier” problems. One of these problems was a similar blowup question for the limit of the Navier–Stokes problem with the viscosity term removed. This is known as the regularity problem for the Euler equations, and our agents surprised us by resolving this question. The specific variant of the question that they resolved was the unforced version, where no external force is applied to the fluid. Nearly 100 agents worked together for approximately 50 hours to produce our Euler regularity disproof1.

Once we saw the Euler solution, we thought that Navier–Stokes was the most promising problem to work on. Thus, we decided to devote our resources to Navier–Stokes. To do so, we shifted agents away from the other Millennium Problems and prompted these agents with the Euler resolution. When a further trained version of our internal model became available over the course of the effort, we updated our agents to that model.

We encouraged different groups of agents to explore a diversity of approaches. After some time, we cross-pollinated the agent groups by using Codex to consolidate the most useful insights from each agent group. These follow-up prompts drew on the agents’ own intermediate results. The group that found the solution to Navier–Stokes was guided in such a way.

The agents arrived at their resolution on Saturday, September 5, about 88 hours after the first agents were launched. Lean formalization and verification took an additional 17 hours via GPT‑6 Astra.

Across all attempted problems, the agents sent 4.9 million messages and used about 300 billion output tokens. In the process of resolving the Navier–Stokes problem, the agents sent 2.7 million messages and used approximately 130 billion output tokens.

Concurrent work

Our effort began on September 1st after hearing a rumor which we later realized was related to Levent Alpöge, an Anthropic employee, and Tristan Buckmaster, a math professor at NYU.2 After the completion of our full project and Lean verification (on September 6th), believing from the rumor they also had a solution of Navier–Stokes, we reached out to them to offer a concurrent release of our result and to recognize their priority in a joint announcement. At that point we found out that, using an internal Anthropic model, they had produced a resolution of the forced Euler problem. In these discussions we offered them visibility into all of the prompts we used and later to see the proof. We recognize the priority of their work on forced Euler and congratulate them on their remarkable mathematical achievement.

We (the researchers and the agents) did not see any of their work through any means until they released it publicly — in particular, no specific user data was accessed in order to solve this problem.

Following an investigation, we have confirmed that Buckmaster’s Codex prompts over the two months preceding this announcement and paper on September 8, 2026, could not have influenced the system in any way, including through training. The OpenAI internal model used for this result was developed through large-scale reinforcement learning on top of a previously pretrained model. Our proofs also differ significantly. In the Euler case, Alpöge and Buckmaster proved a result with external forcing, while OpenAI’s system proved a result without external forcing.

Progress and responsibility

Our goal in releasing this result is to report on the substantial progress of our AI models. We do not intend to claim the Millennium Prize for this result.

This milestone represents substantial work by mathematicians and AI researchers. However, this is not a culmination, but rather a snapshot in time, of progress on AI development.

We believe we are now in the next period of AI progress⁠, and today’s results provide further evidence of this. We are focusing on understanding this model, and using what we learn to help us guide and pace how we pursue further advances in capability. One of our key goals⁠ is to build AI systems which are steerable, accountable, and connected to people, which may require more deliberate choices about the pace of progress, as we continue our mission to ensure AGI benefits all of humanity.

Sharing AI progress in mathematics | OpenAI

October 6, 2026

Research
Publication
Sharing AI progress in mathematics
View on GitHub
(opens in a new window)
Listen to article
2:04
Share

We’re releasing a broad range of new mathematical results produced by an internal frontier model.

As we look to improve how we share results with the math community, we’ve been consulting with the independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence at the Institute for Advanced Study⁠
(opens in a new window)
 to develop best practices, and we have drawn on their advice and public recommendations⁠
(opens in a new window)
 to inform how we release these results.

For this release, we’re publishing the results in a GitHub repository, with protocols for paper revisions and citations. We’re continuing to explore other community-hosted alternatives for this release which meet the committee’s guidelines. For future releases, we are committed to further improving the quality of the papers via the citations, mathematical exposition, and presentation of the results for better understanding.

As part of our GitHub repository, we are sharing formalizations of many of the proofs in Lean, a programming language that allows mathematical proofs to be checked by a computer. We will update the repository with more formalizations as we obtain them.

To promote scientific transparency and openness, we are also publishing additional details about how we obtained the results in the repository. These include 10 summaries of the model’s reasoning, estimations of compute spent in terms of Pro usage on ChatGPT, and statistics about the number of attempted problems. The average result used the equivalent compute of roughly three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking.

We want this progress to push the frontier of human knowledge and enable further progress in mathematics. We will be funding a series of workshops, conferences, and special programs around the understanding of major results produced by AI—we will share more on this in the near future.

We want to directly empower scientists with state-of-the-art capabilities and are working to responsibly release the model that produced these results. This is why it is important to continue to evaluate our internal frontier models on mathematics and other sciences, so we can accelerate developing the tools to advance those fields. We will continue to act on feedback from the community and update our standards for future disclosures of major scientific advancements.

"{\"len\":3306,\"text\":\"Readme This repository contains mathematical manuscripts and supporting proof artifacts produced by an internal OpenAI model. As part of model development, we evaluate our models on open research problems. We expanded these evaluations after performance on our existing mathematical evaluations saturated. Some outputs build upon earlier results produced by the models. This collection includes results at different stages of verification. Not all have accompanying Lean formalizations. We will continue to update this repository with Lean formalizations as we obtain them. Some of the unformalized results could have issues. We will endeavor to fix any such issues quickly. We are also exploring community-hosted repositories for these materials. Navigating the collection The current catalogue contains 719 manuscripts organized into 372 families. A family groups related papers, which may include a principal result, companion arguments, consequences, or alternative proofs. Each family is classified by mathematical discipline. Start with the overview for descriptions of the families. Use the manuscript map to find individual papers and their supporting materials. The preprints/ directory contains PDFs, source files, and manuscript-specific citation and build instructions. The Lean library and formalization catalogue describe the available formal proofs, their associated papers, and verification configurations. See the Comparator instructions for additional checking instructions. The repository has ~42% top-line results formalized. Updates to the repo are described in the history. Reasoning summaries We are also releasing abridged summaries of the model's reasoning, covering the following results: Family Subject 007 Ordinary two-point correlations of multiplicative functions 017 The irrationality exponent of π 087 Symmetric and general Mahler conjectures 102 Ordinary NP-hardness at the basic semidefinite threshold 159 Quasipolynomial bounds for arithmetic progressions 197 Kaplansky's direct-finiteness conjecture in characteristic two 221 The Mézard–Parisi formula for diluted spin glasses 271 Spontaneous magnetization in the quantum Heisenberg ferromagnet 287 Isomorphism of free group factors 362 The three-dimensional relativistic Vlasov–Maxwell system How the results were produced The vast majority of results were obtained with the same procedure using an unreleased internal OpenAI model. On average, each result used three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking compute with that model. Over the course of the evaluation, the model was posed approximately 4,000 problems. Aggregating the output into result families and manuscripts and requiring an appropriate level of significance led to the catalog outlined above. Exceptions to this fixed procedure include work on a zero-free region for the Riemann zeta function and proof of the Hodge Conjecture for CM abelian varieties. Additionally, the writeup for the Re(s) > 11/12 zero-free region for the Riemann zeta function was human edited for readability. Versions and citations We will preserve the public release history of this collection. Corrections and revisions will be recorded as new versions, with previously released versions remaining accessible. To cite the individual manuscript, use the BibTeX block in its directory.\"}"

For any updated papers, previously published editions remain accessible through the version notes in their README. October 7, 2026 Withdrawals In “Algebraicity of Weil classes on split abelian eightfolds” a sign error invalidates a stabilization-trace cancellation argument and the construction used by two dependent papers. As a result, we have withdrawn the following three manuscripts: Algebraicity of Weil classes on split abelian eightfolds Algebraicity of Kuga–Satake Correspondences for K3 Surfaces The rational Hodge conjecture for products of K3 surfaces The withdrawn papers now carry notices explaining the gap and linking to the archived manuscripts. Fixes We have revised 14 other manuscripts with proof repairs, corrected statements, clearer hypotheses and dependencies, and one correction to an obsolete citation. The changes include: Lipschitz heights and Ashkin–Teller currents (4 manuscripts): repaired crossing, boundary-attachment, conditioning and convergence arguments, including additional work on the real-Lipschitz interface proof. Kähler minimal model programs and abundance (6 manuscripts): expanded positivity and contraction arguments and clarified which results are used as inputs, with their required hypotheses. Taming and hypersymplectic deformation (2 manuscripts): corrected the cone-equality claim in Taming implies compatibility, added a strict-inclusion example, and removed an unnecessary cone-comparison dependency from the hypersymplectic paper. Incompressible Box Transport and Finite Computation: revised the torus-projection and common-clock estimates. Exact Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer Formula from Low Selmer Corank: removed an obsolete introductory citation to a removed supporting manuscript. Also, as a consequence of these fixes we updated 13 additional manuscripts to cite the revised editions of companion papers. These changes update references and version dates. Additional Formalizations We have added an additional 6 formalizations and 5 other additions covering supporting results. This brings the total percentage of top-line results formalized to 300 / 719 = ~42%.\"}"

content.text:
Don't push yet; tell the other session to hold. The code and simulations reproduce, but checking the atlas against its sources turned up errors, and the repo is public. I applied the patch in a scratch worktree off `main` (b5854fc). Your `rtg-0` tree is untouched, and nothing is committed or pushed.

## What reproduces

- **Patch and hashes:** the patch applies cleanly, and your two Downloads `.md` files are identical to the copies inside it. Every seal hash and every source hash in the receipts matches.
- **Tests:** 29 new tests, 128 in the full suite, all passing. Both verifiers regenerate their receipts exactly, apart from timestamps.
- **Simulations:** `results2.json` and `results2b.json` come out byte for byte. Run 1's `results.json` doesn't: on Node 24.19 under Windows, 24 numbers differ in the last digit. Its summary and prediction checks are identical, so "byte for byte" holds for run 1 only on the original machine.
- **Quoted results:** the 5-of-6 and 3-of-6 prediction records, the 20–29% share of patches with a flipped label, and "score-only selection raised readout" all check.

## One correction to the new results

The 8/13 blind range holds only if the memorized items are a random sample of the set. A loop fed its own failures, which is the case the ceiling check exists for, crosses the ceiling after patching 4/25 of the set. That is 8/13 of the *failed items*: same formula, different denominator. The ceiling law in the insertions (§D) and the addendum sentence should state both cases.

The 3-nearest-neighbour simulation adds a third case. It patched 25% of the set at n=4000 and its reported score stayed at 0.759, under the 0.90 ceiling, because one added point doesn't overturn a 3-vote majority.

## Checking the atlas against its sources

I read the primary sources as full text in the browser pane, not through summaries. OpenAI's chart data turned out to be embedded in its page. Most figures hold; these don't:

| Case | Atlas says | Source says |
|---|---|---|
| OpenAI | 722 manuscripts; 162 formalized in Lean, ≈22% | Repo history: 3 manuscripts withdrawn 7 Oct over a sign error, 14 revised; now 719, with "300 / 719 = ~42%" of top-line results formalized |
| OpenAI | Feedback channel "not stated" | Mid-run they "updated our agents" to a further-trained model, and fed intermediate results back across agent groups via Codex. README: "Some outputs build upon earlier results produced by the models" |
| METR | Doubling times of 131 and 89 days (from a Manifold page) | METR's own data: 128.7 days from 2023 on (CI 104–158), and no since-2024 fit. The Mythos point (1044.78 min) is confirmed, with a CI of 8.5–55 h. METR added its 16-hour caveat the same day it added that point |
| Anthropic | Weights are person-time after automation, so a task that got faster weighs less | Each sampled person's week is split evenly across the tasks they touched. That counts tasks, not hours, so this mechanism doesn't follow. A bias that does follow: work no sampled person touched never enters the basket |
| Anthropic | 59% exact agreement "is the relevant figure" | For a count at the AL3/AL4 line, 59% is only a lower bound. What's needed is agreement on which side of that line a task falls, plus which way disagreements lean |
| AIDE² | Meaning of ± unknown; ALE-Bench contrast 1.90 SE | ± is one standard error of the benchmark mean. The 1858 vs 1796 contrast is across models (Gemini 3 Flash with the step-85 harness vs Fable 5 with the initial one). With the model held fixed, Table 1 gives 1790±9 vs 1536±33, about 7.4 SE. The step-85 harness beats the initial one by at least 2.6 SE on all four benchmarks |
| AIDE² | Number of readout checkpoints unknown | Two, chosen by position: the incumbent within the first 50 nodes, and the final incumbent |

Everything else the atlas attributes to these sources is as quoted. That covers OpenAI's dates, quotes and swarm scale; Anthropic's 15,000 / 542 / 378 tasks, 59 / 35 / 97% agreement, 26% and >90%; METR's suite and freeze date; AIDE²'s steps, grades, models, benchmark sizes and 55/39/32%; and the Princeton paper's budgets, models, grades and limitations. Smaller points worth adding:

- **OpenAI chart:** the by-eye values were right. The internal model runs 0.262→0.474 and GPT-6 Astra 0.084→0.170, with ±1 SE error bars. Every pass rate is a whole multiple of 1/382.
- **Princeton:** the runs needed three human interventions, including a 24-hour deadline extension, and the authors come from about ten institutions.
- **AIDE²:** about a quarter of the rejected rewrites beat the incumbent on the signal the agent could see, then lost on the private grade. That bears directly on the feedback argument.

I didn't check CellCog, DataLearner, the X screenshot or Engadget; the primaries above replace the first three, and no card cites Engadget.

## On the push

The headline survives: none of the five gives a model-weights gain from one generation to the next on a sealed readout. It reads differently, though. AIDE²'s held-out gains are much stronger than the 1.90 figure suggests, and OpenAI's run has feedback channels the atlas says weren't stated. The module, tests and insertions are fine to commit once the ceiling law states both cases.

If you'd like, I'll make these fixes here. That means editing the atlas and `configs/rsi_claim_cards.json`, re-running the verifier (its OpenAI and METR checks change), and committing to a local `feedback-channel-and-rsi-atlas` branch off `main`. You could then push from here or hand the corrected patch back. The scratch worktree is at `…\scratchpad\wt`.

# Takeoff-evidence examples for the evaluation design calculus

Draft 0.1 — inspected 2026-10-11.

This atlas applies [the calculus](evaluation_design_calculus.md) and the
[suggested feedback insertions](evaluation_feedback_insertions.md) to five
published claims that bear on AI-driven AI research and development. These are
design analyses and proposed studies. No model was called and no published
result was reproduced.

Each case distinguishes **observed**, **interpretation**, and **proposed
variation**, as the [Prime Intellect atlas](prime_intellect_eval_atlas.md) does.

**Reading caveat.** Every source below was read on the inspection date through
a fetch tool that returns a summary of the page, not its bytes. One chart was
read from a screenshot in a third-party post. Figures are as that tool returned
them. A line-level check against the originals is outstanding and should
precede any circulation. Source levels are marked per case:

- *primary, summarized*: the publisher's own page or paper, through the tool.
- *secondary*: a report about the source.
- *screenshot*: an image of the source reproduced by a third party.

## 1. The question put to each case

A forecast of compounding needs one estimand: the gain from one generation of
controllers to the next, repeated, on a readout the improvement process did not
touch. In the notation of the insertions, that is a series of \(V^{r}_{\pi_g}\)
with \(r\) sealed, together with a ledger showing that it stayed sealed.

| Card field | What to look for in a takeoff claim |
|---|---|
| \(\Pi\) | What improves: weights, harness, test-time budget, or the mix of who does the work |
| \(D\) | How scored items were chosen, and whether the choice followed a look at results |
| \(Z\) | Whether what was kept depends on how it scored |
| \(J\) | Who or what judges, and whether the judge shares errors with the judged |
| Feedback | Whether scores or items from the scored set reached the improvement process |
| Readout | Whether any reported number comes from a set declared sealed |
| \(C\) | Which estimand the evidence supports, as against the one the headline implies |

40	
41	## B. §3, operator table
42	
43	Suggested row:
44	
45	| Proposed operator | Primary effect | Required detail |
46	|---|---|---|
47	| \(\operatorname{Feedback}_{s,q}\) | Controller roster/protocol of a later generation | Source set \(s\); access class \(q\in\{\text{sealed},\text{score-only},\text{item-level}\}\); whether the consumer selects among candidates or supplies a training input; generation scope. |
48	
49	Suggested sentence beneath the table:
50	
51	> Feedback is not \(\operatorname{Rescore}\), which is offline, and not
52	> \(\operatorname{Observe}\), which changes what the evaluator records. It reads
53	> \(J\) restricted to \(s\) and writes \(\Pi\) for the next generation. Declaring
54	> a set sealed while a score from it reaches the loop is ill-typed.
55	
56	## C. §4, after the sentence on `Repeat` and reset/carry maps
57	
58	> Generations joined by Feedback are not independent blocks. The carry map
59	> carries the controller, and with it whatever of \(s\) the channel transmitted.
60	> Aggregating a per-generation score across such generations as if each were a
61	> fresh draw of the same experiment mistakes the unit.
62	
63	## D. §5, three laws and one observation
64	
65	**Coarsening law.**
66	
67	> The access classes are ordered: sealed is a deterministic function of the
68	> score, and the score is a deterministic function of the per-item outcomes.
69	> Total-variation distance between two controllers' feedback therefore cannot
70	> increase from item-level to score-only to sealed. Two controllers that fail
71	> different items with equal totals are separated completely by item-level
72	> feedback and not at all by a score.
73	
74	Support: `access_order_fixture`; the ordering is checked for every pair of
75	distributions on a rational grid over two-item outcomes.
76	
77	**Selection law.**
78	
79	> Keeping the best of \(K\) candidates by score on \(s\), then reporting that
80	> score, overstates: \(\mathbb E[\max_k\hat S_k]\ge\max_k\mathbb E[\hat S_k]\).
81	> This is the same convexity as the mixture law, with the candidate index in
82	> place of the mixture component. For candidates of equal true value
83	> one half, two candidates and one item give a reported value of three quarters.
84	
85	Support: `selection_inflation`, checked against independent enumeration of
86	every outcome matrix in seven small cells. Exact gaps for two candidates at
87	\(p=\tfrac12\) are \(\tfrac14\), \(\tfrac{35}{256}\), about 0.0700 and about
88	0.0352 at 1, 4, 16 and 64 items; multiplied by \(\sqrt n\) these are 0.250,
89	0.273, 0.280 and 0.282. The value \(1/(2\sqrt\pi)\approx0.2821\) is the
90	standard Gaussian figure for the larger of two draws. The fixture verifies the
91	listed cells and no limit.
92	
93	Boundary: one generation, equal candidates, independent items. Accumulation
94	across generations is a simulation result, not an exact one.
95	
96	**Ceiling law.**
97	
98	> With labels flipped independently at rate \(\varepsilon<\tfrac12\), no
99	> predictor blind to the flips exceeds \(1-\varepsilon\) on observed labels.
100	> A controller that has memorized a share \(m/n\) of \(s\), and scores \(v\)
101	> elsewhere, scores \(m/n+(1-m/n)v\) on \(s\). It crosses the ceiling only when
102	> \(m/n>(1-\varepsilon-v)/(1-v)\). Below that share a ceiling check is silent.
103	
104	Support: `ceiling_detection_threshold`. With clean accuracy \(\tfrac45\) and
105	\(\varepsilon=\tfrac1{10}\): \(v=\tfrac{37}{50}\), threshold \(\tfrac8{13}\).
106	The formula assumes a memorized item has no effect on any other item, which the
107	nearest-neighbour learner in the simulations did not satisfy.
108	
109	**Observation on what item-level feedback selects.**
110	
111	> An item the controller fails is more likely than an average item to carry a
112	> wrong label, whenever the controller is better than chance:

## B. §3, operator table

Suggested row:

| Proposed operator | Primary effect | Required detail |
|---|---|---|
| \(\operatorname{Feedback}_{s,q}\) | Controller roster/protocol of a later generation | Source set \(s\); access class \(q\in\{\text{sealed},\text{score-only},\text{item-level}\}\); whether the consumer selects among candidates or supplies a training input; generation scope. |

Suggested sentence beneath the table:

> Feedback is not \(\operatorname{Rescore}\), which is offline, and not
> \(\operatorname{Observe}\), which changes what the evaluator records. It reads
> \(J\) restricted to \(s\) and writes \(\Pi\) for the next generation. Declaring
> a set sealed while a score from it reaches the loop is ill-typed.

## C. §4, after the sentence on `Repeat` and reset/carry maps

> Generations joined by Feedback are not independent blocks. The carry map
> carries the controller, and with it whatever of \(s\) the channel transmitted.
> Aggregating a per-generation score across such generations as if each were a
> fresh draw of the same experiment mistakes the unit.

## D. §5, three laws and one observation

**Coarsening law.**

> The access classes are ordered: sealed is a deterministic function of the
> score, and the score is a deterministic function of the per-item outcomes.
> Total-variation distance between two controllers' feedback therefore cannot
> increase from item-level to score-only to sealed. Two controllers that fail
> different items with equal totals are separated completely by item-level
> feedback and not at all by a score.

Support: `access_order_fixture`; the ordering is checked for every pair of
distributions on a rational grid over two-item outcomes.

**Selection law.**

> Keeping the best of \(K\) candidates by score on \(s\), then reporting that
> score, overstates: \(\mathbb E[\max_k\hat S_k]\ge\max_k\mathbb E[\hat S_k]\).
> This is the same convexity as the mixture law, with the candidate index in
> place of the mixture component. For candidates of equal true value
> one half, two candidates and one item give a reported value of three quarters.

Support: `selection_inflation`, checked against independent enumeration of
every outcome matrix in seven small cells. Exact gaps for two candidates at
\(p=\tfrac12\) are \(\tfrac14\), \(\tfrac{35}{256}\), about 0.0700 and about
0.0352 at 1, 4, 16 and 64 items; multiplied by \(\sqrt n\) these are 0.250,
0.273, 0.280 and 0.282. The value \(1/(2\sqrt\pi)\approx0.2821\) is the
standard Gaussian figure for the larger of two draws. The fixture verifies the
listed cells and no limit.

Boundary: one generation, equal candidates, independent items. Accumulation
across generations is a simulation result, not an exact one.

**Ceiling law.**

> With labels flipped independently at rate \(\varepsilon<\tfrac12\), no
> predictor blind to the flips exceeds \(1-\varepsilon\) on observed labels.
> A controller that has memorized a share \(m/n\) of \(s\), and scores \(v\)
> elsewhere, scores \(m/n+(1-m/n)v\) on \(s\). It crosses the ceiling only when
> \(m/n>(1-\varepsilon-v)/(1-v)\). Below that share a ceiling check is silent.

Support: `ceiling_detection_threshold`. With clean accuracy \(\tfrac45\) and
\(\varepsilon=\tfrac1{10}\): \(v=\tfrac{37}{50}\), threshold \(\tfrac8{13}\).
The formula assumes a memorized item has no effect on any other item, which the
nearest-neighbour learner in the simulations did not satisfy.

**Observation on what item-level feedback selects.**

> An item the controller fails is more likely than an average item to carry a
> wrong label, whenever the controller is better than chance:
> \(\Pr[\text{flipped}\mid\text{failed}]=\varepsilon a/(\varepsilon a+(1-\varepsilon)(1-a))\),
> which exceeds \(\varepsilon\) exactly when \(a>\tfrac12\). Feeding failures
> back concentrates label noise in what the next controller is built from.

Support: `failed_item_noise_share`; \(\tfrac4{13}\) against a base rate of
\(\tfrac1{10}\) in the fixture. In the second simulation the measured share
among patched items was 20–29% against the same 10% base rate. This is the
reason the unchecked answer in the Proposer–Solver recipe (atlas §11) matters
once its output is fed back.

Suggested closing sentence, matching the section's existing last line:

> No unconditional claim is made that feedback lowers readout performance. In
> the simulations, score-only selection of fresh training batches raised it.

## E. §7, after the definition of the order effect

def memorized_selection_score(clean_accuracy: Q, flip: Q, patch_share: Q) -> Q:
    """Selection-set score after memorizing a share of its observed labels.

    Memorized items score one; the remainder keep the base observed accuracy.
    Collateral effects of a patch on other items are assumed absent, which a
    real learner need not satisfy.
    """

    if not 0 <= patch_share <= 1:
        raise ValueError("patch share must lie in [0, 1]")
    base = observed_accuracy(clean_accuracy, flip)
    return patch_share + (1 - patch_share) * base


def ceiling_detection_threshold(clean_accuracy: Q, flip: Q) -> Q:
    """Patch share above which the selection score exceeds the noise ceiling.

    Below this share the ceiling check is silent however much was memorized.
    """

    base = observed_accuracy(clean_accuracy, flip)
    if base >= 1:
        raise ValueError("base observed accuracy must be below one")
    return max(Q(0), (noise_ceiling(flip) - base) / (1 - base))


def failed_item_noise_share(clean_accuracy: Q, flip: Q) -> Q:
    """Probability that an item the base predictor fails has a flipped label.

    The predictor errs on the clean label independently of the flip.  It fails
    the observed label either by being right about a flipped item or wrong
    about an unflipped one.
    """

    wrong_because_flipped = flip * clean_accuracy
    wrong_unflipped = (1 - flip) * (1 - clean_accuracy)
    if wrong_because_flipped + wrong_unflipped == 0:
        raise ValueError("the predictor never fails an observed label")
    return wrong_because_flipped / (wrong_because_flipped + wrong_unflipped)


def noise_ceiling_fixture() -> dict[str, Q]:
    clean, flip = Q(4, 5), Q(1, 10)
    return {
        "clean_accuracy": clean, "flip_probability": flip,
        "base_observed_accuracy": observed_accuracy(clean, flip),
        "noise_ceiling": noise_ceiling(flip),
        "score_half_memorized": memorized_selection_score(clean, flip, Q(1, 2)),
        "score_fully_memorized": memorized_selection_score(clean, flip, Q(1)),
        "ceiling_detection_threshold": ceiling_detection_threshold(clean, flip),
        "failed_item_noise_share": failed_item_noise_share(clean, flip),
    }

def verify() -> dict[str, object]:
    """Run all exact fixtures and return machine-readable checks."""

    order = access_order_fixture()
    smallest = selection_inflation(1, 2, Q(1, 2))
    ladder = {n: selection_inflation(n, 2, Q(1, 2))["readout_gap"] for n in (1, 4, 16, 64)}
    widening = {k: selection_inflation(4, k, Q(1, 2))["readout_gap"] for k in (1, 2, 4, 16)}
    noise = noise_ceiling_fixture()
    ledgers = run_ledger_fixture()
    flags = divergence_flags(((0, Q(7, 10), Q(7, 10)), (50, Q(4, 5), Q(37, 50)),
                              (100, Q(83, 100), Q(73, 100))), Q(1, 50))
    checks = {
        "item_level_separates_equal_scores_and_score_only_does_not":
            order["gaps"]["same_score"] == {"sealed": Q(0), "score_only": Q(0), "item_level": Q(1)},
        "access_classes_ordered": order["access_classes_ordered_by_coarsening"],
        "two_candidates_one_item_gap_is_quarter": smallest["readout_gap"] == Q(1, 4),
        "single_candidate_has_no_selection_gap": widening[1] == 0,
        "selection_gap_shrinks_with_items": ladder[1] > ladder[4] > ladder[16] > ladder[64] > 0,
        "selection_gap_grows_with_candidates": widening[1] < widening[2] < widening[4] < widening[16],
        "full_memorization_exceeds_noise_ceiling":
            noise["score_fully_memorized"] == 1 > noise["noise_ceiling"],
        "half_memorization_stays_below_ceiling":
            noise["score_half_memorized"] < noise["noise_ceiling"],
        "ceiling_check_threshold_is_eight_thirteenths":
            noise["ceiling_detection_threshold"] == Q(8, 13),
        "failed_items_enriched_for_flipped_labels":
            noise["failed_item_noise_share"] == Q(4, 13) > noise["flip_probability"],
        "respected_ledger_leaves_readout_evaluable":
            ledgers["respected"]["declarations_respected"]
            and ledgers["respected"]["readout"]["R"]["endpoint_status"] == "evaluable",
        "breached_ledger_withholds_endpoint":
            ledgers["breached"]["readout"]["R"]["endpoint_status"] == "not_evaluated"
            and bool(ledgers["breached"]["selection"]["S"]["breaches"]),
        "selection_scores_never_endpoints":
            not ledgers["respected"]["selection"]["S"]["selection_scores_usable_as_endpoints"],
        "divergence_flags_fire_when_selection_outruns_readout":
            [row["flagged"] for row in flags] == [True, True]
            and flags[1]["readout_gain"] < 0 < flags[1]["selection_gain"],
    }
    return {"evidence_status": "exact_synthetic_fixtures_not_model_or_agent_evidence",
            "checks": checks, "all_passed": all(checks.values()),
            "access_order": order,
            "selection_inflation": {"one_item_two_candidates": smallest,
                                    "gap_by_items_two_candidates": ladder,
                                    "gap_by_candidates_four_items": widening},
            "noise_ceiling": noise, "ledger": ledgers, "divergence": flags}

# Feedback channel: suggested insertions for the evaluation design calculus

Draft 0.1 — 2026-10-11. Suggestions only.

This file changes nothing in `evaluation_design_calculus.md` or
`evaluation_game_testbed.md`. Each block names a location in those documents,
offers text for it, and states what supports the text. Where a block is adopted,
its wording should be made the author's own. Where it is not, the executable
fixtures still stand by themselves.

The gap being addressed: the calculus already says that a judgment "shown during
play or used for learning ... also enters observations or controller updates"
(§2), and that frozen-controller sensitivity differs from sensitivity "after
retraining, selecting another controller" (§7). It has no operator for that
channel, no estimand for what the channel does to a score, and no record of how
often it was used. A self-improvement loop is that channel applied once per
generation.

## Evidence behind the suggestions

| Level | Source | What it supplies |
|---|---|---|
| Finite verified example | `src/spiral_ln/evaluation_game_feedback.py`, 29 tests, receipt under `output/evaluation_game_feedback/` | Access-class ordering, one-generation selection gap, noise-ceiling threshold, failed-item enrichment, ledger enforcement |
| Synthetic mechanism result | `output/eval_reuse_toys/` (two seeded simulations, predictions hashed before each run) | Multi-generation behaviour of the gap under score-only and item-level feedback |
| Not available | — | Any language-model loop, any observed controller |

The simulations are JavaScript, seeded, and not exact. Their prediction record
is 5 of 6 in the first run and 3 of 6 in the second, and both overpredicted the
size of the gap. One arm of the second run was added after its sealed results
were seen and is marked exploratory in its own files.

## A. §2, after "Maintain three distinctions"

# Feedback channel: suggested insertions for the evaluation design calculus

Draft 0.1 — 2026-10-11. Suggestions only.

This file changes nothing in `evaluation_design_calculus.md` or
`evaluation_game_testbed.md`. Each block names a location in those documents,
offers text for it, and states what supports the text. Where a block is adopted,
its wording should be made the author's own. Where it is not, the executable
fixtures still stand by themselves.

The gap being addressed: the calculus already says that a judgment "shown during
play or used for learning ... also enters observations or controller updates"
(§2), and that frozen-controller sensitivity differs from sensitivity "after
retraining, selecting another controller" (§7). It has no operator for that
channel, no estimand for what the channel does to a score, and no record of how
often it was used. A self-improvement loop is that channel applied once per
generation.

## Evidence behind the suggestions

| Level | Source | What it supplies |
|---|---|---|
| Finite verified example | `src/spiral_ln/evaluation_game_feedback.py`, 29 tests, receipt under `output/evaluation_game_feedback/` | Access-class ordering, one-generation selection gap, noise-ceiling threshold, failed-item enrichment, ledger enforcement |
| Synthetic mechanism result | `output/eval_reuse_toys/` (two seeded simulations, predictions hashed before each run) | Multi-generation behaviour of the gap under score-only and item-level feedback |
| Not available | — | Any language-model loop, any observed controller |

The simulations are JavaScript, seeded, and not exact. Their prediction record
is 5 of 6 in the first run and 3 of 6 in the second, and both overpredicted the
size of the gap. One arm of the second run was added after its sealed results
were seen and is marked exploratory in its own files.

## A. §2, after "Maintain three distinctions"

Suggested fourth distinction:

> 4. A judgment that reaches whatever produces the next controller is a channel.
> Its source set, its access class, and the number of times it was used belong
> in the experiment record. A score measured on a set that fed this channel is a
> selection score. A capability claim needs a set that did not.

## B. §3, operator table

Suggested row:

| Proposed operator | Primary effect | Required detail |
|---|---|---|
| \(\operatorname{Feedback}_{s,q}\) | Controller roster/protocol of a later generation | Source set \(s\); access class \(q\in\{\text{sealed},\text{score-only},\text{item-level}\}\); whether the consumer selects among candidates or supplies a training input; generation scope. |

Suggested sentence beneath the table:

> Feedback is not \(\operatorname{Rescore}\), which is offline, and not
> \(\operatorname{Observe}\), which changes what the evaluator records. It reads
> \(J\) restricted to \(s\) and writes \(\Pi\) for the next generation. Declaring
> a set sealed while a score from it reaches the loop is ill-typed.

## C. §4, after the sentence on `Repeat` and reset/carry maps

> Generations joined by Feedback are not independent blocks. The carry map
> carries the controller, and with it whatever of \(s\) the channel transmitted.
> Aggregating a per-generation score across such generations as if each were a
> fresh draw of the same experiment mistakes the unit.

## D. §5, three laws and one observation

**Coarsening law.**

> The access classes are ordered: sealed is a deterministic function of the
> score, and the score is a deterministic function of the per-item outcomes.
> Total-variation distance between two controllers' feedback therefore cannot
> increase from item-level to score-only to sealed. Two controllers that fail
> different items with equal totals are separated completely by item-level
> feedback and not at all by a score.

Support: `access_order_fixture`; the ordering is checked for every pair of
distributions on a rational grid over two-item outcomes.

**Selection law.**

> Keeping the best of \(K\) candidates by score on \(s\), then reporting that
> score, overstates: \(\mathbb E[\max_k\hat S_k]\ge\max_k\mathbb E[\hat S_k]\).
> This is the same convexity as the mixture law, with the candidate index in
> place of the mixture component. For candidates of equal true value
> one half, two candidates and one item give a reported value of three quarters.

Support: `selection_inflation`, checked against independent enumeration of
every outcome matrix in seven small cells. Exact gaps for two candidates at
\(p=\tfrac12\) are \(\tfrac14\), \(\tfrac{35}{256}\), about 0.0700 and about
0.0352 at 1, 4, 16 and 64 items; multiplied by \(\sqrt n\) these are 0.250,
0.273, 0.280 and 0.282. The value \(1/(2\sqrt\pi)\approx0.2821\) is the
standard Gaussian figure for the larger of two draws. The fixture verifies the
listed cells and no limit.

Boundary: one generation, equal candidates, independent items. Accumulation
across generations is a simulation result, not an exact one.

**Ceiling law.**

> With labels flipped independently at rate \(\varepsilon<\tfrac12\), no
> predictor blind to the flips exceeds \(1-\varepsilon\) on observed labels.
> A controller that has memorized a share \(m/n\) of \(s\), and scores \(v\)
> elsewhere, scores \(m/n+(1-m/n)v\) on \(s\). It crosses the ceiling only when
> \(m/n>(1-\varepsilon-v)/(1-v)\). Below that share a ceiling check is silent.

Support: `ceiling_detection_threshold`. With clean accuracy \(\tfrac45\) and
\(\varepsilon=\tfrac1{10}\): \(v=\tfrac{37}{50}\), threshold \(\tfrac8{13}\).
The formula assumes a memorized item has no effect on any other item, which the
nearest-neighbour learner in the simulations did not satisfy.

**Observation on what item-level feedback selects.**

> An item the controller fails is more likely than an average item to carry a
> wrong label, whenever the controller is better than chance:
> \(\Pr[\text{flipped}\mid\text{failed}]=\varepsilon a/(\varepsilon a+(1-\varepsilon)(1-a))\),
> which exceeds \(\varepsilon\) exactly when \(a>\tfrac12\). Feeding failures
> back concentrates label noise in what the next controller is built from.

Support: `failed_item_noise_share`; \(\tfrac4{13}\) against a base rate of
\(\tfrac1{10}\) in the fixture. In the second simulation the measured share
among patched items was 20–29% against the same 10% base rate. This is the
reason the unchecked answer in the Proposer–Solver recipe (atlas §11) matters
once its output is fed back.

Suggested closing sentence, matching the section's existing last line:

> No unconditional claim is made that feedback lowers readout performance. In
> the simulations, score-only selection of fresh training batches raised it.

## E. §7, after the definition of the order effect

> For a controller \(\pi_g\) produced with feedback from \(s\), and a sealed set
> \(r\) from the same sampling law, define the readout gap
> \(\rho_g=V^{s}_{\pi_g}-V^{r}_{\pi_g}\). It compares two measurements of one
> controller, not two designs, so it is not a design difference. A gain series
> computed on \(s\) estimates the change in value plus the change in \(\rho\).

## F. §11, the evaluation card

Suggested amendment to item 6:

> ... and whether any score feeds back into play *or into the production of a
> later controller*.

Suggested additional item:

> 10. **Feedback ledger:** for each evaluation set, its role (selection or
> readout), declared access class, score queries, items fed back, number and
> generation of readouts, and the rule that retires it.

## G. `evaluation_game_testbed.md`, estimand table

Suggested fifth row:

| Estimand | Definition | It is not |
|---|---|---|
| Readout gap | \(\rho=V^{s}_\pi-V^{r}_\pi\), with \(s\) having fed judgment to the loop and \(r\) sealed | A baseline gain, or evidence that capability changed |

Suggested section, placed after "Executable confirmation and adversarial
checks":

> ### Feedback channel and multi-generation ledger
>
> `evaluation_game_feedback.py` extends the single split enforced by `confirm()`
> to a sequence of generations. Sets are declared with a role and an access
> class. Events record a score reaching the loop, items reaching the loop, or an
> experimenter reading a sealed set. Malformed declarations raise, including a
> readout set not declared sealed and identifiers shared across sets. Breaches
> of a well-formed declaration are recorded instead, and move the readout
> endpoint to `not_evaluated`: a breach is a finding about the run. Reads of the
> sealed set are budgeted, since a stop-or-continue decision taken on a readout
> is itself adaptive. Identifiers detect recorded overlap. They do not certify
> independence.
>
> ```powershell
> $env:PYTHONPATH = "src"
> python scripts/verify_evaluation_game_feedback.py --output output/evaluation_game_feedback/feedback_v0_1.json
> python -m pytest tests/test_evaluation_game_feedback.py -q
> ```

## H. What is not delivered

- `Feedback` is not implemented against `hive_lab` adapters or any external
  policy. The module checks declarations and arithmetic.
- No loop with a language model has been run. The first observed-controller
  study would pair a small model with a declared selection set and a sealed
  readout, and report the ledger.
- Partial leakage, where the loop learns failure categories and not items, has
  no fixture.
- The simulations fix one parameter set each. No sweep over candidate count,
  decay rate, or label-noise rate was run.

> With labels flipped independently at rate \(\varepsilon<\tfrac12\), no
> predictor blind to the flips exceeds \(1-\varepsilon\) in expectation on
> observed labels. Let \(v\) be the controller's observed accuracy before any
> item of \(s\) is memorized. If it memorizes a share \(m/n\) of \(s\) chosen
> without regard to its outcomes, it scores \(m/n+(1-m/n)v\) on \(s\) and
> crosses the ceiling only when \(m/n>(1-\varepsilon-v)/(1-v)\). If it memorizes
> items it failed, which is what item-level feedback supplies, it scores
> \(v+m/n\) and crosses when \(m/n>1-\varepsilon-v\): the same threshold
> \((1-\varepsilon-v)/(1-v)\), now as a share of the failed items. Below the
> threshold a ceiling check is silent.

`targeted_ceiling_detection_threshold`. With clean accuracy \(\tfrac45\) and
\(\varepsilon=\tfrac1{10}\): \(v=\tfrac{37}{50}\). Memorizing at random, the
check is silent below \(\tfrac8{13}\) of the set. Patching failures, it is
silent below \(\tfrac4{25}\) of the set, which is \(\tfrac8{13}\) of the failed
items. Both formulas assume a memorized item has no effect on any other item.
The nearest-neighbour learner in the second simulation did not satisfy that,
and it also did not reliably absorb a patch: at \(n=4000\) it patched a quarter
of the set and its reported score stayed at 0.759, below the 0.90 ceiling.

# Feedback channel: suggested insertions for the evaluation design calculus

Draft 0.2 — 2026-10-12. Suggestions only. Draft 0.2 states the ceiling law for
failure-targeted patching as well as for patching chosen at random.

This file changes nothing in `evaluation_design_calculus.md` or
`evaluation_game_testbed.md`. Each block names a location in those documents,
offers text for it, and states what supports the text. Where a block is adopted,
its wording should be made the author's own. Where it is not, the executable
fixtures still stand by themselves.

The gap being addressed: the calculus already says that a judgment "shown during
play or used for learning ... also enters observations or controller updates"
(§2), and that frozen-controller sensitivity differs from sensitivity "after
retraining, selecting another controller" (§7). It has no operator for that
channel, no estimand for what the channel does to a score, and no record of how
often it was used. A self-improvement loop is that channel applied once per
generation.

## Evidence behind the suggestions

| Level | Source | What it supplies |
|---|---|---|
| Finite verified example | `src/spiral_ln/evaluation_game_feedback.py`, 30 tests, receipt under `output/evaluation_game_feedback/` | Access-class ordering, one-generation selection gap, noise-ceiling threshold, failed-item enrichment, ledger enforcement |
| Synthetic mechanism result | `output/eval_reuse_toys/` (two seeded simulations, predictions hashed before each run) | Multi-generation behaviour of the gap under score-only and item-level feedback |
| Not available | — | Any language-model loop, any observed controller |

The simulations are JavaScript, seeded, and not exact. Their prediction record
is 5 of 6 in the first run and 3 of 6 in the second, and both overpredicted the
size of the gap. One arm of the second run was added after its sealed results
were seen and is marked exploratory in its own files.

## A. §2, after "Maintain three distinctions"

Suggested fourth distinction:

> 4. A judgment that reaches whatever produces the next controller is a channel.
> Its source set, its access class, and the number of times it was used belong
> in the experiment record. A score measured on a set that fed this channel is a
> selection score. A capability claim needs a set that did not.

## B. §3, operator table

Suggested row:

| Proposed operator | Primary effect | Required detail |
|---|---|---|
| \(\operatorname{Feedback}_{s,q}\) | Controller roster/protocol of a later generation | Source set \(s\); access class \(q\in\{\text{sealed},\text{score-only},\text{item-level}\}\); whether the consumer selects among candidates or supplies a training input; generation scope. |

Suggested sentence beneath the table:

> Feedback is not \(\operatorname{Rescore}\), which is offline, and not
> \(\operatorname{Observe}\), which changes what the evaluator records. It reads
> \(J\) restricted to \(s\) and writes \(\Pi\) for the next generation. Declaring
> a set sealed while a score from it reaches the loop is ill-typed.

## C. §4, after the sentence on `Repeat` and reset/carry maps

> Generations joined by Feedback are not independent blocks. The carry map
> carries the controller, and with it whatever of \(s\) the channel transmitted.
> Aggregating a per-generation score across such generations as if each were a
> fresh draw of the same experiment mistakes the unit.

## D. §5, three laws and one observation

**Coarsening law.**

> The access classes are ordered: sealed is a deterministic function of the
> score, and the score is a deterministic function of the per-item outcomes.
> Total-variation distance between two controllers' feedback therefore cannot
> increase from item-level to score-only to sealed. Two controllers that fail
> different items with equal totals are separated completely by item-level
> feedback and not at all by a score.

Support: `access_order_fixture`; the ordering is checked for every pair of
distributions on a rational grid over two-item outcomes.

**Selection law.**

> Keeping the best of \(K\) candidates by score on \(s\), then reporting that
> score, overstates: \(\mathbb E[\max_k\hat S_k]\ge\max_k\mathbb E[\hat S_k]\).
> This is the same convexity as the mixture law, with the candidate index in
> place of the mixture component. For candidates of equal true value
> one half, two candidates and one item give a reported value of three quarters.

Support: `selection_inflation`, checked against independent enumeration of
every outcome matrix in seven small cells. Exact gaps for two candidates at
\(p=\tfrac12\) are \(\tfrac14\), \(\tfrac{35}{256}\), about 0.0700 and about
0.0352 at 1, 4, 16 and 64 items; multiplied by \(\sqrt n\) these are 0.250,
0.273, 0.280 and 0.282. The value \(1/(2\sqrt\pi)\approx0.2821\) is the
standard Gaussian figure for the larger of two draws. The fixture verifies the
listed cells and no limit.

Boundary: one generation, equal candidates, independent items. Accumulation
across generations is a simulation result, not an exact one.

**Ceiling law.**

> With labels flipped independently at rate \(\varepsilon<\tfrac12\), no
> predictor blind to the flips exceeds \(1-\varepsilon\) on observed labels.
> A controller that has memorized a share \(m/n\) of \(s\), and scores \(v\)
> elsewhere, scores \(m/n+(1-m/n)v\) on \(s\). It crosses the ceiling only when
> \(m/n>(1-\varepsilon-v)/(1-v)\). Below that share a ceiling check is silent.

Support: `ceiling_detection_threshold`. With clean accuracy \(\tfrac45\) and
\(\varepsilon=\tfrac1{10}\): \(v=\tfrac{37}{50}\), threshold \(\tfrac8{13}\).
The formula assumes a memorized item has no effect on any other item, which the
nearest-neighbour learner in the simulations did not satisfy.

**Observation on what item-level feedback selects.**

> An item the controller fails is more likely than an average item to carry a
> wrong label, whenever the controller is better than chance:
> \(\Pr[\text{flipped}\mid\text{failed}]=\varepsilon a/(\varepsilon a+(1-\varepsilon)(1-a))\),
> which exceeds \(\varepsilon\) exactly when \(a>\tfrac12\). Feeding failures
> back concentrates label noise in what the next controller is built from.

Support: `failed_item_noise_share`; \(\tfrac4{13}\) against a base rate of
\(\tfrac1{10}\) in the fixture. In the second simulation the measured share
among patched items was 20–29% against the same 10% base rate. This is the
reason the unchecked answer in the Proposer–Solver recipe (atlas §11) matters
once its output is fed back.

Suggested closing sentence, matching the section's existing last line:

> No unconditional claim is made that feedback lowers readout performance. In
> the simulations, score-only selection of fresh training batches raised it.

## E. §7, after the definition of the order effect

> For a controller \(\pi_g\) produced with feedback from \(s\), and a sealed set
> \(r\) from the same sampling law, define the readout gap
> \(\rho_g=V^{s}_{\pi_g}-V^{r}_{\pi_g}\). It compares two measurements of one
> controller, not two designs, so it is not a design difference. A gain series
> computed on \(s\) estimates the change in value plus the change in \(\rho\).

## F. §11, the evaluation card

Suggested amendment to item 6:

> ... and whether any score feeds back into play *or into the production of a
> later controller*.

Suggested additional item:

> 10. **Feedback ledger:** for each evaluation set, its role (selection or
> readout), declared access class, score queries, items fed back, number and
> generation of readouts, and the rule that retires it.

## G. `evaluation_game_testbed.md`, estimand table

Suggested fifth row:

| Estimand | Definition | It is not |
|---|---|---|
| Readout gap | \(\rho=V^{s}_\pi-V^{r}_\pi\), with \(s\) having fed judgment to the loop and \(r\) sealed | A baseline gain, or evidence that capability changed |

Suggested section, placed after "Executable confirmation and adversarial
checks":

> ### Feedback channel and multi-generation ledger
>
> `evaluation_game_feedback.py` extends the single split enforced by `confirm()`
> to a sequence of generations. Sets are declared with a role and an access
> class. Events record a score reaching the loop, items reaching the loop, or an
> experimenter reading a sealed set. Malformed declarations raise, including a
> readout set not declared sealed and identifiers shared across sets. Breaches
> of a well-formed declaration are recorded instead, and move the readout
> endpoint to `not_evaluated`: a breach is a finding about the run. Reads of the
> sealed set are budgeted, since a stop-or-continue decision taken on a readout
> is itself adaptive. Identifiers detect recorded overlap. They do not certify
> independence.
>
> ```powershell
> $env:PYTHONPATH = "src"
> python scripts/verify_evaluation_game_feedback.py --output output/evaluation_game_feedback/feedback_v0_1.json
> python -m pytest tests/test_evaluation_game_feedback.py -q
> ```

## H. What is not delivered

- `Feedback` is not implemented against `hive_lab` adapters or any external
  policy. The module checks declarations and arithmetic.
- No loop with a language model has been run. The first observed-controller
  study would pair a small model with a declared selection set and a sealed
  readout, and report the ledger.
- Partial leakage, where the loop learns failure categories and not items, has
  no fixture.
- The simulations fix one parameter set each. No sweep over candidate count,
  decay rate, or label-noise rate was run.

`paper/evaluation_feedback_insertions.md`. They are JavaScript, not exact, and
involve no language model. Files are stored as run; `output/**` is not

|---|---|

| `sim2b.js`, `results2b.json` | Post hoc arm added after run 2's results were seen. Exploratory. Hashes appended to `SEAL_2.txt` afterwards. |

seal on the run.

Reproduce with plain Node, from a scratch copy so existing results are kept:

```powershell
node sim.js
node sim2.js
node sim2b.js
```

overpredicted the size of the gap between reported and true accuracy.

A re-run from a scratch copy on the same day reproduced all three results
files byte for byte.

A chart titled "Performance of GPT-6 Astra and our Internal Model on a curated
set of open math problems" plots pass rate against test-time compute on a log
scale, with error bars. Read by eye from a screenshot, the internal model runs
from about 0.26 to about 0.48 over six points and GPT-6 Astra from about 0.09 to
about 0.17 over five. The chart could not be retrieved from the page text.

The 6 October release reports 722 manuscripts in 372 result families, about
4,000 problems posed, 162 main results formalized in Lean, ten reasoning
summaries, and an average result using "the equivalent compute of roughly three
hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking." Its README says: "We expanded these evaluations
after performance on our existing mathematical evaluations saturated."
[Primary, summarized](https://openai.com/index/sharing-ai-progress-in-mathematics/);
counts from a [secondary reading of the repository](https://cellcog.ai/blog/openai-math-results/).
input.new_string:
billion output tokens, with Lean formalization taking a further 17 hours.
Two details of the run bear on feedback. Partway through, OpenAI moved the
agents to a further-trained version of the internal model. And it
cross-pollinated agent groups, using Codex to turn each group's intermediate
results into follow-up prompts; the group that found the result was guided
this way.
[Primary](https://openai.com/index/navier-stokes-solution/)

A chart titled "Performance of GPT-6 Astra and our Internal Model on a curated
set of open math problems" plots pass rate against test-time compute on a log
scale, with error bars. Its data is embedded in the page. The internal model
runs from 0.262 to 0.474 over six points, at relative compute 2.6 to 93; GPT-6
Astra runs from 0.084 to 0.170 over five points, at 1.4 to 31. Error bars are
one standard error. Every pass rate is a whole multiple of 1/382, which fits
382 scored attempts, for example 191 problems tried twice; the page does not
say which.
[Primary, embedded data](https://openai.com/index/navier-stokes-solution/)

The 6 October release reports ten reasoning summaries and an average result
using "the equivalent compute of roughly three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking."
The repository README lists 719 manuscripts in 372 families from about 4,000
problems posed, and states that roughly 42% of top-line results are formalized
in Lean; the history file gives 300 of 719. The release went out with 722
manuscripts. On 7 October a sign error led OpenAI to withdraw three and revise
fourteen others. The README also says that some outputs build on earlier
results produced by the models, and that results entered the catalogue only if
judged significant enough. Its README says: "We expanded these evaluations
after performance on our existing mathematical evaluations saturated."
[Primary](https://openai.com/index/sharing-ai-progress-in-mathematics/);
[repository](https://github.com/openai/math) and
[history](https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/history.md).

input.new_string:
1. The headline is a threshold count at one boundary of a six-level scale.
   Neither published agreement figure is the one it needs. Exact agreement,
   59%, is a lower bound on how often judge and human put a node on the same
   side of the AL3/AL4 line. Agreement within one level, 97%, does not bound it
   either way, since AL3 against AL4 is within one level. The headline needs
   agreement on that binary call and the direction of the disagreements:
   disagreements that cancel leave the share unbiased.
2. Weights come from staff weeks sampled in July 2026. Each sampled person's
   week is one unit, split evenly across the tasks they worked on. That counts
   tasks touched, not time spent, so a task that became faster does not lose
   weight for that reason. The scheme has a different blind spot: work that no
   sampled person touched in a sampled week never enters the basket. Fully
   delegated work is the most likely to be missed, so the finding that no
   subset is fully autonomous partly reflects how the basket was built.
3. It is a measurement of who does the work. It is the \(p\) of an Amdahl
   bound, not a gain per generation.

graded on a 1–6 scale, knowing the work was AI-generated: 2/6 and 1/6. Stated
limitations are five runs on two papers, non-blind grading by the original
authors, researcher degrees of freedom in question selection, possible
under-elicitation including a scaffold bug, and evaluation awareness. The
authors found no significant reward hacking, and report five instances of
subagents misrepresenting results that the orchestrator caught.
[Primary, summarized](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27191)

**Interpretation.** Using unpublished questions seals the item set against
pretraining, a choice none of the other four makes for its items. The opening
is at \(J\): the judge knows the condition and wrote the reference answer. In
the terms of the v3 protocol's provenance block, `scorer_blinded` would be
false, and there is no negative control. A human-written submission graded
under the same label would say how much of the score belongs to the label.

The models tested predate the internal model of §3. The result is silent on
that model.

**Proposed variation.** Blind grading with human-written decoys mixed in, on
more questions, with the authors of each question grading only the others'.

**Claim boundary.** Failure on two questions under an unblinded judge supports
"not demonstrated here". It does not bound what a later controller does.

## 8. What these examples add to the calculus

1. **Feedback class and ledger.** Only one case of five declares whether scores
   from a scored set reached the process being measured. The card should ask.
2. **Saturation as Hide.** A fixed suite outgrown by its subjects loses
   discrimination without any change to the game. The ceiling belongs on the
   card as a property of \(Z\).
3. **Acquisition conditioned on judgment.** Publishing what scored well makes
   \(Z\) depend on \(J\). Counts of what was attempted are then part of the
   evidence, not a courtesy.
4. **A judge that shares errors with the judged.** Agreement statistics must be
   reported at the boundary the headline is counted at.
5. **Estimand named against headline.** Amplification slope, task share,
   horizon, harness gain and open-ended failure are five different quantities.
   A statement about compounding needs a sixth, which none supplies.

The machine-readable companion is `configs/rsi_claim_cards.json`.
`scripts/verify_rsi_claims_atlas.py` verifies manifest structure and the
derived arithmetic only; its receipt is under `output/rsi_claims_atlas/`.

"""Check takeoff-claims atlas structure and derived arithmetic; no models are run."""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from fractions import Fraction as Q
from hashlib import sha256
import json
from pathlib import Path


ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
SOURCE_KINDS = {"primary", "primary_embedded_data"}
FEEDBACK_CLASSES = {"score_only", "item_level", "score_only_or_item_level", "item_level_within_run"}
REQUIRED = ("observed_contract", "what_improves", "estimand_supported", "headline_estimand",
            "missing_declarations", "proposed_axes", "independent_unit", "claim_boundary")


def _z_squared(row):
    a, sa, b, sb = (Q(value) for value in row)
    return (a - b) ** 2 / (sa ** 2 + sb ** 2)


def verify(manifest):
    checks = []

    def check(name, passed, **evidence):
        checks.append({"name": name, "passed": bool(passed), "evidence": evidence})

    cards = manifest["cards"]
    check("five_distinct_cards",
          len(cards) == manifest["cases"] == 5 and len({c["id"] for c in cards}) == 5)
    check("every_source_is_primary_and_dated",
          all(c["sources"] and all(s["kind"] in SOURCE_KINDS and s["url"].startswith("https://")
                                   and s["read_on"] == manifest["inspected_date"]
                                   for s in c["sources"]) for c in cards))
    check("sources_declared_checked_line_by_line", manifest["sources_verified_line_by_line"] is True)
    check("all_studies_explicitly_proposed",
          manifest["model_evaluations_run"] == 0
          and all(c["study_status"] == "proposed_not_executed" for c in cards))
    check("cards_carry_estimand_boundary_and_missing_declarations",
          all(all(c[key] for key in REQUIRED) for c in cards))

"""Check takeoff-claims atlas structure and derived arithmetic; no models are run."""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from fractions import Fraction as Q
from hashlib import sha256
import json
from pathlib import Path


ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
SOURCE_KINDS = {"primary_summarized", "secondary", "screenshot", "search_excerpt"}
REQUIRED = ("observed_contract", "what_improves", "estimand_supported", "headline_estimand",
            "missing_declarations", "proposed_axes", "independent_unit", "claim_boundary")


def verify(manifest):
    checks = []

    def check(name, passed, **evidence):
        checks.append({"name": name, "passed": bool(passed), "evidence": evidence})

    cards = manifest["cards"]
    check("five_distinct_cards",
          len(cards) == manifest["cases"] == 5 and len({c["id"] for c in cards}) == 5)
    check("every_source_has_a_declared_reading_level",
          all(c["sources"] and all(s["kind"] in SOURCE_KINDS and s["url"].startswith("https://")
                                   and s["read_on"] == manifest["inspected_date"]
                                   for s in c["sources"]) for c in cards))
    check("no_card_rests_on_secondary_reading_alone",
          all(any(s["kind"] == "primary_summarized" for s in c["sources"]) for c in cards))
    check("all_studies_explicitly_proposed",
          manifest["model_evaluations_run"] == 0
          and all(c["study_status"] == "proposed_not_executed" for c in cards))
    check("cards_carry_estimand_boundary_and_missing_declarations",
          all(all(c[key] for key in REQUIRED) for c in cards))
    check("headline_and_supported_estimands_differ_on_every_card",
          all(c["estimand_supported"] != c["headline_estimand"] for c in cards))
    declared = [c["id"] for c in cards
                if c["loop_present"] == "yes" and c["feedback_access_declared"]
                and c["sealed_readout_declared"] is True]
    check("one_case_declares_feedback_and_a_sealed_readout",
          len(declared) == manifest["cases_with_declared_feedback_and_sealed_readout"] == 1,
          case=declared)
    check("no_case_supplies_the_compounding_estimand",
          manifest["cases_supplying_weight_level_gain_ratio_on_sealed_readout"] == 0
          and not any(c["what_improves"].startswith("model_weights") for c in cards))

    f = manifest["derived_fixtures"]
    m = f["openai_math"]
    check("openai_ratios",
          Q(m["manuscripts"], m["problems_posed_approx"]) == Q(m["manuscripts_per_problem"])
          and Q(m["families"], m["problems_posed_approx"]) == Q(m["families_per_problem"])
          and Q(m["lean_main_results"], m["manuscripts"]) == Q(m["lean_share_of_manuscripts"])
          and Q(m["problems_posed_approx"], m["families"]) == Q(m["problems_per_family"]),
          scope="Ratios of reported counts; the problem count is approximate in the source")
    check("openai_swarm_scale",
          m["swarm_agents"] * m["swarm_hours"] == m["swarm_agent_hours_upper_bound"]
          and Q(m["output_tokens"], m["messages"]) == Q(m["tokens_per_message"]),
          tokens_per_message=float(Q(m["tokens_per_message"])))

    a = f["anthropic_index"]
    check("amdahl_ceiling_for_leads_share",
          1 / (1 - Q(a["leads_share"])) == Q(a["amdahl_ceiling_if_leads_share_free"]),
          scope="Illustrative; post-automation person-time is not a pre-automation time share")
    check("judge_agrees_with_humans_more_than_humans_agree",
          Q(a["exact_agreement_model_human"]) > Q(a["exact_agreement_human_human"])
          and a["leaves"] < a["nodes"])

    t = f["metr"]
    hours = Q(t["top_frontier_minutes"]) / 60
    check("top_frontier_point_above_stated_ceiling",
          hours == Q(t["top_frontier_hours"]) and hours > t["stated_reliable_ceiling_hours"]
          and t["exceeds_ceiling"], hours=float(hours))

    d = f["aide2"]
    steps = d["accepted_steps"]
    check("aide2_acceptance_arithmetic",
          Q(len(steps), d["proposals"]) == Q(d["acceptance_rate"])
          and (Q(d["grade_end"]) - Q(d["grade_start"])) / len(steps)
          == Q(d["mean_grade_gain_per_acceptance"])
          and [b - a_ for a_, b in zip(steps, steps[1:])] == d["acceptance_intervals"]
          and sum(s <= 49 for s in steps) == d["accepted_first_half"]
          and sum(s >= 50 for s in steps) == d["accepted_second_half"]
          and d["proposals"] - steps[-1] == d["proposals_after_last_acceptance"])
    variance = sum(v * v for v in d["ale_pm"])
    z_squared = Q(d["ale_contrast"] ** 2, variance)
    check("ale_contrast_below_conventional_threshold_if_independent_standard_errors",
          variance == d["ale_combined_variance"] and z_squared == Q(d["ale_z_squared"])
          and (z_squared < Q(196, 100) ** 2) == d["ale_below_1_96_if_independent_standard_errors"],
          z_squared=float(z_squared), scope="Conditional on what the plus-or-minus figures denote")
    check("reward_hacking_counts_consistent_with_rounded_percentages",
          all(round(100 * Q(count, d["reward_hacking_pairs"])) == pct
              for count, pct in zip(d["reward_hacking_counts_inferred"],
                                    d["reward_hacking_percentages"])),
          scope="Counts are inferred from rounding, not reported")

    p = f["princeton"]
    check("princeton_sample_is_two_questions",
          p["questions"] == len(p["scores"]) == 2 and p["runs"] == 5
          and all(1 <= s <= p["scale_max"] for s in p["scores"]))
    return checks


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("--manifest", type=Path, default=ROOT / "configs/rsi_claim_cards.json")
    parser.add_argument("--output", type=Path)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    manifest_bytes = args.manifest.read_bytes()
    checks = verify(json.loads(manifest_bytes))
    report = {
        "schema_version": "0.1",
        "generated_at_utc": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
        "evidence_status": "manifest_structure_and_exact_derived_arithmetic_only",
        "model_evaluations_run": 0,
        "sources_verified_line_by_line": False,
        "manifest_sha256": sha256(manifest_bytes).hexdigest(),
        "verifier_sha256": sha256(Path(__file__).read_bytes()).hexdigest(),
        "check_count": len(checks),
        "all_passed": all(c["passed"] for c in checks),
        "checks": checks,
    }
    serialized = json.dumps(report, indent=2) + "\n"
    if args.output:
        args.output.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        with args.output.open("x", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
            handle.write(serialized)
        print(json.dumps({"all_passed": report["all_passed"], "checks": len(checks),
                          "output": str(args.output.resolve())}))
    else:
        print(serialized)
    return 0 if report["all_passed"] else 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())
