178	   sampled person touched in a sampled week never enters the basket. Fully
179	   delegated work is the most likely to be missed, so the finding that no
180	   subset is fully autonomous partly reflects how the basket was built.
181	3. It is a measurement of who does the work. It is the \(p\) of an Amdahl
182	   bound, not a gain per generation.
183	
184	**Derived arithmetic** (illustrative only: 26% is a share of task-touch
185	weights, not of time):
186	
187	\[
188	\frac{1}{1-\tfrac{13}{50}}=\frac{50}{37}\approx1.35 .
189	\]
190	
191	That is the ceiling on overall speedup if the "leads" share became free and
192	nothing else changed.
193	
194	**Proposed variation.** Blind human re-rating of a stratified sample of nodes
195	near the AL3/AL4 boundary, with the headline reported as an interval under a
196	one-level perturbation of the judge. Separately, weights from a time-use
197	survey, compared with the task-touch weights.
198	
199	**Claim boundary.** There is no scored item set here, so feedback and readout
200	do not apply. The index supports a statement about task mix under a declared
201	judge. It does not measure whether each generation improves the next by more.
202	
203	## 5. METR's time horizon: a suite that hides by saturating
204	
205	**Observed.** Time Horizon 1.1 fits a logistic curve of success against human
206	task duration over "over a hundred diverse software tasks" from RE-Bench, HCAST
207	and shorter novel tasks, and reads off the 50% point. The page states:
208	"Measurements above 16 hrs are unreliable with our current task suite." It
209	carries a notice dated 8 September 2026 that it is no longer actively updated.
210	It mentions private tasks without giving the public/private split. METR added
211	the 16-hour notice on 8 May 2026, in the same update that added Claude Mythos
212	Preview (early).
213	[Primary](https://metr.org/time-horizons/)
214	
215	The page embeds its data. Claude Mythos Preview (early), released 7 April
216	2026, has a 50% horizon of 1044.78 minutes, with an interval of 508.9 to
217	3304.3 minutes, and an average score of 0.852 on the suite. METR's
218	fitted doubling time for models from 2023 on is 128.7 days, with an interval of
219	104.4 to 158.0; a stitched all-time fit gives 187.8 days. No fit restricted to
220	2024 onward is published. The page does not state the level of its intervals.
221	[Primary, embedded data](https://metr.org/time-horizons/)
222	
223	**Interpretation.** In the testbed's terms a saturated suite is an
224	observation-only Hide. Once a controller's ability exceeds the hardest items,
225	distinct controllers push forward to the same record, and the discrimination
226	gap between them goes to zero. No change in the game is involved.
227	
228	The suite is fixed and reused across model generations and developers, and its
229	scores are published. At the level of the field that is at least score-only
230	feedback over years. Nothing read asserts that any developer trained against
231	it. An average score of 0.852 for the top model is consistent with a suite
232	near saturation.
233	
234	**Derived arithmetic.**
235	
236	\[
237	\frac{1044.78}{60}\approx17.41\ \text{hours}>16,\qquad
238	\frac{508.9}{60}\approx8.48<16<\frac{3304.3}{60}\approx55.07 .
239	\]
240	
241	The highest frontier point lies above the bound the instrument's owner calls
242	reliable, and METR said so when it published the point. Its interval runs from
243	about half the bound to more than three times it.
244	
245	**Proposed variation.** Report, per model, the count of items above its
246	estimated ability. Extend the suite with long tasks held sealed. Declare the
247	freeze date as part of the instrument.
248	
249	**Claim boundary.** Below the ceiling the horizon supports a statement about
250	released models on this task family. Above it, neither a plateau nor an
251	acceleration is identified.
252	
253	## 6. AIDE²: the case with a declared readout
254	
255	**Observed.** An agent proposes rewrites of its own harness; candidates are
256	scored on a selection suite of ML engineering, heuristic algorithm engineering
257	and harness engineering tasks; scoring uses private data averaged into a grade.
258	Inner agents see only a public signal. The outer agent "reads the previously
259	proposed agents and their grades", and its reviewer "explores the evaluation
260	artifacts". The main run lasted eight days: one initial agent and 99 proposals,
261	seven accepted at steps 2, 6, 28, 39, 47, 63 and 85, raising the incumbent grade
262	from 0.703 to 0.778. The outer loop ran on Claude Opus 4.7 and the inner agents
263	on Gemini 3 Flash. Two further runs accepted two and four rewrites.
264	
265	Held-out reporting uses ALE-Bench (10 tasks, 10 seeds), MLE-Bench (22 tasks, 3
266	seeds), FML-Bench (18 tasks, 3 seeds) and WeatherBench 2 (1 task, 3 seeds).
267	Gains there are described as "positive throughout but not monotone"; the step-47
268	agent is best on two of the four. Reward hacking on 38 held-out KernelBench
269	pairs fell from 55% to 39% to 32%, against 39% for the human-engineered agent.
270	The authors state that the selection trace cannot show generalization because
271	candidates were selected on the grade, and that the outer loop's role "cannot
272	be decisively distinguished" from a strong baseline. The two evolved agents
273	reported on the external benchmarks are fixed by position: the incumbent within
274	the first 50 nodes (step 47) and the final incumbent (step 85). About a quarter
275	of the graded rewrites that were rejected beat the incumbent on the signal the
276	agent could see and lost on the private grade.
277	[Primary](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.26457v1)
278	
279	Table 1 reports the external benchmarks at a fixed model, with \(\pm\) one
280	standard error of the benchmark mean. On ALE-Bench the initial harness scores
281	\(1536\pm33\), step 47 \(1713\pm26\) and step 85 \(1790\pm9\). A separate
282	comparison across models, at a $20 budget per run, has Gemini 3 Flash with the
283	step-85 harness at \(1858\pm22\) against Fable 5 with the initial harness at
284	\(1796\pm24\). On MLE-Bench, with Fable 5, the step-85 harness is within one
285	standard error of the initial one.
286	
287	**Interpretation.** This is the only case of the five that separates a
288	selection set from a readout and says which numbers came from which. In ledger
289	terms:
290	
291	- Selection set: one fixed suite, 99 score queries. Declared access is at least
292	  score-only; the reviewer's reading of evaluation artifacts may make it
293	  item-level. The rise from 0.703 to 0.778 is a selection score.
294	- Readout: four external benchmarks, read at two evolved checkpoints chosen by
295	  position, not by readout score. Both are reported on every benchmark, not the
296	  best per benchmark, which is the reporting a ledger asks for. Whether the

## 5. METR's time horizon: a suite that hides by saturating

**Observed.** Time Horizon 1.1 fits a logistic curve of success against human
task duration over "over a hundred diverse software tasks" from RE-Bench, HCAST
and shorter novel tasks, and reads off the 50% point. The page states:
"Measurements above 16 hrs are unreliable with our current task suite." It
carries a notice dated 8 September 2026 that it is no longer actively updated.
It mentions private tasks without giving the public/private split. METR added
the 16-hour notice on 8 May 2026, in the same update that added Claude Mythos
Preview (early).
[Primary](https://metr.org/time-horizons/)

The page embeds its data. Claude Mythos Preview (early), released 7 April
2026, has a 50% horizon of 1044.78 minutes, with an interval of 508.9 to
3304.3 minutes, and an average score of 0.852 on the suite. METR's
fitted doubling time for models from 2023 on is 128.7 days, with an interval of
104.4 to 158.0; a stitched all-time fit gives 187.8 days. No fit restricted to
2024 onward is published. The page does not state the level of its intervals.
[Primary, embedded data](https://metr.org/time-horizons/)

**Interpretation.** In the testbed's terms a saturated suite is an
observation-only Hide. Once a controller's ability exceeds the hardest items,
distinct controllers push forward to the same record, and the discrimination
gap between them goes to zero. No change in the game is involved.

The suite is fixed and reused across model generations and developers, and its
scores are published. At the level of the field that is at least score-only
feedback over years. Nothing read asserts that any developer trained against
it. An average score of 0.852 for the top model is consistent with a suite
near saturation.

**Derived arithmetic.**

\[
\frac{1044.78}{60}\approx17.41\ \text{hours}>16,\qquad
\frac{508.9}{60}\approx8.48<16<\frac{3304.3}{60}\approx55.07 .
\]

The highest frontier point lies above the bound the instrument's owner calls
reliable, and METR said so when it published the point. Its interval runs from
about half the bound to more than three times it.

**Proposed variation.** Report, per model, the count of items above its
estimated ability. Extend the suite with long tasks held sealed. Declare the
freeze date as part of the instrument.

**Claim boundary.** Below the ceiling the horizon supports a statement about
released models on this task family. Above it, neither a plateau nor an
acceleration is identified.

## 6. AIDE²: the case with a declared readout

**Observed.** An agent proposes rewrites of its own harness; candidates are
scored on a selection suite of ML engineering, heuristic algorithm engineering
and harness engineering tasks; scoring uses private data averaged into a grade.
Inner agents see only a public signal. The outer agent "reads the previously
proposed agents and their grades", and its reviewer "explores the evaluation
artifacts". The main run lasted eight days: one initial agent and 99 proposals,
seven accepted at steps 2, 6, 28, 39, 47, 63 and 85, raising the incumbent grade
from 0.703 to 0.778. The outer loop ran on Claude Opus 4.7 and the inner agents
on Gemini 3 Flash. Two further runs accepted two and four rewrites.

Held-out reporting uses ALE-Bench (10 tasks, 10 seeds), MLE-Bench (22 tasks, 3
seeds), FML-Bench (18 tasks, 3 seeds) and WeatherBench 2 (1 task, 3 seeds).
Gains there are described as "positive throughout but not monotone"; the step-47
agent is best on two of the four. Reward hacking on 38 held-out KernelBench
pairs fell from 55% to 39% to 32%, against 39% for the human-engineered agent.
The authors state that the selection trace cannot show generalization because
candidates were selected on the grade, and that the outer loop's role "cannot
be decisively distinguished" from a strong baseline. The two evolved agents
reported on the external benchmarks are fixed by position: the incumbent within
the first 50 nodes (step 47) and the final incumbent (step 85). About a quarter
of the graded rewrites that were rejected beat the incumbent on the signal the
agent could see and lost on the private grade.
[Primary](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.26457v1)

Table 1 reports the external benchmarks at a fixed model, with \(\pm\) one
standard error of the benchmark mean. On ALE-Bench the initial harness scores
\(1536\pm33\), step 47 \(1713\pm26\) and step 85 \(1790\pm9\). A separate
comparison across models, at a $20 budget per run, has Gemini 3 Flash with the
step-85 harness at \(1858\pm22\) against Fable 5 with the initial harness at
\(1796\pm24\). On MLE-Bench, with Fable 5, the step-85 harness is within one
standard error of the initial one.

**Interpretation.** This is the only case of the five that separates a
selection set from a readout and says which numbers came from which. In ledger
terms:

- Selection set: one fixed suite, 99 score queries. Declared access is at least
  score-only; the reviewer's reading of evaluation artifacts may make it
  item-level. The rise from 0.703 to 0.778 is a selection score.
- Readout: four external benchmarks, read at two evolved checkpoints chosen by
  position, not by readout score. Both are reported on every benchmark, not the
  best per benchmark, which is the reporting a ledger asks for. Whether the
  positions were fixed before the run is not stated.
- The quarter of rejected rewrites that won on the visible signal and lost on
  the private grade measures how far the loop's two signals diverge. It is the
  within-task analogue of the readout gap.
- What improves is the harness. The model is frozen, so this is not evidence
  about weights improving weights.

**Derived arithmetic.**

\[
\frac{7}{99}\approx0.071,\qquad
\frac{0.778-0.703}{7}=\frac{3}{280}\approx0.0107 .
\]

Intervals between acceptances are 4, 22, 11, 8, 16 and 22 steps; five of the
seven fall in steps 1–49 and two in steps 50–99, with none in the last 14.

**Reading note.** Draft 0.1 was written from a fetch tool that returns a
summary of each page, with one chart read by eye from a screenshot and several
figures taken from secondary pages. For draft 0.2 every figure attributed to a
source below was checked against the source's full text in a browser, or
against the data embedded in the source's page. The secondary pages and the
screenshot are superseded and no longer cited. §9 lists what the check changed.
Source levels are marked per case:

- *primary*: the publisher's own page, paper or repository, read in full.
- *primary, embedded data*: the data behind a chart or table on the
  publisher's page.

## 1. The question put to each case

A forecast of compounding needs one estimand: the gain from one generation of
controllers to the next, repeated, on a readout the improvement process did not
touch. In the notation of the insertions, that is a series of \(V^{r}_{\pi_g}\)
with \(r\) sealed, together with a ledger showing that it stayed sealed.

| Card field | What to look for in a takeoff claim |
|---|---|
| \(\Pi\) | What improves: weights, harness, test-time budget, or the mix of who does the work |
| \(D\) | How scored items were chosen, and whether the choice followed a look at results |
| \(Z\) | Whether what was kept depends on how it scored |
| \(J\) | Who or what judges, and whether the judge shares errors with the judged |
| Feedback | Whether scores or items from the scored set reached the improvement process |
| Readout | Whether any reported number comes from a set declared sealed |
| \(C\) | Which estimand the evidence supports, as against the one the headline implies |

## 2. The example set

| Case | Source level | What improves | Scored set fed back? | Sealed readout declared? | Estimand supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| OpenAI internal model, mathematics | primary; chart from embedded data | Test-time compute at one checkpoint; the controller was also replaced during the run | Within the run, yes; into training, not stated | No | Amplification slope |
| Anthropic R&D Automation Index | primary | Share of work led by the model | Not applicable | Not applicable | Task-share under a learned judge |
| METR time horizon | primary; values from embedded data | Released models over years | Not stated; suite reused | No | Horizon on a fixed suite, below its ceiling |
| AIDE² harness self-improvement | primary | Agent harness, model frozen | Yes, by design | Yes, four external benchmarks | Held-out gain across harness generations |
| Princeton-led (CRUX) shadow evaluation | primary | Nothing; a single-generation test | No loop | Yes, against pretraining | Failure on two open-ended questions under one judge |

None of the five supplies a generation-over-generation gain ratio for model
weights on a sealed readout. The fourth comes closest, at the level of the
harness, and its held-out gains at a fixed model are large relative to their
standard errors.

RSI atlas 0.2: line-level source check; ceiling law for targeted patching

Draft 0.1 of the atlas was written from a summarizing fetch tool, a
screenshot and secondary pages. Every figure it attributes to a source was
checked against the full text, or the data embedded in the source page, and
the secondary citations are dropped. Changes:

- OpenAI: 719 manuscripts after three withdrawals on 2026-10-07 (722 at
  release); about 42% of top-line results in Lean (300/719), not 162/722.
  The run declares within-run feedback and replaced its model partway.
  Chart values come from the page's Vega-Lite data (multiples of 1/382).
- Anthropic: weights split each sampled person-week evenly across tasks,
  so the "fast task weighs less" mechanism is withdrawn; 59% exact
  agreement is a lower bound at the AL3/AL4 line, not the needed figure.
- METR: doubling time 128.7 days from 2023 on (104.4-158.0), from METR's
  data; the 131/89-day figures came from a market page. The top point's
  interval (8.5-55 h) straddles the 16 h bound.
- AIDE-squared: plus-or-minus is one standard error; the 1.90-SE contrast
  is cross-model, while fixed-model gains are 2.6-7.4 SE. Readout
  checkpoints are two, fixed by position.
- Princeton-led study: interventions and affiliations noted.

The cards manifest and verifier follow (28 checks, receipt regenerated).
A mutation test confirms the verifier rejects the draft 0.1 count and the
89-day doubling time.

Feedback module: the ceiling threshold 8/13 holds for memorization chosen
independently of outcomes. Item-level feedback patches failures, and then
the check is silent only below 4/25 of the set (8/13 of the failures).
Adds targeted_patch_selection_score and
targeted_ceiling_detection_threshold, one test, one verify() check, and
the matching text in the insertions (draft 0.2). Receipt now
feedback_v0_2.json.

Toy-run README: run 1 reproduces to its reported precision but not to the
byte on Node 24.19 under Windows (24 values differ in the last digit).

content.text:
Yes, partly, and mostly on my side.

**What stayed on target.** The feedback module and the insertions are mathematics of the notation. They propose a new operator, Feedback_{s,q}, with three access classes and three laws:
- **Coarsening law:** item-level, score-only and sealed feedback are successively coarser, so what the loop can learn about its failures can only shrink down that order.
- **Selection law:** keeping the best of several candidates and reporting its score overstates, with an exact one-generation gap that tends to 1/(2√(πn)).
- **Ceiling law:** a check for scores above the label-noise ceiling stays silent until enough of the set has been memorized.

They also define a readout-gap estimand. My one mathematical contribution was the ceiling-law correction: a loop that patches its failures crosses the ceiling after 4/25 of the set, against 8/13 under random memorization.

**What went afield.** The atlas applies the notation to five published claims. Most of my effort in this session went into fact-checking that atlas's sources: OpenAI's counts, METR's doubling times, Anthropic's weighting. That checked claims about the world, not the notation. It mattered because the other session was asking whether to push to a public repo, but it did nothing for your research question. I should have said so before offering to do it.

**What the detour turned up for the notation.** Three points are worth keeping:
- **Controller swap:** OpenAI changed its model partway through a run. The calculus has no way to say the controller changed inside a generation; the carry map assumes it changes only between generations.
- **Visible vs. hidden signal:** in AIDE², about a quarter of rejected rewrites scored better on the signal the agent could see and worse on the private grade. That is a within-task version of the readout gap, and could be defined formally.
- **Counts at a boundary:** a headline counted at one level boundary needs agreement on which side of the line each item falls. Exact agreement only bounds that from below. This belongs with the judge-related laws in §5.

**Getting back to the mathematics.** These are the open problems, in the order I'd take them:
1. **Partial leakage as a lattice.** The insertions list partial leakage (the loop sees categories of failure, not items) as having no fixture. Each partition of the items gives its own access class, and the classes are ordered by refinement. The coarsening law should extend to the whole lattice as a data-processing inequality. This is small, exact, and closes a gap the insertions name.
2. **Multi-generation selection gap.** The exact results stop at one generation, and accumulation across generations exists only in the simulations. An exact result for reusing the same set over several generations is the quantity a compounding claim needs, and it's the main open problem.
3. **Feedback's laws with the other operators.** How Feedback composes with Repeat, Hide and Rescore, and which of those orderings commute.

I'd start with 1 as a warm-up that yields a clean theorem, then put the real effort into 2. Want me to start on the lattice?

1	# Evaluation-game estimands and incentive-response testbed
2	
3	## Scope
4	
5	This is a small exact, finite synthetic testbed. It does not call a model,
6	collect transcripts, simulate interacting agents, or identify strategic intent.
7	It builds on the separation among game, case distribution, measurement, and
8	claim in [evaluation_design_calculus.md](evaluation_design_calculus.md). It
9	does not alter the frozen v3 sandbagging results or protocol.
10	
11	```powershell
12	$env:PYTHONPATH = "src"
13	python scripts/verify_evaluation_game_testbed.py --output output/evaluation_game_testbed.json
14	python -m pytest tests/test_evaluation_game_testbed.py -q
15	```
16	
17	The output is exact synthetic fixture evidence, not model or agent evidence.
18	It stores rational values as strings and will not overwrite an existing output.
19	
20	## Four non-interchangeable estimands
21	
22	Fix \(\mathcal E=\langle G,\Pi,D,Z,J,\mathcal A,C\rangle\). A score alone
23	does not say which object changed.
24	
25	| Estimand | Definition | It is not |
26	|---|---|---|
27	| Baseline gain | \(B=V_{\pi_1}(d)-V_{\pi_0}(d)\) with a named case law and judgment | Robustness or strategic stability |
28	| Robust regret | \(R(\pi;\mathcal Q)=\max_{q\in\mathcal Q}[\max_{\pi'}V_{\pi'}(q)-V_\pi(q)]\) | A baseline gain or a measurement gap |
29	| Discrimination gap | \(\mathrm{TV}(Z_\#P_{\pi_1},Z_\#P_{\pi_0})\) | Utility, regret, or player information |
30	| Exploitability | \(\max_i[\sup_{\pi_i'}\mathbb EU_i(\pi_i',\pi_{-i})-\mathbb EU_i(\pi)]\) | Generalization or welfare |
31	
32	The finite fixtures make baseline gain and robust regret both one half. Their
33	matching numbers are intentional: their source objects and interpretation remain
34	different, so they must not be combined or relabeled as each other.
35	Both policies in the corrected baseline fixture receive the revealed state:
36	the baseline always chooses left and the candidate follows the observation.
37	The game and case law are consequently fixed for that comparison.
38	
39	## Observation-only Hide versus player-facing hiding
40	
41	Observation-only `Hide` belongs to acquisition. After players act, apply a
42	common Markov kernel \(H(z'\mid z)\) to each completed record:
43	
44	\[
45	P_H(z'\mid\pi)=\sum_z H(z'\mid z)P(z\mid\pi).
46	\]
47	
48	It does not change legal actions, player histories, transitions, or payoffs.
49	In the fixture, perfectly correct and perfectly wrong traces have visible
50	total-variation discrimination gap one. The common kernel maps both to
51	`redacted`, leaving an acquired-record gap of zero and demonstrating finite
52	data processing: \(\mathrm{TV}(H_\#P,H_\#Q)\leq\mathrm{TV}(P,Q)\).
53	
54	Removing information from a player before action instead changes \(O_i\) in
55	\(G\). In the two-location game, the optimal value falls from one to one half.
56	That is a game intervention, not offline measurement redaction. An adapter that
57	removes player feedback must type it that way irrespective of its method name.
58	
59	## Strategic checks, costs, and falsifiers
60	
61	The social-dilemma fixture enumerates a pure equilibrium set and reports the
62	selected outcome under `enumerate_pure_nash_then_lexicographically_select`; it
63	does not present the outcome as controller behavior. At `share, share`, exact
64	exploitability is two. Searching only the `share` deviation returns zero, which
65	is marked as a lower bound rather than exploitability. A matching-pennies
66	fixture separately checks equal primal maximin and dual minimax witnesses at
67	zero. It is not a generic equilibrium solver.
68	
69	Falsifiers for an applied strategic interpretation are an illegal deviation
70	class, private state leaked to the search, an unspecified adaptation or
71	equilibrium-selection rule, dependent payoff estimates, or calling a restricted
72	search exact exploitability. Report the restriction and withhold that stronger
73	claim when any appears.
74	
75	## Incentive-response design for sandbagging investigation
76	
77	The estimand is a behavioral incentive-response contrast, not intent. Let
78	\(Y_{c,d,g}\) be a blinded score with condition \(c\), difficulty \(d\), and
79	grader-severity stratum \(g\):
80	
81	\[
82	Y=\mu+\alpha_c+\beta_d+\gamma_g+\eta_{c,d}+\varepsilon.
83	\]
84	
85	Match paired control/incentive tasks within \((d,g)\), estimate
86	\(\tau_d=\mathbb E[Y_{0,d,g}-Y_{1,d,g}]\), and reserve untouched blocks to
87	test \(\iota=\tau_{hard}-\tau_{easy}\). Pairing cancels additive difficulty
88	and grader severity; it does not establish prompt equivalence or intent.
89	Selection of strata, allocation, and any target family remains in training data;
90	the interaction is tested only in the held-out confirmation data.
91	
92	For acquisition, condition 0 gives the ordinary task and performance objective;
93	condition 1 adds a preregistered evaluation-contingent incentive frame while
94	holding task instructions, tools, time budget, scoring rubric, and stated role
95	fixed. The frame is shown to the participant before acting, so it is a
96	presentation/incentive intervention on the game, not observation-only Hide.
97	Use held-out isomorphic task forms matched by difficulty calibrated on separate
98	data; randomize form-to-condition and AB/BA order in reset contexts. A negative
99	control uses comparably sized neutral framing with no changed incentive. This
100	design checks sensitivity to the chosen frame, not compliance with an assumed
101	internal utility function. Semantic equivalence must be reviewed independently.
102	
103	Estimate grader severity on independent anchor responses with condition labels
104	removed. Cross each grader/severity stratum with both conditions and both
105	difficulties using the same rubric and version; do not assign strict graders
106	only to the incentive arm. Save response, form, block, assignment, scorer, and
107	calibration identifiers. Difficulty- or condition-dependent grading errors
108	require an expanded nuisance model and separate checks. The executable fixture
109	encodes known additive severity, not estimated severity or verified blinding.
110	
111	The fixture has four equal-weight equal-variance strata and a 96-score budget.
112	Each matched pair costs two scored responses. It enumerates the 48-pair integer
113	allocation minimizing \(\sum_h(1/4)^2/n_h\) and obtains 12 pairs per stratum.
114	This optimization is conditional on its equal-variance and equal-cost premise.
115	In an applied study, preregister variance/cost estimates, retain minimum stratum
116	coverage, and use the resulting Neyman-style allocation without holdout tuning.
117	
118	The fixture deliberately has no latent intent variable and records
119	`intent_identified: false`. A contrast can arise from strategic response, benign
120	role constraints, task changes, condition-dependent scoring, or distribution
121	shift. Falsifiers include an interaction in negative-incentive controls, failed
122	prompt-equivalence review, unblinded scoring, grader severity not linked within
123	pairs, or a selection/holdout block overlap. Any falsifier defeats the strategic
124	interpretation; it is not evidence of a zero effect.
125	
126	## Executable confirmation and adversarial checks
127	
128	`evaluation_game_confirmation.py` now enforces the split on actual synthetic
129	pair and block records. Every block contains all four difficulty/grader strata.
130	Duplicate pairs, missing strata, mixed block metadata, reused training IDs,
131	and confirmation of a different family all raise errors. The selected family
132	is chosen by training mean gap with lexical ties, before confirmation rows are
133	generated. Identifiers can detect recorded overlap; they cannot independently
134	certify independence or prevent an operator from relabeling reused observations.
135	
136	The saved fixture has two families with eight training blocks each (64 pairs,
137	128 score operations), then 12 target and 12 negative-control blocks for the
138	selected family (96 pairs, 192 score operations). The total is **320**. These
139	are constructed score values, not paid model calls or independent model trials.
140	The older four-cell arithmetic illustration records eight score values and a
141	separate *planned* 96-score target allocation; that plan is not an acquisition
142	receipt. Calibration, prompt review, and scorer qualification costs remain
143	outside this synthetic count and must be budgeted for an observed study.
144	
145	Each confirmation block produces an equal-weight incentive-response contrast
146	and a hard-minus-easy interaction. Two exact two-sided sign tests receive
147	alpha/2 each, with ties discarded. These test directional consistency under
148	independent blocks and equiprobable nonzero signs under the null; they do not
149	test the population mean. The fixture reports the arithmetic means separately.
150	Its interaction is 1/5, with sign p-value 1/2048 across 12 positive blocks.
151	This deterministic positive fixture does not measure statistical coverage or
152	false-positive rates. Training-only effects return a holdout p-value of one.
153	This budget covers one selected-family evaluation. Multiple subjects or added

# Evaluation-game estimands and incentive-response testbed

## Scope

This is a small exact, finite synthetic testbed. It does not call a model,
collect transcripts, simulate interacting agents, or identify strategic intent.
It builds on the separation among game, case distribution, measurement, and
claim in [evaluation_design_calculus.md](evaluation_design_calculus.md). It
does not alter the frozen v3 sandbagging results or protocol.

```powershell
$env:PYTHONPATH = "src"
python scripts/verify_evaluation_game_testbed.py --output output/evaluation_game_testbed.json
python -m pytest tests/test_evaluation_game_testbed.py -q
```

The output is exact synthetic fixture evidence, not model or agent evidence.
It stores rational values as strings and will not overwrite an existing output.

## Four non-interchangeable estimands

Fix \(\mathcal E=\langle G,\Pi,D,Z,J,\mathcal A,C\rangle\). A score alone
does not say which object changed.

| Estimand | Definition | It is not |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline gain | \(B=V_{\pi_1}(d)-V_{\pi_0}(d)\) with a named case law and judgment | Robustness or strategic stability |
| Robust regret | \(R(\pi;\mathcal Q)=\max_{q\in\mathcal Q}[\max_{\pi'}V_{\pi'}(q)-V_\pi(q)]\) | A baseline gain or a measurement gap |
| Discrimination gap | \(\mathrm{TV}(Z_\#P_{\pi_1},Z_\#P_{\pi_0})\) | Utility, regret, or player information |
| Exploitability | \(\max_i[\sup_{\pi_i'}\mathbb EU_i(\pi_i',\pi_{-i})-\mathbb EU_i(\pi)]\) | Generalization or welfare |

The finite fixtures make baseline gain and robust regret both one half. Their
matching numbers are intentional: their source objects and interpretation remain
different, so they must not be combined or relabeled as each other.
Both policies in the corrected baseline fixture receive the revealed state:
the baseline always chooses left and the candidate follows the observation.
The game and case law are consequently fixed for that comparison.

## Observation-only Hide versus player-facing hiding

Observation-only `Hide` belongs to acquisition. After players act, apply a
common Markov kernel \(H(z'\mid z)\) to each completed record:

\[
P_H(z'\mid\pi)=\sum_z H(z'\mid z)P(z\mid\pi).
\]

It does not change legal actions, player histories, transitions, or payoffs.
In the fixture, perfectly correct and perfectly wrong traces have visible
total-variation discrimination gap one. The common kernel maps both to
`redacted`, leaving an acquired-record gap of zero and demonstrating finite
data processing: \(\mathrm{TV}(H_\#P,H_\#Q)\leq\mathrm{TV}(P,Q)\).

Removing information from a player before action instead changes \(O_i\) in
\(G\). In the two-location game, the optimal value falls from one to one half.
That is a game intervention, not offline measurement redaction. An adapter that
removes player feedback must type it that way irrespective of its method name.

## Strategic checks, costs, and falsifiers

The social-dilemma fixture enumerates a pure equilibrium set and reports the
selected outcome under `enumerate_pure_nash_then_lexicographically_select`; it
does not present the outcome as controller behavior. At `share, share`, exact
exploitability is two. Searching only the `share` deviation returns zero, which
is marked as a lower bound rather than exploitability. A matching-pennies
fixture separately checks equal primal maximin and dual minimax witnesses at
zero. It is not a generic equilibrium solver.

Falsifiers for an applied strategic interpretation are an illegal deviation
class, private state leaked to the search, an unspecified adaptation or
equilibrium-selection rule, dependent payoff estimates, or calling a restricted
search exact exploitability. Report the restriction and withhold that stronger
claim when any appears.

## Incentive-response design for sandbagging investigation

The estimand is a behavioral incentive-response contrast, not intent. Let
\(Y_{c,d,g}\) be a blinded score with condition \(c\), difficulty \(d\), and
grader-severity stratum \(g\):

\[
Y=\mu+\alpha_c+\beta_d+\gamma_g+\eta_{c,d}+\varepsilon.
\]

Match paired control/incentive tasks within \((d,g)\), estimate
\(\tau_d=\mathbb E[Y_{0,d,g}-Y_{1,d,g}]\), and reserve untouched blocks to
test \(\iota=\tau_{hard}-\tau_{easy}\). Pairing cancels additive difficulty
and grader severity; it does not establish prompt equivalence or intent.
Selection of strata, allocation, and any target family remains in training data;
the interaction is tested only in the held-out confirmation data.

For acquisition, condition 0 gives the ordinary task and performance objective;
condition 1 adds a preregistered evaluation-contingent incentive frame while
holding task instructions, tools, time budget, scoring rubric, and stated role
fixed. The frame is shown to the participant before acting, so it is a
presentation/incentive intervention on the game, not observation-only Hide.
Use held-out isomorphic task forms matched by difficulty calibrated on separate
data; randomize form-to-condition and AB/BA order in reset contexts. A negative
control uses comparably sized neutral framing with no changed incentive. This
design checks sensitivity to the chosen frame, not compliance with an assumed
internal utility function. Semantic equivalence must be reviewed independently.

Estimate grader severity on independent anchor responses with condition labels
removed. Cross each grader/severity stratum with both conditions and both
difficulties using the same rubric and version; do not assign strict graders
only to the incentive arm. Save response, form, block, assignment, scorer, and
calibration identifiers. Difficulty- or condition-dependent grading errors
require an expanded nuisance model and separate checks. The executable fixture
encodes known additive severity, not estimated severity or verified blinding.

The fixture has four equal-weight equal-variance strata and a 96-score budget.
Each matched pair costs two scored responses. It enumerates the 48-pair integer
allocation minimizing \(\sum_h(1/4)^2/n_h\) and obtains 12 pairs per stratum.
This optimization is conditional on its equal-variance and equal-cost premise.
In an applied study, preregister variance/cost estimates, retain minimum stratum
coverage, and use the resulting Neyman-style allocation without holdout tuning.

The fixture deliberately has no latent intent variable and records
`intent_identified: false`. A contrast can arise from strategic response, benign
role constraints, task changes, condition-dependent scoring, or distribution
shift. Falsifiers include an interaction in negative-incentive controls, failed
prompt-equivalence review, unblinded scoring, grader severity not linked within
pairs, or a selection/holdout block overlap. Any falsifier defeats the strategic
interpretation; it is not evidence of a zero effect.

## Executable confirmation and adversarial checks

`evaluation_game_confirmation.py` now enforces the split on actual synthetic
pair and block records. Every block contains all four difficulty/grader strata.
Duplicate pairs, missing strata, mixed block metadata, reused training IDs,
and confirmation of a different family all raise errors. The selected family
is chosen by training mean gap with lexical ties, before confirmation rows are
generated. Identifiers can detect recorded overlap; they cannot independently
certify independence or prevent an operator from relabeling reused observations.

The saved fixture has two families with eight training blocks each (64 pairs,
128 score operations), then 12 target and 12 negative-control blocks for the
selected family (96 pairs, 192 score operations). The total is **320**. These
are constructed score values, not paid model calls or independent model trials.
The older four-cell arithmetic illustration records eight score values and a
separate *planned* 96-score target allocation; that plan is not an acquisition
receipt. Calibration, prompt review, and scorer qualification costs remain
outside this synthetic count and must be budgeted for an observed study.

Each confirmation block produces an equal-weight incentive-response contrast
and a hard-minus-easy interaction. Two exact two-sided sign tests receive
alpha/2 each, with ties discarded. These test directional consistency under
independent blocks and equiprobable nonzero signs under the null; they do not
test the population mean. The fixture reports the arithmetic means separately.
Its interaction is 1/5, with sign p-value 1/2048 across 12 positive blocks.
This deterministic positive fixture does not measure statistical coverage or
false-positive rates. Training-only effects return a holdout p-value of one.
This budget covers one selected-family evaluation. Multiple subjects or added
confirmatory contrasts require a frozen campaign correction; do not reuse the
same alpha independently for each subject or retune on confirmation outcomes.

Negative controls must have exactly zero paired differences for this fixture's
support flag. This is an arithmetic diagnostic, not an empirical equivalence
test; observed controls would need uncertainty, tolerance margins, adequate
sample sizes, and a preregistered inference procedure. A control bias withholds
the support flag. Passing that flag still leaves `intent_identified: false`.

The allocation optimizer solves the finite integer problem with supplied
weights, paired-difference variances, pair costs, budget, and minimum stratum
counts. Independent exhaustive enumeration checks it with unequal costs and
variances. Its variance objective assumes independent strata. Covariances of
contrasts measured in common blocks require a different objective; the block
confirmation fixture is not claimed to attain that independent-stratum bound.

Additional checks cover 625 rational binary distribution/channel combinations
for total-variation contraction, malformed kernel rejection, and a falsifier
where different policy-specific channels manufacture discrimination. A general
finite matrix certificate reports primal and dual bounds and refuses to certify
an inferior matching-pennies strategy. A coordination-game example reports its
complete Nash set (two pure profiles and one uniformly mixed profile) alongside
two explicit update paths: simultaneous best responses cycle from (0,1), while
row-then-column updates reach (1,1). The former equilibrium enumeration rule is
a selection convention; these new paths supply actual finite adaptation rules.

The verifier's schema 1.1 includes confirmation, allocation, adaptation, and
primal/dual results and source hashes. Run the expanded regressions with:

```powershell
python -m pytest tests/test_evaluation_game_testbed.py tests/test_evaluation_game_confirmation.py -q
```

1	# A calculus of evaluation design
2	
3	Version 0.1 — 2026-09-11. A proposed synthesis for Spiral.
4	
5	**An evaluation is a designed game, a population of controllers, and an evidence-producing experiment.** Its notation should expose what can be composed, what a transformation preserves, and what the observations support. This document connects game-design concepts to a small mathematical core. It does not claim a universal algebra of games or a validated measure of general intelligence.
6	
7	The accompanying exact examples are in `configs/evaluation_design_calculus_examples.json`; `scripts/verify_evaluation_design_calculus.py` checks their arithmetic and selected finite instances of the laws. These are mathematical fixtures, not model evaluations. Existing Spiral campaigns remain unchanged.
8	
9	For applications to published environments, see the [Prime Intellect example atlas](prime_intellect_eval_atlas.md), including proof feedback, 2048 interfaces, simulated users, poker, and learned judges.
10	
11	## 1. What the literature contributes
12	
13	| Foundation | Established contribution | Our adaptation |
14	|---|---|---|
15	| [Hunicke, LeBlanc, and Zubek, MDA (2004)](https://www.cs.northwestern.edu/~hunicke/MDA.pdf) | Distinguishes mechanics, their runtime dynamics, and players' aesthetic experience. | Separate specified mechanisms from observed behavior and the capability claim. This is an adaptation; evidence is not a replacement definition of MDA's aesthetics. |
16	| [Juul, emergence and progression (2002)](https://jesperjuul.net/text/openandtheclosed.html) | Distinguishes interacting rules that generate varied play from prescribed sequences of challenges. | Record whether success requires particular steps or allows alternative successful strategies. |
17	| [Sicart, game mechanics (2008)](https://www.gamestudies.org/0802/articles/sicart) | Analyzes mechanics as methods by which agents interact with a game world. | Give mechanics action types, legal preconditions, and state effects. |
18	| [Dormans, Machinations (2011)](https://pure.hva.nl/ws/portalfiles/portal/141880/556168_dormans_simulating_mechanics.pdf) | Represents resource flows and feedback structures in game economies. | Use explicit resource ledgers, flow constraints, and local response analysis. |
19	| [Operational logics, UCSC research group](https://eis.ucsc.edu/analyses-and-approaches/operational-logics/) | Connects abstract computational operations with their communicative role. | Keep state semantics and their presentation to the participant separately inspectable. |
20	| [Piette et al., Ludii (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.05013) | Describes games through composable, understandable game concepts called ludemes. | Define reusable evaluation primitives such as inspection, commitment, resource transfer, and termination. These are our primitives, not a claimed Ludii extension. |
21	| [Thielscher, GDL-II (2010)](https://cgi.cse.unsw.edu.au/~mit/Papers/AAAI10a.pdf) | Extends formal game descriptions to nondeterminism and restricted information. | Specify legal actions, transitions, private observations, and termination independently. |
22	| [Ghani et al., compositional game theory (2018)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.04641) | Uses open games with sequential and parallel composition, including strategic context. | Borrow the insistence on typed interfaces; distinguish execution composition from composition of strategic incentives. |
23	| [Nash (1950)](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.36.1.48), [Harsanyi (1967)](https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/abs/10.1287/mnsc.14.3.159) | Equilibrium under unilateral deviations; games with private types and beliefs. | State a strategic reference model and measure deviation opportunities without assuming observed agents optimize the assigned payoff. |
24	
25	The tuple, operator names, effect annotations, design derivatives, and project mappings below are our proposed synthesis. The linear algebra, probability composition, inclusion–exclusion identities, and elementary equilibrium calculations are standard mathematical constructions applied here. Their general applicability does not follow merely from their game-design inspiration.
26	
27	## 2. Three objects, three kinds of claim
28	
29	Write an evaluation as
30	
31	\[
32	\mathcal E=\langle G,\Pi,D,Z,J,\mathcal A,C\rangle.
33	\]
34	
35	- \(G\): game specification.
36	- \(\Pi\): the controller roster and execution protocol, including model or policy, instructions, memory, tools, decoding, retries, and resource budgets.
37	- \(D\): sampling and assignment of game instances, counterparts, conditions, and independent run blocks.
38	- \(Z\): evidence acquisition; what the evaluator observes and records.
39	- \(J\): judgment of an acquired trace.
40	- \(\mathcal A\): aggregation and uncertainty procedure.
41	- \(C\): claim, target population, and assumptions required for interpretation.
42	
43	One run produces a full trajectory \(\tau\), an acquired record \(z\), and a judgment \(y\):
44	
45	\[
46	\tau\sim P_{G,\Pi,D},\qquad z\sim Z(\cdot\mid\tau),\qquad y=J(z).
47	\]
48	
49	Aggregation operates across declared independent blocks, not automatically across every action or message. The claim is an interpretation of the experiment, not another deterministic output of the state machine.
50	
51	Use this game record:
52	
53	\[
54	G=\langle N,X,\Theta,p_0,\{A_i,O_i\}_{i\in N},T,U,H,F\rangle.
55	\]
56	
57	Here \(N\) is the player set, \(X\) the world state, \(\Theta\) private types, \(p_0\) their joint initial distribution with the state, \(A_i\) legal moves, \(O_i\) observation channels, \(T\) transitions, \(U\) assigned trajectory utilities, \(H\) the stopping rule, and \(F\) the presentation layer. A turn scheduler can be encoded in the state, with inactive players given a no-op. Information includes any feedback from legality checks, errors, timing, and rewards.
58	
59	A controller acts from its accessible history: \(\pi_i(a_i\mid h_i)\). A privileged experiment recorder may inspect the full trajectory; a player must not receive that trajectory accidentally through its integration wrapper. A fixed scripted counterparty is part of the environment from the focal player's perspective. Merely naming it a second agent does not make the run evidence of mutual strategic adaptation.
60	
61	Maintain three distinctions:
62	
63	1. Assigned utility \(U_i\) specifies a game-theoretic objective; a controller's actual optimization of it is an empirical question.
64	2. Judgment \(J\) can measure welfare, accuracy, or cost separately from that utility. If judgment is shown during play or used for learning, it also enters observations or controller updates.
65	3. Claim \(C\) can concern mechanism feasibility, a particular controller, or a target population. These require different evidence.
66	
67	## 3. A design grammar with effect annotations
68	
69	Give each transformation a signature, preconditions, scope, and read/write footprint. Denote a valid application by
70	
71	\[
72	\Gamma\vdash d:\mathcal E\longrightarrow\mathcal E'
73	\quad [\operatorname{read}(d);\operatorname{write}(d)].
74	\]
75	
76	\(\Gamma\) records facts such as the existence of an inspection action, the absence of leaked private information, or the availability of an external resource account.
77	
78	| Proposed operator | Primary effect | Required detail |
79	|---|---|---|
80	| \(\operatorname{Restrict}_B\) | Legal actions | What actions remain; empty action sets require a defined fallback. |
81	| \(\operatorname{Budget}_{b,c}\) | State, legality, and resource costs | Initial budget, cost schedule, replenishment, and who sees spending. |
82	| \(\operatorname{Hide}_{i,q}\) | Player \(i\)'s observations | A specified projection or stochastic channel; include indirect disclosures. |
83	| \(\operatorname{Observe}_{q}\) | Evaluator acquisition \(Z\) | Sampling and attribution process; whether participants learn the setting. |
84	| \(\operatorname{Message}_{c}\) | Actions, observations, and possibly costs | Sender, receiver, timing, alphabet, cost, and whether messages bind. |
85	| \(\operatorname{Commit}_{k}\) | Legal future actions or payoffs | Acceptance, enforcement, default, expiry, and within-round or episode scope. |
86	| \(\operatorname{Repeat}_{H,m}\) | Horizon, state, and controller memory | Identity persistence, reset map, termination knowledge, and payoff discounting. |
87	| \(\operatorname{Payoff}_{u}\) | Assigned utility | Whether implementation also changes resources, displayed feedback, or training. |
88	| \(\operatorname{Reframe}_{f}\) | Presentation | A bijective semantic mapping, or an explicit admission that task meaning changed. |
89	| \(\operatorname{Controller}_{\pi}\) | Controller roster/protocol | Which players change, with what information and budget. |
90	| \(\operatorname{Rescore}_{j}\) | Judgment | Only offline rescoring is automatically outside the game. |
91	
92	These are distinct types of operation. A resource injection is not just a reward edit. Giving an evaluator access to hidden state does not give a player that access. A message channel is not a signal-count variable unless it actually carries content that another controller can interpret.
93	
94	Mechanics form a feasible design space constrained by \(\Gamma\), not an unrestricted Cartesian product. A commitment to unavailable actions or a private message without a recipient channel is ill-typed. Record rejected combinations rather than silently dropping them from a factorial study.
95	
96	## 4. Composition: execution first, strategic context second
97	
98	For finite state interfaces, an executed fragment with fixed controllers can be represented by a stochastic kernel \(K:X\rightsquigarrow Y\). Carry relevant history and accumulated payoff in the interfaces. Define
99	
100	\[
101	(K;L)(z\mid x)=\sum_y K(y\mid x)L(z\mid y).
102	\]
103	
104	The interface types must match. Finite summation proves
105	
106	\[
107	(K;L);M=K;(L;M),\qquad \mathrm{id};K=K=K;\mathrm{id}.
108	\]
109	
110	Parallel independent execution has
111	
112	\[
113	(K\otimes L)(y_1,y_2\mid x_1,x_2)
114	=K(y_1\mid x_1)L(y_2\mid x_2).
115	\]
116	
117	With matching interfaces and independent factors,
118	
119	\[
120	(K_1\otimes K_2);(L_1\otimes L_2)
121	=(K_1;L_1)\otimes(K_2;L_2).
122	\]
123	
124	Shared capital, shared randomness, or controllers coordinating across fragments violate that factorization unless explicitly represented in the interface. Repeating a kernel also requires a declared reset/carry map; independent episodes and a repeated strategic relationship have different semantics.
125	
126	These laws describe execution distributions. An equilibrium of each isolated fragment need not remain an equilibrium when downstream incentives are introduced. Open-game theory supplies richer strategic interfaces, including continuation utility; this document does not implement that formalism or prove an embedding into it. [Ghani et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.04641)
127	
128	## 5. Laws, counterexamples, and preservation levels
129	
130	Use a preservation annotation \(d:G\xrightarrow{P}G'\). Useful predicates \(P\) include conservation, legal-trace correspondence, information correspondence, payoff correspondence, and best-response correspondence. Measurement validity is a separate obligation.
131	
132	**Projection law.** A deterministic deletion of a fixed set of visible fields is idempotent: \(H(H(o))=H(o)\). Two fresh independent sampling passes with retention \(q\), however, retain with probability \(q^2\). Reapplying random observation loss is not idempotent.
133	
134	**Disjoint-update law.** Two pure, deterministic transformations commute if neither writes anything the other reads or writes, including implicit dependencies, metadata, and randomness. This is a sufficient condition, not a necessary one. The claim is about transformations applied at design time; it does not say their effects on behavior are additive.
135	
136	**Order effect.** Granting two budget units and capping the balance at five do not commute. Starting at four, cap-after-grant yields five; grant-after-cap yields six. Thus an expression's order belongs in its saved design record.
137	
138	**Renaming law.** A bijection on states, actions, observations, and payoffs preserves corresponding strategic possibilities when policies and measurements are transported through the same bijection. An unchanged language model receiving new prose is not a transported policy. Its sensitivity is a result to measure, not a contradiction of game isomorphism.
139	
140	**Utility law.** For expected-utility comparisons, replacing each player's total trajectory utility by \(a_iU_i+b_i\), \(a_i>0\), preserves that player's best responses and therefore Nash equilibria. A per-step constant can change preferences when episode lengths differ. An arbitrary increasing nonlinear transformation need not preserve preferences over lotteries: a fair lottery paying zero or four has mean two, below a sure 2.1; squaring outcomes reverses the ordering, giving eight versus 4.41. This says nothing about whether a prompted model is invariant to rescaling.
141	
142	**Mixture law.** For a fixed controller and compatible scalar measurement, expectation under a mixture is the corresponding weighted expectation. Optimizing after revealing which component was selected is a different experiment. In general \(\max_\pi\sum_i w_iV_i(\pi)\leq\sum_iw_i\max_\pi V_i(\pi)\). Averaging separately optimal scores can overstate achievable performance in a hidden mixture.
143	
144	No unconditional claim is made that hiding information lowers observed performance, that additional tools raise it, or that repetition produces cooperation.
145	
146	## 6. A resource-flow calculus
147	
148	Following Machinations' emphasis on stocks, flows, and feedback, represent stocks of one declared resource type by \(x_t\), flows by \(f_t\), and net incidence by \(B\):
149	
150	\[
151	x_{t+1}=x_t+Bf_t+s_t-d_t.
152	\]
153	
154	Here \(s_t,d_t\) are external sources and drains. Admissibility requires nonnegative balances, capacities, action authorization, and sufficient resources at the moment each transfer fires. A feasible final balance alone does not guarantee a sequential execution exists.
155	
156	If \(w^TB=0\), then
157	
158	\[
159	w^Tx_{t+1}-w^Tx_t=w^T(s_t-d_t).
160	\]
161	
162	This is a direct conservation proof. Transfers cancel; external creation and destruction remain explicit. Separate resource types need separate ledgers or justified conversion rates. One cannot add money, privacy, and success percentages into a conservation equation.
163	
164	A simple three-account example starts at \((10,0,0)\). Transfer three from account one to two and two from account two to three. The final stock is \((7,1,2)\), with total ten. An explicit source of four changes the total to fourteen. In Spiral, a coordination-income bonus must appear as such a source; its configured contribution is not evidence of discovered productivity.
165	
166	For a smooth deterministic approximation \(x_{t+1}=F(x_t,a_t;\lambda)\), a differentiable fixed feedback policy \(a_t=\pi(x_t)\) gives the local state Jacobian
167	
168	\[
169	J_x=\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}
170	+\frac{\partial F}{\partial a}\frac{\partial\pi}{\partial x}.
171	\]
172	
173	At a fixed point, spectral radius below one is a sufficient local stability condition for this differentiable discrete-time system. Discrete actions, thresholds, stochastic controllers, and changes of equilibrium require separate treatment. This is an optional approximation for feedback analysis, not an established stability result for the existing simulator.
174	
175	## 7. A calculus of design effects
176	
177	Let \(V_\pi(d)\) be the expected scalar measurement for a frozen controller protocol, target sampling law, and design \(d\). Define a design difference
178	
179	\[
180	\Delta_aV_\pi(d)=V_\pi(a(d))-V_\pi(d).
181	\]
182	
183	For two independent binary settings, define their interaction on a chosen outcome scale:
184	
185	\[
186	\Delta_{ab}V=V_{11}-V_{10}-V_{01}+V_{00}.
187	\]
188	
189	This asks whether the combined effect exceeds the sum of the individual effects. It differs from an order effect,
190	
191	\[
192	\Omega_{a,b}V(d)=V(a(b(d)))-V(b(a(d))).
193	\]
194	
195	Two commuting configuration switches can have a large interaction. Noncommuting transformations require the order to be specified before constructing the four cells.
196	
197	For a fully feasible set of binary mechanics \(M\), use the subset lattice:
198	
199	\[
200	\beta_S=\sum_{T\subseteq S}(-1)^{|S|-|T|}V(T),
201	\qquad
202	V(S)=\sum_{T\subseteq S}\beta_T.
203	\]
204	
205	This inclusion–exclusion expansion separates baseline, individual contributions, and higher-order interactions relative to the all-off design. It is an exact representation of the cell means, not a proof of causality. It requires all relevant subset cells; nested ablations alone cannot identify every interaction. Effects depend on the chosen measurement scale.
206	
207	For a continuous parameter, a finite difference
208	
209	\[
210	D_hV(\lambda)=\frac{V(\lambda+h)-V(\lambda)}{h}
211	\]
212	
213	can approximate a derivative where smoothness is justified. Preserve it as a finite difference around discontinuities. Always distinguish frozen-controller sensitivity from sensitivity after retraining, selecting another controller, or selecting another equilibrium.
214	
215	Estimate paired differences within independent run blocks, using matched exogenous cases and separate random streams for independent mechanisms. A common seed alone is insufficient when conditions consume different random draws. Freeze sampling, outcome scale, counterpart roster, multiplicity handling, and stopping before confirmation. A notation does not repair a confounded design.
216	
217	## 8. Exact example: information and usable alternatives
218	
219	There are two locations, left and right. Exactly one contains a unit-valued resource, each with probability one half. A single player chooses a location once.
220	
221	- \(I=0\): the player cannot see which location contains the resource.
222	- \(I=1\): the location is revealed before action.
223	- \(B=0\): only the left action is legal.
224	- \(B=1\): either action is legal.
225	
226	Use the optimal admissible decision rule in each cell, explicitly marking this as an analytical ceiling \(V^*\), not a model score.
227	
228	| | Left only | Either location |
229	|---|---:|---:|

# A calculus of evaluation design

Version 0.1 — 2026-09-11. A proposed synthesis for Spiral.

**An evaluation is a designed game, a population of controllers, and an evidence-producing experiment.** Its notation should expose what can be composed, what a transformation preserves, and what the observations support. This document connects game-design concepts to a small mathematical core. It does not claim a universal algebra of games or a validated measure of general intelligence.

The accompanying exact examples are in `configs/evaluation_design_calculus_examples.json`; `scripts/verify_evaluation_design_calculus.py` checks their arithmetic and selected finite instances of the laws. These are mathematical fixtures, not model evaluations. Existing Spiral campaigns remain unchanged.

For applications to published environments, see the [Prime Intellect example atlas](prime_intellect_eval_atlas.md), including proof feedback, 2048 interfaces, simulated users, poker, and learned judges.

## 1. What the literature contributes

| Foundation | Established contribution | Our adaptation |
|---|---|---|
| [Hunicke, LeBlanc, and Zubek, MDA (2004)](https://www.cs.northwestern.edu/~hunicke/MDA.pdf) | Distinguishes mechanics, their runtime dynamics, and players' aesthetic experience. | Separate specified mechanisms from observed behavior and the capability claim. This is an adaptation; evidence is not a replacement definition of MDA's aesthetics. |
| [Juul, emergence and progression (2002)](https://jesperjuul.net/text/openandtheclosed.html) | Distinguishes interacting rules that generate varied play from prescribed sequences of challenges. | Record whether success requires particular steps or allows alternative successful strategies. |
| [Sicart, game mechanics (2008)](https://www.gamestudies.org/0802/articles/sicart) | Analyzes mechanics as methods by which agents interact with a game world. | Give mechanics action types, legal preconditions, and state effects. |
| [Dormans, Machinations (2011)](https://pure.hva.nl/ws/portalfiles/portal/141880/556168_dormans_simulating_mechanics.pdf) | Represents resource flows and feedback structures in game economies. | Use explicit resource ledgers, flow constraints, and local response analysis. |
| [Operational logics, UCSC research group](https://eis.ucsc.edu/analyses-and-approaches/operational-logics/) | Connects abstract computational operations with their communicative role. | Keep state semantics and their presentation to the participant separately inspectable. |
| [Piette et al., Ludii (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.05013) | Describes games through composable, understandable game concepts called ludemes. | Define reusable evaluation primitives such as inspection, commitment, resource transfer, and termination. These are our primitives, not a claimed Ludii extension. |
| [Thielscher, GDL-II (2010)](https://cgi.cse.unsw.edu.au/~mit/Papers/AAAI10a.pdf) | Extends formal game descriptions to nondeterminism and restricted information. | Specify legal actions, transitions, private observations, and termination independently. |
| [Ghani et al., compositional game theory (2018)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.04641) | Uses open games with sequential and parallel composition, including strategic context. | Borrow the insistence on typed interfaces; distinguish execution composition from composition of strategic incentives. |
| [Nash (1950)](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.36.1.48), [Harsanyi (1967)](https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/abs/10.1287/mnsc.14.3.159) | Equilibrium under unilateral deviations; games with private types and beliefs. | State a strategic reference model and measure deviation opportunities without assuming observed agents optimize the assigned payoff. |

The tuple, operator names, effect annotations, design derivatives, and project mappings below are our proposed synthesis. The linear algebra, probability composition, inclusion–exclusion identities, and elementary equilibrium calculations are standard mathematical constructions applied here. Their general applicability does not follow merely from their game-design inspiration.

## 2. Three objects, three kinds of claim

Write an evaluation as

\[
\mathcal E=\langle G,\Pi,D,Z,J,\mathcal A,C\rangle.
\]

- \(G\): game specification.
- \(\Pi\): the controller roster and execution protocol, including model or policy, instructions, memory, tools, decoding, retries, and resource budgets.
- \(D\): sampling and assignment of game instances, counterparts, conditions, and independent run blocks.
- \(Z\): evidence acquisition; what the evaluator observes and records.
- \(J\): judgment of an acquired trace.
- \(\mathcal A\): aggregation and uncertainty procedure.
- \(C\): claim, target population, and assumptions required for interpretation.

One run produces a full trajectory \(\tau\), an acquired record \(z\), and a judgment \(y\):

\[
\tau\sim P_{G,\Pi,D},\qquad z\sim Z(\cdot\mid\tau),\qquad y=J(z).
\]

Aggregation operates across declared independent blocks, not automatically across every action or message. The claim is an interpretation of the experiment, not another deterministic output of the state machine.

Use this game record:

\[
G=\langle N,X,\Theta,p_0,\{A_i,O_i\}_{i\in N},T,U,H,F\rangle.
\]

Here \(N\) is the player set, \(X\) the world state, \(\Theta\) private types, \(p_0\) their joint initial distribution with the state, \(A_i\) legal moves, \(O_i\) observation channels, \(T\) transitions, \(U\) assigned trajectory utilities, \(H\) the stopping rule, and \(F\) the presentation layer. A turn scheduler can be encoded in the state, with inactive players given a no-op. Information includes any feedback from legality checks, errors, timing, and rewards.

A controller acts from its accessible history: \(\pi_i(a_i\mid h_i)\). A privileged experiment recorder may inspect the full trajectory; a player must not receive that trajectory accidentally through its integration wrapper. A fixed scripted counterparty is part of the environment from the focal player's perspective. Merely naming it a second agent does not make the run evidence of mutual strategic adaptation.

Maintain three distinctions:

1. Assigned utility \(U_i\) specifies a game-theoretic objective; a controller's actual optimization of it is an empirical question.
2. Judgment \(J\) can measure welfare, accuracy, or cost separately from that utility. If judgment is shown during play or used for learning, it also enters observations or controller updates.
3. Claim \(C\) can concern mechanism feasibility, a particular controller, or a target population. These require different evidence.

## 3. A design grammar with effect annotations

Give each transformation a signature, preconditions, scope, and read/write footprint. Denote a valid application by

\[
\Gamma\vdash d:\mathcal E\longrightarrow\mathcal E'
\quad [\operatorname{read}(d);\operatorname{write}(d)].
\]

\(\Gamma\) records facts such as the existence of an inspection action, the absence of leaked private information, or the availability of an external resource account.

| Proposed operator | Primary effect | Required detail |
|---|---|---|
| \(\operatorname{Restrict}_B\) | Legal actions | What actions remain; empty action sets require a defined fallback. |
| \(\operatorname{Budget}_{b,c}\) | State, legality, and resource costs | Initial budget, cost schedule, replenishment, and who sees spending. |
| \(\operatorname{Hide}_{i,q}\) | Player \(i\)'s observations | A specified projection or stochastic channel; include indirect disclosures. |
| \(\operatorname{Observe}_{q}\) | Evaluator acquisition \(Z\) | Sampling and attribution process; whether participants learn the setting. |
| \(\operatorname{Message}_{c}\) | Actions, observations, and possibly costs | Sender, receiver, timing, alphabet, cost, and whether messages bind. |
| \(\operatorname{Commit}_{k}\) | Legal future actions or payoffs | Acceptance, enforcement, default, expiry, and within-round or episode scope. |
| \(\operatorname{Repeat}_{H,m}\) | Horizon, state, and controller memory | Identity persistence, reset map, termination knowledge, and payoff discounting. |
| \(\operatorname{Payoff}_{u}\) | Assigned utility | Whether implementation also changes resources, displayed feedback, or training. |
| \(\operatorname{Reframe}_{f}\) | Presentation | A bijective semantic mapping, or an explicit admission that task meaning changed. |
| \(\operatorname{Controller}_{\pi}\) | Controller roster/protocol | Which players change, with what information and budget. |
| \(\operatorname{Rescore}_{j}\) | Judgment | Only offline rescoring is automatically outside the game. |

These are distinct types of operation. A resource injection is not just a reward edit. Giving an evaluator access to hidden state does not give a player that access. A message channel is not a signal-count variable unless it actually carries content that another controller can interpret.

Mechanics form a feasible design space constrained by \(\Gamma\), not an unrestricted Cartesian product. A commitment to unavailable actions or a private message without a recipient channel is ill-typed. Record rejected combinations rather than silently dropping them from a factorial study.

## 4. Composition: execution first, strategic context second

For finite state interfaces, an executed fragment with fixed controllers can be represented by a stochastic kernel \(K:X\rightsquigarrow Y\). Carry relevant history and accumulated payoff in the interfaces. Define

\[
(K;L)(z\mid x)=\sum_y K(y\mid x)L(z\mid y).
\]

The interface types must match. Finite summation proves

\[
(K;L);M=K;(L;M),\qquad \mathrm{id};K=K=K;\mathrm{id}.
\]

Parallel independent execution has

\[
(K\otimes L)(y_1,y_2\mid x_1,x_2)
=K(y_1\mid x_1)L(y_2\mid x_2).
\]

With matching interfaces and independent factors,

\[
(K_1\otimes K_2);(L_1\otimes L_2)
=(K_1;L_1)\otimes(K_2;L_2).
\]

Shared capital, shared randomness, or controllers coordinating across fragments violate that factorization unless explicitly represented in the interface. Repeating a kernel also requires a declared reset/carry map; independent episodes and a repeated strategic relationship have different semantics.

These laws describe execution distributions. An equilibrium of each isolated fragment need not remain an equilibrium when downstream incentives are introduced. Open-game theory supplies richer strategic interfaces, including continuation utility; this document does not implement that formalism or prove an embedding into it. [Ghani et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.04641)

## 5. Laws, counterexamples, and preservation levels

Use a preservation annotation \(d:G\xrightarrow{P}G'\). Useful predicates \(P\) include conservation, legal-trace correspondence, information correspondence, payoff correspondence, and best-response correspondence. Measurement validity is a separate obligation.

**Projection law.** A deterministic deletion of a fixed set of visible fields is idempotent: \(H(H(o))=H(o)\). Two fresh independent sampling passes with retention \(q\), however, retain with probability \(q^2\). Reapplying random observation loss is not idempotent.

**Disjoint-update law.** Two pure, deterministic transformations commute if neither writes anything the other reads or writes, including implicit dependencies, metadata, and randomness. This is a sufficient condition, not a necessary one. The claim is about transformations applied at design time; it does not say their effects on behavior are additive.

**Order effect.** Granting two budget units and capping the balance at five do not commute. Starting at four, cap-after-grant yields five; grant-after-cap yields six. Thus an expression's order belongs in its saved design record.

**Renaming law.** A bijection on states, actions, observations, and payoffs preserves corresponding strategic possibilities when policies and measurements are transported through the same bijection. An unchanged language model receiving new prose is not a transported policy. Its sensitivity is a result to measure, not a contradiction of game isomorphism.

**Utility law.** For expected-utility comparisons, replacing each player's total trajectory utility by \(a_iU_i+b_i\), \(a_i>0\), preserves that player's best responses and therefore Nash equilibria. A per-step constant can change preferences when episode lengths differ. An arbitrary increasing nonlinear transformation need not preserve preferences over lotteries: a fair lottery paying zero or four has mean two, below a sure 2.1; squaring outcomes reverses the ordering, giving eight versus 4.41. This says nothing about whether a prompted model is invariant to rescaling.

**Mixture law.** For a fixed controller and compatible scalar measurement, expectation under a mixture is the corresponding weighted expectation. Optimizing after revealing which component was selected is a different experiment. In general \(\max_\pi\sum_i w_iV_i(\pi)\leq\sum_iw_i\max_\pi V_i(\pi)\). Averaging separately optimal scores can overstate achievable performance in a hidden mixture.

No unconditional claim is made that hiding information lowers observed performance, that additional tools raise it, or that repetition produces cooperation.

## 6. A resource-flow calculus

Following Machinations' emphasis on stocks, flows, and feedback, represent stocks of one declared resource type by \(x_t\), flows by \(f_t\), and net incidence by \(B\):

\[
x_{t+1}=x_t+Bf_t+s_t-d_t.
\]

Here \(s_t,d_t\) are external sources and drains. Admissibility requires nonnegative balances, capacities, action authorization, and sufficient resources at the moment each transfer fires. A feasible final balance alone does not guarantee a sequential execution exists.

If \(w^TB=0\), then

\[
w^Tx_{t+1}-w^Tx_t=w^T(s_t-d_t).
\]

This is a direct conservation proof. Transfers cancel; external creation and destruction remain explicit. Separate resource types need separate ledgers or justified conversion rates. One cannot add money, privacy, and success percentages into a conservation equation.

A simple three-account example starts at \((10,0,0)\). Transfer three from account one to two and two from account two to three. The final stock is \((7,1,2)\), with total ten. An explicit source of four changes the total to fourteen. In Spiral, a coordination-income bonus must appear as such a source; its configured contribution is not evidence of discovered productivity.

For a smooth deterministic approximation \(x_{t+1}=F(x_t,a_t;\lambda)\), a differentiable fixed feedback policy \(a_t=\pi(x_t)\) gives the local state Jacobian

\[
J_x=\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}
+\frac{\partial F}{\partial a}\frac{\partial\pi}{\partial x}.
\]

At a fixed point, spectral radius below one is a sufficient local stability condition for this differentiable discrete-time system. Discrete actions, thresholds, stochastic controllers, and changes of equilibrium require separate treatment. This is an optional approximation for feedback analysis, not an established stability result for the existing simulator.

## 7. A calculus of design effects

Let \(V_\pi(d)\) be the expected scalar measurement for a frozen controller protocol, target sampling law, and design \(d\). Define a design difference

\[
\Delta_aV_\pi(d)=V_\pi(a(d))-V_\pi(d).
\]

For two independent binary settings, define their interaction on a chosen outcome scale:

\[
\Delta_{ab}V=V_{11}-V_{10}-V_{01}+V_{00}.
\]

This asks whether the combined effect exceeds the sum of the individual effects. It differs from an order effect,

\[
\Omega_{a,b}V(d)=V(a(b(d)))-V(b(a(d))).
\]

Two commuting configuration switches can have a large interaction. Noncommuting transformations require the order to be specified before constructing the four cells.

For a fully feasible set of binary mechanics \(M\), use the subset lattice:

\[
\beta_S=\sum_{T\subseteq S}(-1)^{|S|-|T|}V(T),
\qquad
V(S)=\sum_{T\subseteq S}\beta_T.
\]

This inclusion–exclusion expansion separates baseline, individual contributions, and higher-order interactions relative to the all-off design. It is an exact representation of the cell means, not a proof of causality. It requires all relevant subset cells; nested ablations alone cannot identify every interaction. Effects depend on the chosen measurement scale.

For a continuous parameter, a finite difference

\[
D_hV(\lambda)=\frac{V(\lambda+h)-V(\lambda)}{h}
\]

can approximate a derivative where smoothness is justified. Preserve it as a finite difference around discontinuities. Always distinguish frozen-controller sensitivity from sensitivity after retraining, selecting another controller, or selecting another equilibrium.

Estimate paired differences within independent run blocks, using matched exogenous cases and separate random streams for independent mechanisms. A common seed alone is insufficient when conditions consume different random draws. Freeze sampling, outcome scale, counterpart roster, multiplicity handling, and stopping before confirmation. A notation does not repair a confounded design.

There are two locations, left and right. Exactly one contains a unit-valued resource, each with probability one half. A single player chooses a location once.

- \(I=0\): the player cannot see which location contains the resource.
- \(I=1\): the location is revealed before action.
- \(B=0\): only the left action is legal.
- \(B=1\): either action is legal.

Use the optimal admissible decision rule in each cell, explicitly marking this as an analytical ceiling \(V^*\), not a model score.

| | Left only | Either location |
|---|---:|---:|
| Hidden resource | 0.5 | 0.5 |
| Revealed resource | 0.5 | 1.0 |

3. **Controllers:** focal policy, counterparts, memory, prompts, tools, budgets, and any learning or selection between episodes.
4. **Design expression:** ordered, scoped operators with preconditions, footprints, and preservation obligations.
5. **Reference model:** fixed-policy baseline, optimal decision rule, Nash/Bayesian/sequential reference, or an explicitly heuristic comparator.
6. **Acquisition and judgment:** privileged versus accessible data, blind scoring where relevant, and whether any score feeds back into play.
7. **Estimand:** main effect, interaction, order effect, frontier, calibration error, welfare, or unilateral-improvement gap.
8. **Inference:** assignment, independent blocks, frozen selection/confirmation boundary, uncertainty, and multiplicity.
9. **Evidence status:** algebraic identity, finite verified example, synthetic mechanism result, observed-controller result, or externally validated claim.

The first implementation priority would be compiling these cards against real adapters and checking observation boundaries. A full game-language compiler, open-game strategic semantics, and real-model campaigns are subsequent goals, not results delivered by this document.

## 12. Exact follow-up: estimands, Hide, and incentive response

The companion [evaluation-game testbed](evaluation_game_testbed.md) makes four
non-interchangeable estimands executable in small rational fixtures: baseline
gain, robust regret, acquired-record discrimination gap, and exploitability.
It types observation-only `Hide` as one common post-play Markov kernel and
checks the resulting loss of measurement discrimination. It separately verifies
that hiding information from a player before action changes the game and can
change optimal value. The testbed also records equilibrium sets and selected
outcomes under a declared adaptation rule, marks restricted best response as a
lower bound, includes a tiny zero-sum primal/dual witness, and documents a
difficulty-matched, grader-severity-stratified held-out incentive interaction.
These are exact synthetic design checks, not model or multi-agent results.
