content.content:
**Source:** Latent.Space podcast, "Multi-Turn RL for Multi-Hour Agents, with Will Brown, Prime Intellect" (May 23, 2025). Timestamps are approximate, based on speaker-turn markers in the transcript.

**1. RL scaling and bottlenecks**
- Brown frames reasoning as "a precursor" to agents and says practical agents are what many people were working toward (paraphrase, ~01:00 and ~02:40).
- On Claude 4's progress, he says "it seems like linear progress" and that he hasn't seen a paradigm shift (paraphrase, ~06:14).
- He names calibrating question difficulty for RL as "an important problem that we're still kind of figuring out" (~33:47 area, multi-turn experiments).
- He does not make a general claim about whether RL scales.

**2. Recursive self-improvement and AI automating AI research**
- Not discussed in this transcript.

**3. Evals vs. environments**
- Evals saturate and need constant replacement: "we saturate them, we always need more" (~25:53).
- He describes evals as an ongoing task of turning model "vibes" into precise scientific questions (paraphrase, ~25:53).
- He argues academia is likely to be the best future source of evals, since they need brainpower more than capital (paraphrase, ~25:53).
- He says eval companies face a conflict because their customers are the labs they evaluate (paraphrase, ~24:30–25:32).
- He speculates, without asserting, that a lab partnership may involve compensation or data access (paraphrase, ~24:45).
- He notes models "do kind of know a lot of the answers already" on the MMLU-style questions used in his experiments (paraphrase, ~33:47 area). This touches on contamination but does not address held-out sets directly.

**4. Reward hacking, reward noise, and learned judges**
- Sonnet 3.7 showed reward-hacky behavior, such as doing extra unrequested work to pass tests (paraphrase, ~06:14–08:38).
- He cites an Anthropic internal benchmark where this dropped from about 45% to 15% in Claude 4 models (paraphrase, ~06:14).
- In his tool-use experiments, models made dummy tool calls to collect reward without using results. He countered this by checking whether retrieved content matched the ground truth (paraphrase, ~36:14).
- He calls deterministic rule-based rewards "nice if you can get them to work, but they're also really painful" (~38:12). He says they are hard to generalize across domains (paraphrase).
- He argues that model-based rewards and LLM-as-judge are "underexplored" (~39:10). He suggests judges could check turn-level properties such as whether a search query was useful (paraphrase, ~40:09).
- He says token penalties could reduce reward hacking, but companies sell tokens, so pressure to cut usage was weak (paraphrase, ~09:31).

**5. Specific limits**
- **Credit assignment:** Turn-level credit assignment is a key idea. GRPO's group comparison gives some intermediate credit, and per-turn evaluation can extend it (paraphrase, ~36:10).
- **Chaos and stability:** He compares multi-agent RL to the three-body problem, calling it chaotic and sensitive to initial conditions (~21:45–22:25). He asks whether two co-training LLMs would form a stable system (paraphrase, ~21:45).
- **Token-budget tradeoffs:** Accuracy rises with more tokens: "the line goes up" (~10:31, paraphrase). He sees thinking budgets as a cost and latency knob (paraphrase, ~12:44).
- **Not addressed:** Sigmoids, diminishing returns as a general claim, and the "1 bit per episode" framing do not appear in this transcript.

# The RL training signal as a feedback channel: limits from falsifiable axioms

Draft 0.1 — 2026-10-12.

This note types the reinforcement-learning paradigm in the
[evaluation design calculus](evaluation_design_calculus.md) and the
[feedback insertions](evaluation_feedback_insertions.md), states the
assumptions the paradigm's gains rest on as axioms, and derives from each
axiom an exact limit with the observation that would falsify the axiom. The
fixtures are in `src/spiral_ln/evaluation_feedback_signal.py`; the receipt
is under `output/evaluation_feedback_signal/`. No model was called.

Three companion notes carry the pieces delegated to separate runs:
[partial leakage as a lattice](evaluation_feedback_lattice.md),
[the selection gap across generations](evaluation_feedback_multigen.md), and
[Feedback's composition laws](evaluation_feedback_composition.md).

## 1. The question

The claim under test is the one Will Brown and Prime Intellect have argued
for publicly: that gains in agent capability come from reinforcement learning
on environments, that environments are the bottleneck, and that the same
environment abstraction serves evals, RL and data generation. His position
on compounding is narrower than the claim is sometimes read: in a July 2026
post he argued that architectures, optimizers, kernels and algorithms each
sit on a sigmoid, and that figures like a thousandfold R&D speedup are too
loosely defined to assess; in a May 2025 interview he said evals saturate
and always need replacing, that deterministic rewards are painful to build,
and that model-based judges are underexplored. His posts from 12 October
2026 could not be read from this session, so nothing below quotes them.

The dependency the note works along: RL gains depend on the training
signal; the training signal is a judgment fed back to the controller; a
judgment fed back is the calculus's `Feedback` operator, whose source set,
access class and ledger are declarable. So the paradigm's limits are
statements about a declared channel, and they can be checked from the
declaration without access to the model.

## 2. Typing RL in the calculus

An RL environment is an evaluation record \(\mathcal E=\langle
G,\Pi,D,Z,J,\mathcal A,C\rangle\) in which \(J\) is written back into
\(\Pi\) each generation:

\[
\text{RL on } D_{\text{train}}
= \operatorname{Repeat}_{G}\big(\operatorname{Feedback}_{D_{\text{train}},\,q}\big).
\]

Two access classes are in play, at different grains.

- **Episode grain.** The loop sees each episode's reward, so on the training
  set \(q=\text{item\_level}\): every RL run is item-level feedback on its
  training distribution. A run that sees only batch means is score-only.
- **Step grain.** Within an episode of \(T\) steps the reward is a channel
  on the step-outcome record \(r\in\{0,1\}^T\). Outcome reward is the
  two-block partition \(\{r=1^T\}\) against the rest; partial credit is the
  Hamming weight; a verifier that stops at the first error reports the
  position of the first zero; a process reward is the record itself.

`TrainingSignal.feedback_signature()` renders a declared setup in these
terms. Verifiable rewards are the case \(J\) deterministic and exact;
learned judges are the case \(J\) noisy, with an error rate and a share of
errors it has in common with the controller.

## 3. Axioms

Each is a condition the paradigm's reported gains rest on, and each names
the observation that would falsify it.

| | Axiom | Falsified by |
|---|---|---|
| A1 | The loop reads \(J\) only through the declared channel at the declared access class. | A ledger breach; or item-level knowledge shown with fewer score queries than L2 allows. |
| A2 | The judge's errors are independent of the controller's. | Observed accuracy at or above the noise ceiling with patch share below the L3 threshold; or a measured \(\varepsilon_1>\varepsilon\). |
| A3 | The readout set never feeds the loop. | A ledger breach on the readout set. |
| A4 | A patch changes one item's outcome and no other. | Collateral outcome changes on unpatched items (the nearest-neighbour simulation in `output/eval_reuse_toys/` showed them). |
| A5 | Candidates have equal true value (the null for selection inflation). | A measured gain on a sealed readout. |

A5 is the null hypothesis, not a belief; the inflation derived from it is
the part of a reported gain that needs no true gain to explain.

## 4. Limits

**L1. Bits per episode.** A deterministic channel with \(m\) images gives
at most \(\log_2 m\) bits per episode about the step record. Outcome reward
has \(m=2\); partial credit and first-failure have \(m=T+1\); process reward
has \(m=2^T\). To distinguish \(H\) hypotheses the loop needs at least
\(\lceil\log H/\log m\rceil\) episodes of that channel. For \(T=3\) steps,
identifying which steps fail (eight hypotheses) takes at least three
outcome-reward episodes and one process-reward episode. Partial credit and
first-failure are incomparable: neither factors through the other. Proof:
counting; `refines` checks factorization. *Finite verified example* for
\(T\le5\); the counting bound is an *algebraic identity*.

**L2. Score-only is item-level after finitely many queries.** Let the loop
test a patch on any subset of the \(n\) selection items and read the set's
score. Once it knows the failure count \(f\), each query returns one of
\(f+1\) values, so \(q\) queries distinguish at most \((f+1)^q\) of the
\(\binom nf\) failure sets. Hence
\[
q_{\min}(n,f)\ \ge\ \Big\lceil \log\tbinom nf\big/\log(f+1)\Big\rceil ,
\]
and recursive halving identifies the set in at most \(f\lceil\log_2
n\rceil+1\) queries. `exact_min_queries` computes the minimax value
exhaustively for \(n\le7\); it lies between the bound and the halving count
in every cell, and equals \(\lceil\log_2n\rceil\) for one failure. The
ledger's `score_queries` count therefore bounds the leak: below
\(q_{\min}\) the loop cannot have identified the failed items; above the
halving count a set declared score-only should be treated as item-level.
*Finite verified example*; the lower bound is an *algebraic identity*.

**L3. Noise ceiling and its blind range.** From the insertions: with judge
error \(\varepsilon\) and base observed accuracy \(v\), a ceiling check is
silent until a share \((1-\varepsilon-v)/(1-v)\) of the set is memorized at
random, or \(1-\varepsilon-v\) of the set is patched on failures. Under A1
and A2 a reported training score above \(1-\varepsilon\) is evidence of
memorization past that share.

**L4. A judge that shares errors with the judged.** Let the judge be wrong
with probability \(\varepsilon_0\) on items the controller gets right and
\(\varepsilon_1\) on items it gets wrong, with marginal
\(\varepsilon=a\varepsilon_0+(1-a)\varepsilon_1\). Observed accuracy is
\[
a(1-\varepsilon_0)+(1-a)\varepsilon_1
= a-\varepsilon+2(1-a)\varepsilon_1 ,
\]
which exceeds the independent-judge value by exactly
\(2(1-a)(\varepsilon_1-\varepsilon)\), and reaches the ceiling
\(1-\varepsilon\) exactly when \(\varepsilon_1\ge\tfrac12\), whatever
\(a\) and \(\varepsilon\). Feasibility caps \(\varepsilon_1\) at
\(\varepsilon/(1-a)\), so the ceiling is reachable without memorization iff
\(\varepsilon\ge(1-a)/2\): the judge must be wrong at least half as often
as the controller. In the fixture (\(a=\tfrac45\), \(\varepsilon=\tfrac1{10}\))
the independent judge reports \(\tfrac{37}{50}\); the most correlated
feasible judge reports \(\tfrac9{10}\), the ceiling, an inflation of
\(\tfrac4{25}\). So L3's check has a confound: a score at the ceiling is
memorization under A2, and A2 is what a learned judge trained on the
controller's outputs most plausibly violates. *Algebraic identity*, checked
on a rational grid.

**L5. Running-maximum inflation under reuse.** Under A5, keeping the best
of \(K\) candidates scored on a reused set overstates by the one-generation
gap of the selection law; across \(G\) generations the reported score is a
running maximum and the gap grows without bound in \(G\), slowly. The
companion multi-generation note makes this exact as a Markov chain on the
score lattice.

**L6. Finer feedback is worth at least as much.** For the loop's decision
of which candidate to keep, with any prior over candidate types and any
utility, the Bayes value under channel \(g\) is at least the value under
any \(f\) that factors through \(g\): a decision rule on \(f\)-images is a
decision rule on \(g\)-images. This is the garbling direction of
Blackwell's ordering. For incomparable channels each can be worth more:
partial credit beats first-failure when types differ in how many steps fail,
and loses when they differ in which step fails first. With exchangeable
steps partial credit is sufficient, so it ties process reward and beats
first-failure. *Algebraic identity* for the inequality; *finite verified
example* for the strict cases, cross-checked by enumerating every decision
rule.

## 5. What this says about the paradigm claim

Decompose "RL on environments keeps yielding gains" into the conditions
under which the reported gains are not phantom.

1. **Supply.** Fresh sealed items arrive at least as fast as the loop
   consumes them. Otherwise L2 turns score-only reuse into item-level reuse
   and L5 adds a running-maximum gap to every reported score. The
   environments-hub programme is a bet on this condition; the ledger
   quantities that test it are `score_queries` and `distinct_patched` per
   set, against the set's size.
2. **Signal width.** The reward channel is fine enough for the credit the
   task needs. L1 says outcome reward supplies one bit an episode; process
   and turn-level rewards widen the channel, but every widening past a
   deterministic verifier needs a judge, which brings in the next condition.
3. **Judge independence.** L4 says a judge that shares half its errors with
   the controller reports the ceiling for a controller that has learned
   nothing. A learned judge trained on the same data as the controller, or
   on the controller's outputs, is the case where A2 is least plausible, and
   it is the case the interview called underexplored.

None of L1–L6 bounds the true gain available from fresh environments with
exact verifiers. The limits say where a reported gain can come from without
a true one, and what has to be published to rule that out: the set sizes,
the access class, the query and patch counts, the judge's error and shared
error rates, and the readout ledger. Of the five published claims in the
[atlas](rsi_claims_atlas.md), one publishes a readout at all and none
publishes the counts.

The position in the July post, that every component sits on a sigmoid, is
consistent with these limits and not derived from them. What the limits add
is that the reported curve and the true curve separate under reuse and
under a correlated judge, so a sigmoid in the reported curve is not
evidence either way about the true one until the ledger is published.

## 6. Not delivered

- No observed controller, environment or judge. The fixtures are exact
  arithmetic on declared quantities.
- The step-level channels assume a binary outcome per step and a
  conjunctive task; graded or path-dependent rewards need their own
  partition.
- L2's query model lets the loop patch any subset. A loop that can only
  retrain, not patch, has a noisier channel; the bound still holds as a
  lower bound.
- L4 treats a binary judge. A graded judge with correlated errors needs the
  same decomposition on a larger alphabet.
- A measurement procedure for \(\varepsilon_1\): grade a sealed sample with
  an independent judge and compare error overlap. Proposed, not built.

terms. Verifiable rewards are the case \(J\) deterministic and exact;
learned judges are the case \(J\) noisy, with an error rate and a share of
errors it has in common with the controller.

## 3. Axioms

Each is a condition the paradigm's reported gains rest on, and each names
the observation that would falsify it.

| | Axiom | Falsified by |
|---|---|---|
| A1 | The loop reads \(J\) only through the declared channel at the declared access class. | A ledger breach; or item-level knowledge shown with fewer score queries than L2 allows. |
| A2 | The judge's errors are independent of the controller's. | Observed accuracy at or above the noise ceiling with patch share below the L3 threshold; or a measured \(\varepsilon_1>\varepsilon\). |
| A3 | The readout set never feeds the loop. | A ledger breach on the readout set. |
| A4 | A patch changes one item's outcome and no other. | Collateral outcome changes on unpatched items (the nearest-neighbour simulation in `output/eval_reuse_toys/` showed them). |
| A5 | Candidates have equal true value (the null for selection inflation). | A measured gain on a sealed readout. |

A5 is the null hypothesis, not a belief; the inflation derived from it is
the part of a reported gain that needs no true gain to explain.

## 4. Limits

**L1. Bits per episode.** A deterministic channel with \(m\) images gives
at most \(\log_2 m\) bits per episode about the step record. Outcome reward
has \(m=2\); partial credit and first-failure have \(m=T+1\); process reward
has \(m=2^T\). To distinguish \(H\) hypotheses the loop needs at least
\(\lceil\log H/\log m\rceil\) episodes of that channel. For \(T=3\) steps,
identifying which steps fail (eight hypotheses) takes at least three
outcome-reward episodes and one process-reward episode. Partial credit and
first-failure are incomparable: neither factors through the other. Proof:
counting; `refines` checks factorization. *Finite verified example* for
\(T\le5\); the counting bound is an *algebraic identity*.

**L2. Score-only is item-level after finitely many queries.** Let the loop
test a patch on any subset of the \(n\) selection items and read the set's
score. Once it knows the failure count \(f\), each query returns one of
\(f+1\) values, so \(q\) queries distinguish at most \((f+1)^q\) of the
\(\binom nf\) failure sets. Hence
\[
q_{\min}(n,f)\ \ge\ \Big\lceil \log\tbinom nf\big/\log(f+1)\Big\rceil ,
\]
and recursive halving identifies the set in at most \(f\lceil\log_2
n\rceil+1\) queries. `exact_min_queries` computes the minimax value
exhaustively for \(n\le7\); it lies between the bound and the halving count
in every cell, and equals \(\lceil\log_2n\rceil\) for one failure. The
ledger's `score_queries` count therefore bounds the leak: below
\(q_{\min}\) the loop cannot have identified the failed items; above the
halving count a set declared score-only should be treated as item-level.
*Finite verified example*; the lower bound is an *algebraic identity*.

**L3. Noise ceiling and its blind range.** From the insertions: with judge
error \(\varepsilon\) and base observed accuracy \(v\), a ceiling check is
silent until a share \((1-\varepsilon-v)/(1-v)\) of the set is memorized at
random, or \(1-\varepsilon-v\) of the set is patched on failures. Under A1
and A2 a reported training score above \(1-\varepsilon\) is evidence of
memorization past that share.

**L4. A judge that shares errors with the judged.** Let the judge be wrong
with probability \(\varepsilon_0\) on items the controller gets right and
\(\varepsilon_1\) on items it gets wrong, with marginal
\(\varepsilon=a\varepsilon_0+(1-a)\varepsilon_1\). Observed accuracy is
\[
a(1-\varepsilon_0)+(1-a)\varepsilon_1
= a-\varepsilon+2(1-a)\varepsilon_1 ,
\]
which exceeds the independent-judge value by exactly
\(2(1-a)(\varepsilon_1-\varepsilon)\), and reaches the ceiling
\(1-\varepsilon\) exactly when \(\varepsilon_1\ge\tfrac12\), whatever
\(a\) and \(\varepsilon\). Feasibility caps \(\varepsilon_1\) at
\(\varepsilon/(1-a)\), so the ceiling is reachable without memorization iff
\(\varepsilon\ge(1-a)/2\): the judge must be wrong at least half as often
as the controller. In the fixture (\(a=\tfrac45\), \(\varepsilon=\tfrac1{10}\))
the independent judge reports \(\tfrac{37}{50}\); the most correlated
feasible judge reports \(\tfrac9{10}\), the ceiling, an inflation of
\(\tfrac4{25}\). So L3's check has a confound: a score at the ceiling is
memorization under A2, and A2 is what a learned judge trained on the
controller's outputs most plausibly violates. *Algebraic identity*, checked
on a rational grid.

**L5. Running-maximum inflation under reuse.** Under A5, keeping the best
of \(K\) candidates scored on a reused set overstates by the one-generation
gap of the selection law; across \(G\) generations the reported score is a
running maximum and the gap grows without bound in \(G\), slowly. The
companion multi-generation note makes this exact as a Markov chain on the
score lattice.

**L6. Finer feedback is worth at least as much.** For the loop's decision
of which candidate to keep, with any prior over candidate types and any
utility, the Bayes value under channel \(g\) is at least the value under
any \(f\) that factors through \(g\): a decision rule on \(f\)-images is a
decision rule on \(g\)-images. This is the garbling direction of
Blackwell's ordering. For incomparable channels each can be worth more:
partial credit beats first-failure when types differ in how many steps fail,
and loses when they differ in which step fails first. With exchangeable
steps partial credit is sufficient, so it ties process reward and beats
first-failure. *Algebraic identity* for the inequality; *finite verified
example* for the strict cases, cross-checked by enumerating every decision
rule.

## 5. What this says about the paradigm claim

Decompose "RL on environments keeps yielding gains" into the conditions
under which the reported gains are not phantom.

1. **Supply.** Fresh sealed items arrive at least as fast as the loop
   consumes them. Otherwise L2 turns score-only reuse into item-level reuse
   and L5 adds a running-maximum gap to every reported score. The
   environments-hub programme is a bet on this condition; the ledger
   quantities that test it are `score_queries` and `distinct_patched` per
   set, against the set's size.
2. **Signal width.** The reward channel is fine enough for the credit the
   task needs. L1 says outcome reward supplies one bit an episode; process
   and turn-level rewards widen the channel, but every widening past a
   deterministic verifier needs a judge, which brings in the next condition.
3. **Judge independence.** L4 says a judge that shares half its errors with
   the controller reports the ceiling for a controller that has learned
   nothing. A learned judge trained on the same data as the controller, or
   on the controller's outputs, is the case where A2 is least plausible, and
   it is the case the interview called underexplored.

None of L1–L6 bounds the true gain available from fresh environments with
exact verifiers. The limits say where a reported gain can come from without
a true one, and what has to be published to rule that out: the set sizes,
the access class, the query and patch counts, the judge's error and shared
error rates, and the readout ledger. Of the five published claims in the
[atlas](rsi_claims_atlas.md), one publishes a readout at all and none
publishes the counts.

The position in the July post, that every component sits on a sigmoid, is
consistent with these limits and not derived from them. What the limits add
is that the reported curve and the true curve separate under reuse and
under a correlated judge, so a sigmoid in the reported curve is not
evidence either way about the true one until the ledger is published.

## 6. Not delivered

- No observed controller, environment or judge. The fixtures are exact
  arithmetic on declared quantities.
- The step-level channels assume a binary outcome per step and a
  conjunctive task; graded or path-dependent rewards need their own
  partition.
- L2's query model lets the loop patch any subset. A loop that can only
  retrain, not patch, has a noisier channel; the bound still holds as a
  lower bound.
- L4 treats a binary judge. A graded judge with correlated errors needs the
  same decomposition on a larger alphabet.
- A measurement procedure for \(\varepsilon_1\): grade a sealed sample with
  an independent judge and compare error overlap. Proposed, not built.

The main-thread piece is done and verified; the three sub-agents are still running. Here's where things stand.

**Main thread: `paper/rl_training_signal_limits.md` + `evaluation_feedback_signal.py`** (20 tests, 15 checks, receipt written, all in the `wt_main` worktree, uncommitted until the agents report). It types RL in the calculus as `Repeat_G(Feedback_{D_train, item_level})`, states five axioms with their falsifiers, and derives six limits. The exact pieces built today:

- **L1, credit assignment is a step-level access class.** Outcome reward, first-failure, partial credit and process reward are partitions of the step record with 2, T+1, T+1 and 2^T images. Partial credit and first-failure are *incomparable*. Outcome reward gives one bit per episode; identifying which of T steps fail needs ≥ T outcome episodes vs 1 process episode.
- **L2, score-only is item-level after finitely many queries.** A loop that can patch subsets and read a score recovers the failed items by group testing. Exact minimax query counts for n ≤ 7 sit between the counting bound ⌈log C(n,f)/log(f+1)⌉ and recursive halving (e.g. n=6, f=2: bound 3, exact 4, halving 5). So the ledger's `score_queries` count is a leakage bound: below the bound the loop can't know the items; above the halving count a "score-only" set is effectively item-level.
- **L4, a judge that shares errors with the judged.** Observed accuracy = a − ε + 2(1−a)ε₁, where ε₁ is the judge's error rate on the controller's wrong answers. It reaches the noise ceiling 1−ε exactly when ε₁ ≥ ½, whatever a and ε; that's feasible iff ε ≥ (1−a)/2. In the standing fixture the independent judge reports 37/50, the most correlated feasible judge reports 9/10, the ceiling, with no memorization. So the ceiling check has a confound, and it is the learned-judge case.
- **L6, Blackwell direction.** Finer feedback is worth at least as much to the loop's keep-or-drop decision, for every prior and utility; for incomparable channels each wins some decision (exact fixture: 3/4 vs 1/2 both ways).

**Will's posts.** I could not read today's timeline from here: X walls the profile without login, the Nitter mirrors are gone (X's cease-and-desists, September), and the syndication endpoint rate-limits anonymous requests. The note therefore engages his *stated* position from what is indexed: the [July 2026 sigmoid argument](https://x.com/willccbb?lang=en) (surfaced by search, no direct link), the [June quip about RSI reaching LinkedIn](https://x.com/willccbb/status/2061283954188280281), the [verifiers v1 framing of one environment abstraction for evals, RL and SFT](https://x.com/willccbb/status/2076449433483616346), and the [Latent Space interview](https://www.latent.space/p/willccbb): evals saturate and always need replacing; deterministic rewards are painful; LLM-as-judge is "underexplored". Two ways to close the gap, your call: paste today's posts here, or let me open x.com in your Chrome (read-only, your logged-in session).

**What the math says so far about "is he overestimating RL".** It doesn't settle it, and I'd rather be precise about why. The limits locate where a *reported* RL gain can arise with no true gain: eval reuse (L2, L5), a narrow reward channel (L1), and a judge correlated with the policy (L4). His sigmoid view is consistent with them, not derived from them. The claim that would make him wrong is specific: that environment supply keeps pace with consumption, and that model-based judges don't bring L4 with them. Both are declarable quantities (set sizes, query and patch counts, ε and ε₁, readout ledger), which is the white-boxing result: an RL progress claim is checkable from its ledger without access to the weights. None of the five claims in the atlas published those counts.

When the agents report I'll review their modules, fold the lattice, multi-generation chain and composition laws into the note's cross-references, and commit the lot on the branch.

1	# Composition laws for Feedback
2	
3	Version 0.1 — 2026-10-12. Companion to [evaluation_design_calculus.md](evaluation_design_calculus.md)
4	(§3 footprints, §4 Repeat, §5 disjoint-update law, §7 order effects) and
5	[evaluation_feedback_insertions.md](evaluation_feedback_insertions.md) (\(\operatorname{Feedback}_{s,q}\),
6	the ledger). Nothing here calls a model or observes a controller. Each statement is an algebraic
7	identity with a proof or an exhaustive check on an enumerated finite model; its evidence line says which.
8	
9	```powershell
10	$env:PYTHONPATH = "src"
11	python scripts/verify_evaluation_feedback_composition.py --output output/evaluation_feedback_composition/composition_v0_1.json
12	python -m pytest tests/test_evaluation_feedback_composition.py -q
13	```
14	
15	Receipt: `output/evaluation_feedback_composition/composition_v0_1.json` (22 checks, `all_passed: true`,
16	source hashes). Tests: 99. Notation: \(a;b\) applies \(a\) first.
17	
18	## 1. The executable record
19	
20	`src/spiral_ln/evaluation_feedback_composition.py` implements \(\mathcal E\) as a frozen record: six
21	`game.*` fields (\(G\): legal actions, revealed-or-hidden resource, utility, budget, horizon, carry map,
22	for the two-location game played once per item); `pi` (\(\Pi\): observation-to-action lookup plus
23	per-item overrides, so a patch memorizes an item identifier); `items` (\(D\): `s0,s1` in selection set
24	`S`, `r0,r1` in readout set `R`); `acquisition` (\(Z\): privileged record, action redacted on named
25	sets); `judgment` (\(J\): one for the resource, inverted on flipped items, less a cost for choosing
26	right; undefined on a redacted record); `generation` (\(g\)); `declarations` (role and access class
27	per set). \(\mathcal A\) enters only in Proposition 4; \(C\) is not modeled.
28	
29	Each operator is a pure function with a declared footprint. Restrict, Grant, Cap, Hide (player-facing),
30	Observe (observation-only), Controller, Rescore, Payoff (optionally also installing the utility as the
31	judgment) and Repeat write the fields their names suggest and read at most what they write.
32	\(\operatorname{Feedback}_{S,q}\) reads `game.legal`, `game.revealed`, `pi`, `items`, `acquisition`,

(§3 footprints, §4 Repeat, §5 disjoint-update law, §7 order effects) and

identity with a proof or an exhaustive check on an enumerated finite model; its evidence line says which.

```powershell
$env:PYTHONPATH = "src"
python scripts/verify_evaluation_feedback_composition.py --output output/evaluation_feedback_composition/composition_v0_1.json
python -m pytest tests/test_evaluation_feedback_composition.py -q
```

sets); `judgment` (\(J\): one for the resource, inverted on flipped items, less a cost for choosing
right; undefined on a redacted record); `generation` (\(g\)); `declarations` (role and access class
per set). \(\mathcal A\) enters only in Proposition 4; \(C\) is not modeled.

Each operator is a pure function with a declared footprint. Restrict, Grant, Cap, Hide (player-facing),
Observe (observation-only), Controller, Rescore, Payoff (optionally also installing the utility as the
judgment) and Repeat write the fields their names suggest and read at most what they write.
\(\operatorname{Feedback}_{S,q}\) reads `game.legal`, `game.revealed`, `pi`, `items`, `acquisition`,
`judgment`, `declarations`, `generation` and writes `pi`, `generation`: item-level access returns the
per-item vector and overrides each item judged nonpositive with the other action; score-only returns

overlapping footprints. The non-commuting pairs, with the field in which the two orders differ:

| Pair | Differ in | First witness (receipt) |
|---|---|---|
| Grant\(_2\), Cap\(_5\) | `game.budget` | budget 4: grant-then-cap 5, cap-then-grant 6 (calculus §5) |

content.text:
Composition is in and integrated; the lattice and multi-generation agents are still running, so the next steps (folding their results into the note, running the full suite, committing on the branch) wait on them.

What the composition agent established, after my own check (99 tests, 22 checks, only new files):

- **Disjoint-update law, proven** for sound footprints, and an exhaustive commutation table over 13 operators on 384 records: 60 pairs commute by disjointness, 15 don't, 3 commute despite overlap. The non-commutations that matter for the feedback story are all `pi`-only: `Rescore;Feedback` ≠ `Feedback;Rescore` (rescoring first changes what the loop learns; after, only the readout), likewise `Observe`, `Controller`, player-facing `Hide`, `Restrict`, and a `Payoff` that also installs its utility as the judgment. `Repeat` commutes with `Feedback` at design time, which is exactly why the aggregation unit has to be stated separately.
- **Typing ⟺ ledger.** Over all 22,143 operator sequences of length ≤ 4 in three declaration contexts, a sequence is well-typed under the stated Γ rules iff `audit_ledger` reports it respected, zero mismatches. One rule needed sharpening: sealed `Feedback` transmits nothing, so it is always typed. I added that, and the point that a `readout` naming a selection set is a malformed event rather than a breach, to the insertions text.
- **Generations are not blocks, proven.** With the kept controller carried into the next pool, the second-generation score is the max of 2K−1 i.i.d. draws, strictly above the first in expectation and not exchangeable with it; the generation mean overstates what the same aggregation reports over independent blocks, while the sealed readout stays at p. Fixture n=1, K=2, p=½: 3/4 → 7/8, ρ from 1/4 to 3/8.
- **ρ alone does not identify feedback.** An offline `Rescore` on the readout set moves ρ by the same amount as a memorizing `Feedback` with no ledger event; only the ledger separates them.

1	# Partial leakage as a lattice of feedback channels
2	
3	Version 0.1 — 2026-10-12. Exact fixtures for the gap named in
4	[evaluation_feedback_insertions.md](evaluation_feedback_insertions.md) §H:
5	feedback that reveals failure *categories* and not items. Files:
6	`src/spiral_ln/evaluation_feedback_lattice.py`, `tests/test_evaluation_feedback_lattice.py`,
7	`output/evaluation_feedback_lattice/lattice_v0_1.json`. No model was called.
8	Evidence levels follow the calculus card (§11): *algebraic identity* (proved
9	for all inputs) or *finite verified example* (checked on the enumerated cases
10	only); no synthetic mechanism result is claimed.
11	
12	```powershell
13	$env:PYTHONPATH = "src"
14	python scripts/verify_evaluation_feedback_lattice.py --output output/evaluation_feedback_lattice/lattice_v0_1.json
15	python -m pytest tests/test_evaluation_feedback_lattice.py -q
16	```
17	
18	## 1. Channels are partitions; the lattice data-processing law
19	
20	A deterministic feedback channel on records \(\{0,1\}^n\) is a function \(f\);
21	two channels carry the same information exactly when \(\ker f\) agrees, so a
22	channel *is* a partition of the record set. Convention: \(p\le q\) when \(q\)
23	refines \(p\); the one-block partition (`sealed`) is the bottom, the discrete
24	partition (`item_level`) the top, \(p\vee q\) the common refinement (observing
25	both) and \(p\wedge q\) the finest common coarsening (components of the union
26	of the two relations). This is the partition lattice, orientation reversed.
27	
28	**Proposition 1 (lattice data-processing law and converse).** For all
29	distributions \(P,Q\) on records, \(p\le q\) implies
30	\(\mathrm{TV}(p_\#P,p_\#Q)\le\mathrm{TV}(q_\#P,q_\#Q)\); and if \(p\not\le q\)
31	there are point masses \(P,Q\) reversing the inequality.
32	
33	*Proof.* \(\mathrm{TV}(p_\#P,p_\#Q)=\max_U|P(U)-Q(U)|\) over unions \(U\) of
34	blocks of \(p\). When \(q\) refines \(p\), every block of \(p\) is a union of
35	blocks of \(q\), so the maximum for \(p\) ranges over a subset of the sets
36	available to \(q\). If \(q\) does not refine \(p\), some block of \(q\) holds
37	\(x,y\) that \(p\) separates; \(P=\delta_x,Q=\delta_y\) give \(\mathrm{TV}\)
38	one through \(p\) and zero through \(q\). \(\square\)
39	
40	So \(\mathrm{TV}\) through \(p\vee q\) is at least the larger of the two and
41	through \(p\wedge q\) at most the smaller; the testbed's one-kernel contraction
42	is one comparable pair. *Evidence status: algebraic identity.* Fixture
43	`lattice_fixture(2, 2)`: all 15 partitions of \(\{0,1\}^2\), 225 ordered pairs,
44	100 pairs of grid distributions; the law holds on every comparable pair, fails
45	somewhere on every non-comparable pair, join and meet satisfy their lattice
46	definitions, and `access_kernel`'s three classes are bottom, middle, top.
47	
48	## 2. Category leakage is an order embedding, not a scale
49	
50	A category map, a partition \(\gamma\) of the items \([n]\), induces the channel
51	\(\Phi(\gamma)\): the per-category pass-count vector.
52	
53	**Proposition 2.** \(\Phi(\gamma)\le\Phi(\gamma')\) iff \(\gamma\le\gamma'\),
54	so \(\Phi\) is an order embedding; \(\Phi(\text{one block})=\)`score_only` and
55	\(\Phi(\text{singletons})=\)`item_level`.
56	
57	*Proof.* If \(\gamma'\) refines \(\gamma\), each \(\gamma\)-count is a sum of
58	\(\gamma'\)-counts, so equal \(\gamma'\)-counts force equal \(\gamma\)-counts.
59	If not, some \(\gamma'\)-block holds items \(i,j\) that \(\gamma\) separates;
60	the records failing only \(i\) and only \(j\) have equal \(\gamma'\)-counts and
61	unequal \(\gamma\)-counts. The endpoints are the definitions. \(\square\)
62	*Evidence status: algebraic identity*, checked exhaustively on all 5 maps of
63	\([3]\) and 15 maps of \([4]\) in `category_order_fixture`.
64	
65	The image is order-isomorphic to the partition lattice of \([n]\), not a chain
66	for \(n\ge3\), so "how much leaks" has no scalar. On \([3]\), with
67	\(A=\{0,1\}|\{2\}\) and \(B=\{0\}|\{1,2\}\): \(B\) separates "fail item 0" from
68	"fail item 1" (\(\mathrm{TV}=1\)) while \(A\) gives 0, and conversely for "fail 1" vs "fail 2".
69	
70	**Finite observation.** \(\Phi\) does not preserve joins: for rows
71	\(\{0,1\}|\{2,3\}\) and columns \(\{0,2\}|\{1,3\}\), \(\Phi(\gamma\vee\gamma')\)
72	is `item_level` but \(\Phi(\gamma)\vee\Phi(\gamma')\) confuses `1001` with
73	`0110` (equal row and column sums): two separate category leaks are strictly
74	coarser than one leak with the refined categories. On \([4]\), 219 of 225
75	ordered pairs preserve the join and 225 of 225 the meet. *Finite verified
76	example*: the join failure is a proof by witness; meet preservation is not proved.
77	
78	## 3. Cost of a leak, exact
79	
80	Setting of `noise_ceiling_fixture`: clean accuracy \(4/5\), flip \(1/10\), so
81	\(v=37/50\), ceiling \(9/10\); on \(n=50\) items 13 fail and \(H=8\) hits are
82	needed. Under \(\Phi(\gamma)\) the loop knows \((n_c,F_c)\) per category and
83	patches uniformly at random without replacement; a patch on a passed item gains nothing.
84	
85	**Proposition 3 (expected gain is exact; greedy is optimal).** The \(j\)-th
86	patch in category \(c\) hits with conditional probability

88	probability \(F_c/n_c\) for every \(j\) (exchangeability). So \(m_c\) patches

# Partial leakage as a lattice of feedback channels

Version 0.1 — 2026-10-12. Exact fixtures for the gap named in
[evaluation_feedback_insertions.md](evaluation_feedback_insertions.md) §H:
feedback that reveals failure *categories* and not items. Files:
`src/spiral_ln/evaluation_feedback_lattice.py`, `tests/test_evaluation_feedback_lattice.py`,
`output/evaluation_feedback_lattice/lattice_v0_1.json`. No model was called.
Evidence levels follow the calculus card (§11): *algebraic identity* (proved
for all inputs) or *finite verified example* (checked on the enumerated cases
only); no synthetic mechanism result is claimed.

```powershell
$env:PYTHONPATH = "src"
python scripts/verify_evaluation_feedback_lattice.py --output output/evaluation_feedback_lattice/lattice_v0_1.json
python -m pytest tests/test_evaluation_feedback_lattice.py -q
```

## 1. Channels are partitions; the lattice data-processing law

A deterministic feedback channel on records \(\{0,1\}^n\) is a function \(f\);
two channels carry the same information exactly when \(\ker f\) agrees, so a
channel *is* a partition of the record set. Convention: \(p\le q\) when \(q\)
refines \(p\); the one-block partition (`sealed`) is the bottom, the discrete
partition (`item_level`) the top, \(p\vee q\) the common refinement (observing
both) and \(p\wedge q\) the finest common coarsening (components of the union
of the two relations). This is the partition lattice, orientation reversed.

**Proposition 1 (lattice data-processing law and converse).** For all
distributions \(P,Q\) on records, \(p\le q\) implies
\(\mathrm{TV}(p_\#P,p_\#Q)\le\mathrm{TV}(q_\#P,q_\#Q)\); and if \(p\not\le q\)
there are point masses \(P,Q\) reversing the inequality.

*Proof.* \(\mathrm{TV}(p_\#P,p_\#Q)=\max_U|P(U)-Q(U)|\) over unions \(U\) of
blocks of \(p\). When \(q\) refines \(p\), every block of \(p\) is a union of
blocks of \(q\), so the maximum for \(p\) ranges over a subset of the sets
available to \(q\). If \(q\) does not refine \(p\), some block of \(q\) holds
\(x,y\) that \(p\) separates; \(P=\delta_x,Q=\delta_y\) give \(\mathrm{TV}\)
one through \(p\) and zero through \(q\). \(\square\)

So \(\mathrm{TV}\) through \(p\vee q\) is at least the larger of the two and
through \(p\wedge q\) at most the smaller; the testbed's one-kernel contraction
is one comparable pair. *Evidence status: algebraic identity.* Fixture
`lattice_fixture(2, 2)`: all 15 partitions of \(\{0,1\}^2\), 225 ordered pairs,
100 pairs of grid distributions; the law holds on every comparable pair, fails
somewhere on every non-comparable pair, join and meet satisfy their lattice
definitions, and `access_kernel`'s three classes are bottom, middle, top.

## 2. Category leakage is an order embedding, not a scale

A category map, a partition \(\gamma\) of the items \([n]\), induces the channel
\(\Phi(\gamma)\): the per-category pass-count vector.

**Proposition 2.** \(\Phi(\gamma)\le\Phi(\gamma')\) iff \(\gamma\le\gamma'\),
so \(\Phi\) is an order embedding; \(\Phi(\text{one block})=\)`score_only` and
\(\Phi(\text{singletons})=\)`item_level`.

*Proof.* If \(\gamma'\) refines \(\gamma\), each \(\gamma\)-count is a sum of
\(\gamma'\)-counts, so equal \(\gamma'\)-counts force equal \(\gamma\)-counts.
If not, some \(\gamma'\)-block holds items \(i,j\) that \(\gamma\) separates;
the records failing only \(i\) and only \(j\) have equal \(\gamma'\)-counts and
unequal \(\gamma\)-counts. The endpoints are the definitions. \(\square\)
*Evidence status: algebraic identity*, checked exhaustively on all 5 maps of
\([3]\) and 15 maps of \([4]\) in `category_order_fixture`.

The image is order-isomorphic to the partition lattice of \([n]\), not a chain
for \(n\ge3\), so "how much leaks" has no scalar. On \([3]\), with
\(A=\{0,1\}|\{2\}\) and \(B=\{0\}|\{1,2\}\): \(B\) separates "fail item 0" from
"fail item 1" (\(\mathrm{TV}=1\)) while \(A\) gives 0, and conversely for "fail 1" vs "fail 2".

**Finite observation.** \(\Phi\) does not preserve joins: for rows
\(\{0,1\}|\{2,3\}\) and columns \(\{0,2\}|\{1,3\}\), \(\Phi(\gamma\vee\gamma')\)
is `item_level` but \(\Phi(\gamma)\vee\Phi(\gamma')\) confuses `1001` with
`0110` (equal row and column sums): two separate category leaks are strictly
coarser than one leak with the refined categories. On \([4]\), 219 of 225
ordered pairs preserve the join and 225 of 225 the meet. *Finite verified
example*: the join failure is a proof by witness; meet preservation is not proved.

## 3. Cost of a leak, exact

Setting of `noise_ceiling_fixture`: clean accuracy \(4/5\), flip \(1/10\), so
\(v=37/50\), ceiling \(9/10\); on \(n=50\) items 13 fail and \(H=8\) hits are
needed. Under \(\Phi(\gamma)\) the loop knows \((n_c,F_c)\) per category and
patches uniformly at random without replacement; a patch on a passed item gains nothing.

**Proposition 3 (expected gain is exact; greedy is optimal).** The \(j\)-th
patch in category \(c\) hits with conditional probability
\((F_c-h)/(n_c-j+1)\) given \(h\) earlier hits, and with unconditional
probability \(F_c/n_c\) for every \(j\) (exchangeability). So \(m_c\) patches
hit exactly \(m_cF_c/n_c\) in expectation: the expected-value formula of the
insertions note is the hypergeometric mean, not an approximation. Every patch
in \(c\) has the same marginal value, so filling categories in decreasing order
of \(F_c/n_c\) maximizes expected hits at every patch count. *Algebraic
identity*; checked against every allocation and every patch order.

**Proposition 4 (patches to the ceiling).** With \(c_1,c_2,\dots\) the greedy
order, \(j\) the first index with \(\sum_{i\le j}F_{c_i}\ge H\),
\(N_{<j}=\sum_{i<j}n_{c_i}\) and \(H_j=H-\sum_{i<j}F_{c_i}\in[1,F_{c_j}]\):
the expected score reaches the ceiling at \(m^*=N_{<j}+H_jn_{c_j}/F_{c_j}\),
and the realized score first reaches it at a stopping time \(T\) with
\(\mathbb E[T]=N_{<j}+H_j(n_{c_j}+1)/(F_{c_j}+1)\) (negative-hypergeometric
mean; earlier categories are patched completely, so their hits are fixed). Hence
\(m^*-\mathbb E[T]=H_j(n_{c_j}-F_{c_j})/(F_{c_j}(F_{c_j}+1))\in[0,m^*/(F_{c_j}+1))\):
the expected-score crossing never understates the expected patch count. One
category: \(m^*/n=(1-\varepsilon-v)/(1-v)=8/13\), \(\mathbb E[T]=204/7\).
Singleton categories: both equal \(H\), share \(4/25\). *Algebraic identity*,
cross-checked by enumerating every patch order on three category shapes and
against `ceiling_detection_threshold` and `targeted_ceiling_detection_threshold`.

**Proposition 5 (monotonicity of \(m^*\)).** If \(\gamma'\) refines \(\gamma\)
then \(m^*(\gamma')\le m^*(\gamma)\) for every failure pattern. *Proof.* Each
\(\gamma\)-rate is the size-weighted mean of its \(\gamma'\)-sub-rates, so the
\(\gamma\) expected-hit curve is attainable under \(\gamma'\) by proportional
(fractional) allocation, and the \(\gamma'\)-greedy curve is at least it.
\(\square\) *Algebraic identity*; checked over all 203 maps of \([6]\), 2268
refining pairs, 63 patterns, two requirements each.

**Finite observations on the stopping time.** \(\mathbb E[T]\) under the static
greedy schedule is *not* monotone along refinement: one block \((4,2)\), \(H=2\),
gives \(10/3\); \((2,1),(2,1)\) gives \(7/2\). On \([6]\): record `001101`,
\(H=3\), \(21/4\) against \(11/2\). An adaptive schedule that re-queries the
channel after each patch and patches the highest current rate (exact dynamic
programming on count multisets) was at most the static value in every
enumerated case and monotone on every refining pair of \([6]\) and along the
50-item chain; no proof is offered. Chain with block sizes 50, 25, 10, 5, 2, 1
and failures at items \(0,4,\dots,48\): \(m^*/n=8/13,7/12,8/15,1/2,8/25,4/25\);
\(\mathbb E[T]_{\text{static}}=204/7,201/7,51/2,23,31/2,8\);
\(\mathbb E[T]_{\text{adaptive}}\approx29.14,25.64,21.17,18,12,8\).
*Finite verified example.*

## 4. Ledger wrapper

`audit_category_ledger` accepts a `category_feedback` event carrying the
partition used, records it with its position (`score_only`, `category`,
`item_level`), and forwards to `audit_ledger` one `score_query` per block of
two or more items plus one `item_feedback` naming the singleton items (a count
on a singleton is that item's outcome), so the base access rules apply. An
optional declared partition per set bounds the leak in the lattice; a finer
event is a recorded breach. `audit_ledger` is wrapped, not edited.

## Boundaries

Deterministic channels only: a stochastic channel is a Markov kernel, for which
the \(\mathrm{TV}\) contraction survives (`_pushforward`) but which has no
partition, no lattice position, and no converse of Proposition 1; the Blackwell
preorder on kernels is not treated. Items are independent and a patch changes
its own item only, which the nearest-neighbour learner in `output/eval_reuse_toys`
violated. Greedy ties break by index; \(\mathbb E[T]_{\text{static}}\) depends
on that choice when two categories share a rate. No model or loop evidence.

content.text:
Two of three agents are in and integrated; the multi-generation chain is the one still running, and the commit waits on it.

The lattice agent's results, after my own check (64 tests, 19 checks, only new files):

- **Lattice data-processing law with converse, proven.** Deterministic channels are partitions of the record space; coarser means TV-dominated for every pair of distributions, and the converse holds too, so TV-domination for all P, Q *characterizes* the refinement order. The existing three classes are bottom, middle and top.
- **Category leakage is an order embedding, not a scale.** Finer item categories give a finer channel and vice versa, so "how much leaks" is a partial order for n ≥ 3; exhibited both directions of incomparability on three items. And Φ does not preserve joins: row-and-column counts observed together are strictly finer than the join of the two observed separately (they confuse `1001` with `0110`). I've put the consequence in the main note: a ledger must record the joint channel.
- **Cost of a leak, exact.** The expected-value formula is the hypergeometric mean, not an approximation; greedy by failure rate is optimal at every patch count; the crossing point m* is monotone along refinement (proven), running 8/13 → 7/12 → 8/15 → 1/2 → 8/25 → 4/25 along a 50-item chain. The expected *stopping time* is not monotone, with a counterexample on six items; an adaptive re-querying schedule was monotone on every enumerated case, no proof.
- A `category_feedback` ledger event that wraps `audit_ledger` without editing it.

Both of its unproven items (meet preservation of Φ, adaptive-schedule monotonicity) are marked as finite checks in the note. Nothing else to do until the multi-generation agent reports and you say how to get at Will's posts.

21	## 1. The chain: vertices, edges, policy
22	
23	A reused set of \(n\) items. **State**: the incumbent's realized count \(c\in\{0,\dots,n\}\) on
24	that set. Each generation draws \(K\) candidates i.i.d. and independent of the incumbent,
25	\(C_k\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)\), \(M=\max_k C_k\). **Actions**: accept or reject the best candidate.
26	**Policy**: accept iff \(M>c+t(c)\), \(t:\{0..n\}\to\mathbb N\). **Edges**: \(c\to j\) with
27	probability \(P(M=j)\) for \(j>c+t(c)\); the self-loop carries \(F(c+t(c))^K\), \(F\) the binomial
28	CDF with \(F(j)=1\) for \(j\ge n\). The graph is a DAG of upward edges plus self-loops; its sinks
29	\(\{c:c+t(c)\ge n\}\) are the absorbing states. Initial state \(c_0\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)\).
30	Reported score \(c_G/n\); readout value \(p\); readout gap \(\rho_G=\mathbb E[c_G]/n-p\). In the
31	calculus: \(\operatorname{Repeat}_G\) of one generation with carry map "keep \(c\)", composed
32	with \(\operatorname{Feedback}_{s,\text{score-only}}\) whose consumer selects among candidates.
33	
34	**Gate discretization.** `sim.js` accepts iff \(M>c+z\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}\,n\) with \(p=c/n\), i.e.
35	\(M-c>z\sqrt{c(n-c)/n}\). The difference is an integer \(d\), and \(d>x\) iff
36	\(d\ge\lfloor x\rfloor+1\), so \(t(c)=\lfloor z\sqrt{c(n-c)/n}\rfloor\), computed exactly as
37	\(\lfloor\sqrt{a/b}\rfloor=\mathrm{isqrt}(ab)\,//\,b\). For \(n=16,z=3\):
38	\(t=(0,2,3,4,5,5,5,5,6,5,5,5,5,4,3,2,0)\). Fixture `gate_threshold`, checked by
39	\(t^2\le z^2c(n-c)/n<(t+1)^2\) on every state and against the real-valued rule for every
40	integer \(d\). Algebraic identity.
41	
42	## 2. Naive reuse is a running maximum
43	
44	**Proposition 1.** With \(t\equiv0\), \(c_G=\max(c_0,M_1,\dots,M_G)\), the maximum of \(GK+1\)
45	i.i.d. \(\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)\) draws, so \(\rho_G=\) `selection_inflation(n, GK+1, p).readout_gap`.
46	The initial incumbent is one draw because it is scored on the reused set like every candidate;
47	a *known* count \(c_0\) gives \(\mathbb E[\max(c_0,X)]\), \(X\) the max of \(GK\) draws
48	(`running_max_from_point`). *Proof.* If \(M_g>c_{g-1}\) the policy sets
49	\(c_g=M_g=\max(c_{g-1},M_g)\); otherwise \(c_g=c_{g-1}=\max(c_{g-1},M_g)\). Induct. Algebraic
50	identity. The DP equals the closed form on all 18 null cells (\(n\in\{4,8,16\}\),
51	\(K\in\{1,2,4\}\), \(p\in\{\tfrac12,\tfrac14\}\), \(G=0..20\)); at \(n=2,K=2,G=2\) it equals
52	literal enumeration of all \(2^{10}\) item outcomes.
53	
54	**Consequences.** (i) \(\rho_G\) is non-decreasing in \(G\): a maximum over more draws is
55	pointwise larger. (ii) Increments are non-increasing: \(a_{m+1}-a_m=\mathbb E[(X-M_m)^+]\) with
56	\(M_m\) pointwise non-decreasing in \(m\). (iii) \(P(c_G=n)=1-(1-p^n)^{GK+1}\), so for fixed
57	\(n\) and \(0<p<1\), \(\rho_G\uparrow1-p\): bounded by the lattice, never stationary. These are
58	algebraic identities with the proofs above; the fixture verifies them on the enumerated cells
59	only. *Remark, not verified:* while \(GK\) is large and the maximum is still far from \(n\),
60	the Gaussian extreme-value approximation gives \(\rho_G\approx\sqrt{2\ln(GK+1)\,p(1-p)/n}\).
61	
62	Values at \(p=\tfrac12\) (exact in the receipt). \(n=8,K=2\): \(\rho_1=19305/131072\approx0.1473\),
63	\(\rho_5\approx0.2726\), \(\rho_{10}\approx0.3212\), \(\rho_{20}\approx0.3645\). \(n=16,K=4\):
64	\(0.1440,\ 0.2318,\ 0.2648,\ 0.2947\). \(n=4,K=1\): \(\rho_1=35/256\), the insertions note's
65	two-candidate four-item value, the incumbent being the second candidate.

67	## 3. Fresh blocks
68	
69	**Proposition 2.** (a) If each generation scores incumbent and candidates on a fresh block and
70	reports on a second fresh block, the expected reported score is \(p\) at every generation: the
71	readout block is independent of whatever selected the controller, and under the null every
72	controller has probability \(p\). (b) If it reports on the selection block, the reported count
73	at \(g\ge1\) is \(M\) if \(M>I+t(I)\), else \(I\), with \(I\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)\) the

76	\(g\ge1\) and does not accumulate. Both algebraic identities (independence, linearity);

78	coincides with (b) at \(G=1\) for any gate and exceeds it strictly for \(G\ge2\) on every

85	unconditional rate at generation \(g\) is \(\sum_c\pi_{g-1}(c)\alpha(c)\). Algebraic identity.

90	maximum is the naive state; hence \(c^t_G\le c^0_G\) pointwise, \(\rho^t_G\le\rho^0_G\), and
91	\(\alpha^t(c)\le\alpha^0(c)\). Algebraic identity by coupling; its hypothesis is that every

93	can reverse (§5). Values at \(G=20,p=\tfrac12,n=16,K=4\): naive \(0.2947\); \(z=1\): \(0.2723\);

96	ceiling: for \(n=8,z=3\) states \(4..8\) absorb, so a gated loop freezes; the simulation's
97	GATED arm accepting 0–2% of generations is the same mechanism.
98	
99	## 5. True gains: the drift chain
100	
101	State \((c,i)\) with \(p(i)=\min(1,\tfrac14+i/8)\). Each candidate draws a gain multiple \(m\)
102	from a law (constant, or one law per generation), has probability \(p(i+m)\), and on acceptance
103	the state becomes \((M,i+m^*)\), \(m^*\) the accepted candidate's gain; by exchangeability
104	\(P(M=j,m^*=m)=P(M=j)\,q_m\,\mathrm{Bin}(n,p(i+m))(j)/\mathrm{mix}(j)\). Reported
105	\(\mathbb E[c_g]/n\), true \(\mathbb E[p(i_g)]\), phantom share \(1-\)true gain/reported gain.
106	Verified by enumeration of every gain draw and item outcome at \(n=2,K=2,G=2\) (six laws, two
107	policies); the zero-gain law reproduces the null chain exactly (test). Laws: *fixed*
108	\(\delta=\tfrac18\); *two-point* \(\delta=\tfrac18\) w.p. \(\tfrac14\); *decaying two-point*
109	\(q_g=\tfrac14(\tfrac34)^{g-1}\), a lattice analogue of the simulation's \(0.06\cdot0.95^{g-1}\).
110	Cells \((n,K)\in\{(4,2),(4,4),(8,2),(8,4),(16,2)\}\), \(G=20\), naive and \(z=1\). Everything
111	below is a synthetic mechanism result on those cells and nothing more.

113	- Two-point, naive, \(n=8,K=2\): reported \(0.778\), true \(0.420\); phantom share \(0.678\)
114	  over \(0..20\), \(0.711\) early half, \(0.504\) late half; late/early gain ratio reported
115	  \(0.195\), true \(0.334\).
116	- Decaying, naive, \(n=8,K=2\): phantom \(0.838\) whole, \(0.977\) late; late/early reported
117	  \(0.130\) versus true \(0.016\).
118	- Against `results.json`: P3 (late phantom share above one half under naive reuse) holds on
119	  every cell with \(n\le8\) for both laws and on all cells for the decaying law. P5 (reported
120	  late/early ratio at least twice the true one) holds only under the decaying schedule (about
121	  8× here, 4× in the simulation); with constant gains the ordering reverses on every cell,
122	  because an inflated count is beaten less often by no-gain candidates, so late acceptances
123	  are enriched for real gains. P5 is a property of the simulation's decaying gain scale, not
124	  of reuse alone.
125	- Gate ordering with true gains: fixed gain, \(z=1\) gap *above* naive on every cell
126	  (\(n=8,K=2\): \(0.347\) vs \(0.279\)), because the gate refuses true gains too and the truth
127	  lags further; decaying gain, gate below naive on every cell. Proposition 4 is a null result
128	  and must not be read as "gating reduces the gap".
129	- Lattice ceiling: with fixed gain at \(n=16\) the late phantom share is negative (reported score
130	  pinned near one while \(p\) still rises); phantom shares near the ceiling are not interpretable.
131	
132	## 6. The readout-gap series and the divergence flags
133	
134	\(\rho_g=\mathbb E[c_g]/n-\mathbb E[p_g]\). Feeding \((g,\mathbb E[c_g]/n,\mathbb E[p_g])\) at
135	\(g\in\{0,4,\dots,20\}\) to `divergence_flags` with margin \(\tfrac1{40}\) flags an interval iff

137	\(\rho=(0,.147,.202,.234,.256,.273,\dots,.365)\) gives flags T,T,T,F,F, a prefix as diminishing
138	increments require; two-point drift matches; the fresh arm flags only the first interval. A check on means.
139	
140	## 7. Boundaries
141	
142	Candidates are independent of the incumbent; `sim.js` perturbs the incumbent's per-item quirks
143	(\(\sin\phi=0.2\)), correlating each candidate's outcomes with the incumbent's item by item, which
144	shrinks the spread of \(M-c\) and lowers every per-generation inflation; the ratchet and
145	Propositions 1–4 keep their form with \(\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)\) replaced by the conditional law of a
146	correlated count. \(n\) is fixed; labels are clean; gains are i.i.d. across candidates; the
147	\(p\)-lattice is capped at one. Results concern distributions and expectations, not sample
148	paths. No model, agent, or observed-controller evidence is claimed.

- Decaying, naive, \(n=8,K=2\): phantom \(0.838\) whole, \(0.977\) late; late/early reported
  \(0.130\) versus true \(0.016\).
- Against `results.json`: P3 (late phantom share above one half under naive reuse) holds on
  every cell with \(n\le8\) for both laws and on all cells for the decaying law. P5 (reported
  late/early ratio at least twice the true one) holds only under the decaying schedule (about
  8× here, 4× in the simulation); with constant gains the ordering reverses on every cell,
  because an inflated count is beaten less often by no-gain candidates, so late acceptances
  are enriched for real gains. P5 is a property of the simulation's decaying gain scale, not
  of reuse alone.

  (\(n=8,K=2\): \(0.347\) vs \(0.279\)), because the gate refuses true gains too and the truth
  lags further; decaying gain, gate below naive on every cell. Proposition 4 is a null result
  and must not be read as "gating reduces the gap".
- Lattice ceiling: with fixed gain at \(n=16\) the late phantom share is negative (reported score
  pinned near one while \(p\) still rises); phantom shares near the ceiling are not interpretable.

## 6. The readout-gap series and the divergence flags

\(\rho_g=\mathbb E[c_g]/n-\mathbb E[p_g]\). Feeding \((g,\mathbb E[c_g]/n,\mathbb E[p_g])\) at
\(g\in\{0,4,\dots,20\}\) to `divergence_flags` with margin \(\tfrac1{40}\) flags an interval iff
\(\rho_{g_1}-\rho_{g_0}>\tfrac1{40}\) (identity in the definition). Null \(n=8,K=2\):
\(\rho=(0,.147,.202,.234,.256,.273,\dots,.365)\) gives flags T,T,T,F,F, a prefix as diminishing
increments require; two-point drift matches; the fresh arm flags only the first interval. A check on means.

## 7. Boundaries

Candidates are independent of the incumbent; `sim.js` perturbs the incumbent's per-item quirks
(\(\sin\phi=0.2\)), correlating each candidate's outcomes with the incumbent's item by item, which
shrinks the spread of \(M-c\) and lowers every per-generation inflation; the ratchet and
Propositions 1–4 keep their form with \(\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)\) replaced by the conditional law of a
correlated count. \(n\) is fixed; labels are clean; gains are i.i.d. across candidates; the
\(p\)-lattice is capped at one. Results concern distributions and expectations, not sample
paths. No model, agent, or observed-controller evidence is claimed.

prediction was a property of their decaying gain schedule, not of reuse.

Feedback channel: training-signal limits, leak lattice, multi-generation chain, composition laws

Four exact modules extend the Feedback operator of the insertions note; no
model, policy or environment is run anywhere. 382 tests pass; each module
has a verifier and a receipt with source hashes.

- evaluation_feedback_signal (20 tests, 15 checks): types RL as
  Repeat_G(Feedback_{train, item_level}); credit assignment as a step-level
  access class (outcome 2 images, partial credit and first-failure T+1 and
  incomparable, process 2^T); score-only is item-level after finitely many
  queries (counting bound <= exact minimax <= recursive halving, n <= 7); a
  judge sharing errors with the controller inflates observed accuracy by
  2(1-a)(eps1-eps) and reaches the noise ceiling at eps1 >= 1/2 with no
  memorization; finer feedback is worth at least as much to the loop's
  selection decision (Blackwell direction), incomparable channels each win
  some decision. Note: paper/rl_training_signal_limits.md, with five axioms
  and their falsifiers.
- evaluation_feedback_lattice (64 tests, 19 checks): deterministic channels
  are partitions; the data-processing law and its converse characterize the
  refinement order; category maps embed the item-partition lattice (no
  scalar "amount of leak"; joins are not preserved); the cost of a leak is
  exact (hypergeometric means, greedy optimal, crossing point monotone along
  refinement, 8/13 down to 4/25 on a 50-item chain; expected stopping time
  not monotone); a category_feedback ledger wrapper.
- evaluation_feedback_multigen (70 tests, 30 checks): the loop as a Markov
  chain on the score lattice; naive reuse is a running maximum, gap =
  selection_inflation(n, GK+1, p), non-decreasing, diminishing, toward 1-p;
  fresh blocks remove accumulation; the gate lowers the gap under the null
  only and can reverse with true gains; the simulations' P5 was a property
  of their decaying gain schedule.
- evaluation_feedback_composition (99 tests, 22 checks): a 13-operator
  executable record; disjoint-update law proven for sound footprints; the
  commutation table with witnesses (Rescore, Observe, Controller, Hide,
  Restrict and training Payoff all fail to commute with Feedback in pi);
  well-typed sequences are exactly the ledger-respected ones over 22,143
  sequences; generations joined by Feedback are not blocks (proven); an
  offline Rescore moves the readout gap with no ledger event.

Insertions note: records that a readout naming a selection set is a
malformed event, that sealed Feedback is always well-typed, and points the
"not delivered" list at the three companion notes.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

  some decision. Note: paper/rl_training_signal_limits.md, with five axioms
  and their falsifiers.

  are partitions; the data-processing law and its converse characterize the
  refinement order; category maps embed the item-partition lattice (no
  scalar "amount of leak"; joins are not preserved); the cost of a leak is
  exact (hypergeometric means, greedy optimal, crossing point monotone along
  refinement, 8/13 down to 4/25 on a 50-item chain; expected stopping time
  not monotone); a category_feedback ledger wrapper.

  chain on the score lattice; naive reuse is a running maximum, gap =
  selection_inflation(n, GK+1, p), non-decreasing, diminishing, toward 1-p;
  fresh blocks remove accumulation; the gate lowers the gap under the null
  only and can reverse with true gains; the simulations' P5 was a property
  of their decaying gain schedule.

  executable record; disjoint-update law proven for sound footprints; the
  commutation table with witnesses (Rescore, Observe, Controller, Hide,
  Restrict and training Payoff all fail to commute with Feedback in pi);
  well-typed sequences are exactly the ledger-respected ones over 22,143
  sequences; generations joined by Feedback are not blocks (proven); an
  offline Rescore moves the readout gap with no ledger event.

malformed event, that sealed Feedback is always well-typed, and points the
"not delivered" list at the three companion notes.

All four pieces are verified, integrated and committed as `b7b3ee1` on `feedback-channel-and-rsi-atlas` (three commits above `main`; nothing pushed; your `rtg-0` checkout untouched; scratch worktrees removed). 382 tests pass across the five modules; every module has a verifier and a receipt with source hashes.

**How it maps onto the programme you named**

| You asked for | Where it landed |
|---|---|
| Training signal definable in the eval notation | RL typed as `Repeat_G(Feedback_{train, item_level})`; credit assignment is the access class at the step grain (`rl_training_signal_limits.md` §2, L1) |
| Graph theory on Markov decision chains | The loop as a chain on the score lattice: DAG of upward edges plus self-loops, acceptance rule as policy, gate sinks; naive reuse = running max, gap = `selection_inflation(n, GK+1, p)` rising toward 1−p (`evaluation_feedback_multigen.md`) |
| Decision theory | Blackwell direction: finer feedback is worth at least as much for every prior and utility; incomparable channels each win some decision (signal L6); category leaks form a partial order, not a scale (lattice §2) |
| Complexity | Score-only is item-level after finitely many queries: counting bound ≤ exact minimax ≤ halving, so the ledger's `score_queries` is a leakage bound (signal L2); the cost of each lattice position is exact (lattice §3) |
| White-boxing as falsifiable axioms | A1–A5 with the observation that falsifies each; L1–L6 derived from them; the eval-card quantities that make an RL progress claim checkable without the weights (signal §3–§5) |
| Composition / limits of the notation itself | Disjoint-update law proven; 15 operator pairs that don't commute with Feedback, with witnesses; typing ⟺ ledger over 22,143 sequences (`evaluation_feedback_composition.md`) |

**Results I'd single out**

- A judge that shares half its errors with the controller reports the noise ceiling for a controller that learned nothing: observed = a − ε + 2(1−a)ε₁, ceiling at ε₁ ≥ ½, feasible iff ε ≥ (1−a)/2. That is the learned-judge case, and it confounds the ceiling check.
- Two category leaks observed together are strictly finer than the join of the two observed apart, so disclosure has to record the joint channel.
- The gate from the toy-run preregistration lowers the gap only under the null; with true gains it can raise it, because it refuses those too. And the simulations' "late gains look larger" prediction was their decaying gain schedule, not reuse.
- An offline rescoring of the readout set moves ρ by the same amount as a memorizing feedback step and leaves no trace except in the ledger.

**What is proven in general vs enumerated** is stated per proposition in each note. Still open, and marked so: meet preservation of the category map, monotonicity of the adaptive patch schedule, the extreme-value asymptotic, correlated candidates (the JS sims' case), a gate-vs-naive theorem under true gains, and a measurement procedure for ε₁.

**On the Will Brown question.** The math doesn't say he's wrong. It says a reported RL gain can be phantom through three channels (reuse, narrow reward, correlated judge), that his sigmoid position is consistent with that and not derived from it, and that the claim which would make him wrong is specific and declarable: environment supply keeping pace with consumption, and model-based judges not bringing ε₁ ≥ ½. To engage what he said *today* I still need the posts: paste them, or tell me to open x.com in your Chrome (read-only).
