timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SearchPlugins
tools.description:
Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task. The user does not need to name a plugin: search when the task depends on their team's own process, systems or data and nothing you already have, the project's own scripts included, covers it.

Examples:
- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]
- "ship this to staging" → keywords ["deploy", "release", "staging"]
- "review this contract against our playbook" → keywords ["legal", "contract", "playbook"]
- "which deals close this week?" → keywords ["sales", "pipeline", "crm"]

Do not search unasked for one-off questions or tasks you can handle directly ("explain this regex", "fix this typo"), or after the user ignored a suggestion in this conversation.

Returns a ranked list with id, name, description, and whether the plugin is already enabled for this session (in a channel session, whether the channel has it). When results fit and SuggestPluginInstall is among your tools, call it to render the install card; otherwise relay the relevant results in text instead. If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

files.description: File paths (absolute or relative to cwd) to send to the user. Always pass an array, even for a single file.

caption.description: Optional short caption for the file(s).

status.description: Use 'proactive' when you're surfacing a file the user hasn't asked for and needs to see now — a generated artifact, a completed report. Use 'normal' when replying to something the user just said.

display.description: How the client should present the file. 'render' opens it inline in the side panel (for HTML, SVG, Mermaid, images, PDFs — anything the user wants to look at now). tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

# Session export: the feedback-channel programme, 2026-10-11 to 2026-10-13

This directory holds the raw export of the Claude Code session that produced
the branch `feedback-channel-and-rsi-atlas` up to commit `6518851`, published
so that other models and people can audit the journey rather than only its
results. The narrative map is `docs/feedback_channel_journey_2026-10-11_13.md`.

## Provenance

- Exported from the Claude desktop app on 2026-10-13 with the session-export
  tool as `session-export-1791887165690.zip` (8,230,922 bytes). SHA-256 of
  that zip: `32248dbc4651f45d41ef001a4afa586704f297e783e57c43e1e3ea60f02b9e58`.
  The zip stays on the author's machine. This directory is its content after
  the redaction below, with the one directory level named after the session
  id flattened away, and with one file added (next item).
- The zip omitted the transcript of one subagent, `agent-af4031af24ee0c5b0`
  (the sampling law of the gold-error estimate and the Dawid–Skene model),
  carrying only its `.meta.json` and `.prefix.json`. That transcript was
  taken from the session's on-disk subagent directory (1,605,454 bytes,
  SHA-256 before redaction
  `2e730122336798f0a32ced37e287c9755f5b557f69c90aadba5316b6463e48f2`) and
  passed through the same redaction as everything else.
- Session title "Eval Notation Math"; model `claude-fable-5-1` for most of
  the session (the first part ran on `claude-opus-5-5`; the switch is in the
  transcript); effort `xhigh`; permission mode `auto`.
- Contents: `transcript.jsonl` (the conversation, one JSON object per line in
  order); `subagents/` (the twelve subagent transcripts, each with a
  `.meta.json` and a `.prefix.json` holding the context it started with);
  `tool-results/` (three tool outputs too large to inline); `metadata.json`
  (the session's configuration, including the app's system-prompt append and
  the schemas of the connected tools); `custom-title.json`;
  `local-session-state.json`; `REDACTIONS.json` and `redact_export.py`
  (below). The zip also held a second copy of the transcript under the
  session id, byte-identical (SHA-256
  `b72a24ce7cceed040946b72347be3da2be3c379673a03f46c4ae4af02580495d`
  before redaction); it is omitted.

## Redaction

The session's first turn carried the assistant's persistent memory index and
the working tree's git status, and every subagent's starting context repeats
them. Both name private security reviews of third-party software whose
findings have not been disclosed, and the memory index summarises those
findings in a few words; three further memory lines describe the author's
own machine and infrastructure. None of that is part of the mathematics, and
the review material does not belong in a public repository, so it was removed
from every file by `redact_export.py` before the content was committed. The
script reads its terms from a JSON file that is **not** committed, because
publishing the terms would defeat the purpose; its report counts replacements
per file and per rule category only. The rules:

1. Memory-index lines about the private reviews are replaced whole by
[memory index entries about the author's other work: withheld]
2. Memory-index lines about the author's machine are replaced whole by
[memory index entries about the author's other work: withheld]
3. Working-tree directory names of the form `*-review/` and the
   like are replaced by `?? [redacted-review-dir]/`.
4. Remaining tokens naming those projects, their maintainers, their headline
   findings, or the author's untracked design-note files for one of them are
   replaced by `[redacted]`, keeping the rest of a file name where there was
   one (so `[redacted]_agents.ts`).

`REDACTIONS.json` lists, per file (paths relative to this directory), how
many replacements each rule made: 405 in all, across the transcript and the
twelve subagent transcripts; no other file was touched. Nothing else was
changed: no text of the assistant, the user, the subagents or the tool
results was edited beyond those tokens, JSON string escapes were left intact
so every line still parses, and line endings are LF.

Checks made on the redacted copy before committing:

- A rescan for every removed term, both by the rules' own patterns and by
  plain case-insensitive substring, finds only false positives: four-letter
  runs inside base64-encoded tool payloads, the words "marketing" and
  "markets", and the name of Claude Code's built-in `security-review` skill
  in the tool listing.
- A scan for key-shaped secrets (GitHub, OpenAI, AWS and Slack token formats,
  private-key headers, bearer tokens, API-key environment variables) finds
  none, in the original or the copy.
- The author's email address appears four times, as the git author identity,
  as it does in the repository's commits.

SHA-256 after redaction: `transcript.jsonl`
`d42aa4aa469ba8e48de4afbc1d3c1911fce97c95140a788db3e002a26316e846`;
`subagents/agent-af4031af24ee0c5b0.jsonl`
`833e02bb9e1530b1aa542a4d40af840e871a2a5057ce7616daf3992c35e11d10`.

## Reading order

1. `docs/feedback_channel_journey_2026-10-11_13.md` for the map: what was
   asked, the commits, the delegations, and the errors found and corrected.
2. `transcript.jsonl`, one JSON object per line in conversation order; tool
   calls and their results are interleaved with the assistant's text.
3. The subagent transcript named in the journey's table for any delegated
   result, then the lead's verification of it, which follows the agent's
   report in the main transcript.

Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

@@ -170,28 +171,40 @@ Algebraic identity; checked to \(10^{-9}\) against the tilt bisection for \(K\in

 in the score there (\(n=2,K=2,p=\tfrac12\): likelihood ratios \(\tfrac14,1,\tfrac74\)).
 
-**D.5 (monotone approach in \(n\); version 0.2).** Let \(X_k\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,\tfrac12)\) i.i.d., \(Y_k=X_k-n/2\) (symmetric about 0), \(M_n(K)=\mathbb E\max_kY_k=n\gamma(n,K,\tfrac12)\), \(a_n(K)=M_n(K)/\sqrt n=\sqrt n\,\gamma\). Then \(r(n,K,\tfrac12)=2a_n(K)/\sqrt{2\lambda_K}\), so \(r\) is monotone in \(n\) iff \(a_n^2=M_n^2/n\) is: a comparison of rationals (`scaled_gap_squared`, integer arithmetic, cross-checked against `selection_inflation`).
+**D.5 (monotone approach in \(n\); versions 0.2–0.3).** Let \(X_k\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,\tfrac12)\) i.i.d., \(Y_k=X_k-n/2\) (symmetric about 0), \(M_n(K)=\mathbb E\max_kY_k=n\gamma(n,K,\tfrac12)\), \(a_n(K)=M_n(K)/\sqrt n=\sqrt n\,\gamma\). Then \(r(n,K,\tfrac12)=2a_n(K)/\sqrt{2\lambda_K}\), so \(r\) is monotone in \(n\) iff \(a_n^2=M_n^2/n\) is: a comparison of rationals (`scaled_gap_squared`, integer arithmetic, cross-checked against `selection_inflation`).
 *Theorem (\(K=2\)).* \(a_n(2)^2=n\binom{2n}n^2/(4\cdot16^n)\), \(a_{n+1}(2)^2/a_n(2)^2=(2n+1)^2/(4n(n+1))=1+1/(4n(n+1))>1\), and \(a_n(2)\uparrow1/(2\sqrt\pi)=\mathbb E[M_2]/2\); so \(r(n,2,\tfrac12)\) increases strictly to \(c_2\) and \(\sup_n=c_2\). *Proof.* \(\max(X_1,X_2)=\frac{X_1+X_2}2+\frac{|X_1-X_2|}2\) and \(X_1-X_2+n=X_1+(n-X_2)\sim\mathrm{Bin}(2n,\tfrac12)\), so \(M_n(2)=\tfrac12\mathbb E|S-n|\), \(S\sim\mathrm{Bin}(2n,\tfrac12)\).
 De Moivre: \(\mathbb E|S-n|=2\sum_{s>n}(s-n)\binom{2n}s4^{-n}\) with \(s\binom{2n}s=2n\binom{2n-1}{s-1}\), \(\sum_{s>n}\binom{2n-1}{s-1}=2^{2n-2}\), \(\sum_{s>n}\binom{2n}s=(4^n-\binom{2n}n)/2\), so \(\mathbb E|S-n|=n\binom{2n}n/4^n\) (enumerated for \(n\le30\); the denominator is \(4^n\), not \(2^{2n-1}\)). Hence the closed form; with \(\binom{2n+2}{n+1}/\binom{2n}n=2(2n+1)/(n+1)\) the step ratio is \(\frac{n+1}n\big(\frac{2n+1}{2n+2}\big)^2=\frac{(2n+1)^2}{4n(n+1)}\), above 1 by the \(+1\) in \((2n+1)^2=4n(n+1)+1\). Telescoping, \(a_n(2)^2=\frac1{16}\prod_{j<n}\frac{(2j+1)^2}{(2j)(2j+2)}\uparrow\frac1{16}\cdot\frac4\pi\) (Wallis). \(\square\) Checked exactly for \(n\le200\); \(4n(1-4\pi a_n^2)=0.99937\) at \(n=200\).
 *Theorem (\(K=3\)).* \(M_n(3)=\tfrac32M_n(2)\), so \(a_n(3)\uparrow3/(4\sqrt\pi)\) strictly and \(\sup_nr(n,3,\tfrac12)=c_3\). *Proof.* Deleting one of \(m\) draws uniformly at random, \(\mathbb EY_{(r:m-1)}=\frac{m-r}m\mathbb EY_{(r:m)}+\frac rm\mathbb EY_{(r+1:m)}\); at \(m=3,r=2\): \(\mathbb EY_{(2:2)}=\frac13\mathbb EY_{(2:3)}+\frac23\mathbb EY_{(3:3)}\), and the median of three symmetric draws has mean 0. \(\square\) The same recurrence gives \(M_n(5)=\tfrac52(M_n(4)-M_n(2))\) (checked exactly, \(n\le200\)): odd \(K\) reduce to even \(K\), which are independent quantities.
-*Finite results (\(a_{n+1}^2\) against \(a_n^2\) as rationals).* Monotone for \(K\in\{3,4,5,10,20\}\), \(n\le200\); smallest step ratio always at \(n=200\): 1.0000062 (\(=160801/160800\), \(K=3\)), 1.0000067, 1.0000074, 1.0000102, 1.0000140. Also monotone for \(K=2..30,40,50,100\) at \(n\le100\) and \(K=1000\) at \(n\le40\). The normalized margin \(\mu_n=4n(n+1)(a_{n+1}^2/a_n^2-1)\) is 1 for \(K=2,3\) and at least 1.083, 1.184, 1.643 (\(K=4,5,10\), at \(n=200\)) and 2.207 (\(K=20\), at \(n=4\): the wobble sits near \(n\approx\log_2K\));
+*Finite results, version 0.2 (\(a_{n+1}^2\) against \(a_n^2\) as rationals; superseded by the 0.3 sweeps below).* Monotone for \(K\in\{3,4,5,10,20\}\), \(n\le200\); smallest step ratio always at \(n=200\): 1.0000062 (\(=160801/160800\), \(K=3\)), 1.0000067, 1.0000074, 1.0000102, 1.0000140. Also \(K=2..30,40,50,100\) at \(n\le100\) and \(K=1000\) at \(n\le40\). The normalized margin \(\mu_n=4n(n+1)(a_{n+1}^2/a_n^2-1)=4n(\rho_n-1)+\rho_n^2\) is 1 for \(K=2,3\);
 \(a_n<\mathbb E[M_K]/2\) throughout, \(a_{200}=0.42288,0.51434,0.58105,0.76859,0.93243\) against limits \(0.42314,0.51469,0.58148,0.76938,0.93374\), with \(n(\mathbb E[M_K]/2-a_n)\approx0.053,0.070,0.086,0.158,0.262\).
 *General \(K\).* Adding a fair bit to every count raises the maximum by one iff a candidate at the maximum draws 1, so \(M_{n+1}-M_n=\tfrac12-\mathbb E[2^{-N_n}]\), \(N_n\) the number of candidates at the maximum (identity, enumerated; \(\mathbb E2^{-N}=\sum_m[\bar F(m)^K-F(m-1)^K]\), \(\bar F\) the midpoint CDF, which is \(\mathrm{Bin}(n+1,\tfrac12)\)'s). With \(\rho_n=2n(M_{n+1}-M_n)/M_n\): \(a_{n+1}^2>a_n^2\iff\rho_n+\rho_n^2/(4n)>1\). The sufficient \(\rho_n\ge1\) (\(M_n(K)/M_n(2)\) non-decreasing) holds with equality for \(K=2,3\) and strictly on every cell swept (minimum 1.000103 at \(K=4,n=200\)), but is unproved: \(\rho_n\to1\) for every \(K\) because \(\binom K2\int\varphi^2\Phi^{K-2}=\mathbb E[M_K]/2\) (parts), so the question is second order in \(1/n\).
 The natural route, \(Z_n\le_{cx}Z_{n+1}\) for standardized counts, is false at every step: \(\mathbb E|Z_{2k}|=\sqrt{2k}\binom{2k}k4^{-k}<\mathbb E|Z_{2k+1}|=\sqrt{2k+1}\binom{2k}k4^{-k}>\mathbb E|Z_{2k+2}|\) (exact) and a stop-loss \((x-c)^+\) separates every pair \(n\le60\) (floats, excess \(\ge3.3\times10^{-3}\)). \(K=2\) escapes the parity oscillation because \(X_1-X_2\) is a \(\mathrm{Bin}(2n)\), always of even order. Status: theorem for \(K=2,3\); finite verified example for the rest.
+*\(K\ge4\), version 0.3: the overlap profile.* Write \(w_m=F_n(m)(1-F_n(m))=P(X\le m<X')\), \(m<n\). Since \(F_n(n-1-m)=1-F_n(m)\), \(M_n(K)=\sum_{m<n}[F_n(m)-F_n(m)^K]=\sum_mP_K(w_m)\) with \(2P_K(u(1-u))=1-u^K-(1-u)^K\) (Newton: \(P_2=w\), \(P_3=\tfrac32w\), \(P_4=2w-w^2\), \(P_5=\tfrac52(w-w^2)\); `tie_polynomial`, checked against `centered_max`, \(n\le40\), \(K\le12\)). With \(S_j=\sum_mw_m^j\): \(M_n(2)=S_1\), \(M_n(4)=2S_1-S_2\), and the pair-of-pairs step of R1, \(M_n(4)=M_n(2)+\tfrac12\mathbb E|Y-Y'|\) with \(Y\) the max of two, has \(\mathbb E|Y-Y'|=2\sum_mF_Y(1-F_Y)=2(S_1-S_2)\): the double sum collapses (identity, \(n\le60\)); also \(\mathbb EY_{(3:4)}=3S_2\) (enumerated, \(n\le4\)). The step \(n\to n+1\) replaces \(F_n\) by the midpoints of \((0,F_n,1)\), so \(v_m=\tfrac12(w_{m-1}+w_m)+\tfrac14q_m^2\), and with the local sums \(L_1=\sum_mq_m^2\), \(L_2=\sum_mq_m^2w_m\), \(L_4=\sum_mq_m^4\): \(S_2^{(n+1)}-S_2^{(n)}=\tfrac14(6L_2-L_1)+\tfrac5{16}L_4\) and \(M_{n+1}(4)-M_n(4)=\tfrac34L_1-\tfrac32L_2-\tfrac5{16}L_4\) (identities, \(n\le60\)). Hence \(\rho_n(4)\ge1\iff S_2\ge n[3L_2+\tfrac58L_4-\tfrac12L_1]\), the \(K=4\) analogue of de Moivre's \(S_1=\tfrac n2L_1\) — but an inequality, not an identity.
+*Why R1 fails.* \(S_2=\mathbb EY_{(3:4)}/3\) is not a local sum, \(L_4=\sum_m\binom nm^4/16^n\) is a Franel-type sum (numerators 1, 2, 18, 164, 1810), and the step ratio \(M_{n+1}(4)/M_n(4)\) is not a rational function of \(n\): the linear system \(p(n)=r_ns(n)\) has full column rank for every degree \(\le6\) (exact; at degree 1 the system is solved by \((2n+1)/(2n)\) for \(K=2,3\)), and likewise for \(\mathbb E|Y-Y'|\). What exists instead: \(u_n=2^{4n+1}M_n(4)\) satisfies an order-4 recurrence with degree-8 integer coefficients (nullity one on 53 terms, verified for \(n\le300\); none of order \(\le3\) through degree 12), characteristic polynomial \((x-16)^2(x+2)(x+4)\) — the double root carries \(16^n\sqrt n\), the roots \(-2,-4\) are exponentially small parity terms. So the \(K=2\) telescoping has no analogue; a proof would be an order-4 interval induction on that recurrence, not attempted. \(K=5\) and \(K=8\) inherit the status of \(K=4\).
+*Why R2 fails.* \(\tfrac12-2^{-j}\ge\tfrac14\) for \(j\ge2\) gives \(M_{n+1}-M_n\ge P(N_n\ge2)/4\), so \(nP(N_n\ge2)\ge2M_n\) would prove \(\rho_n\ge1\); \(P(N\ge2)=\sum_m[F(m)^K-F(m-1)^K-Kq_mF(m-1)^{K-1}]\) and \(P(N=j)=\sum_m\binom Kjq_m^jF(m-1)^{K-j}\) (exact, enumerated). The bound is an identity for \(K=2\) (\(N\le2\)) and fails at every \(n\) for \(K=3\), where \(\rho_n=1\): by \(m\to n-m\), \(P(N\ge2)=\tfrac32\sum q_m^2-\tfrac12\sum q_m^3\), so \(nP(N\ge2)-2M_n(3)=-\tfrac n2\sum_mq_m^3<0\) exactly (\(-\tfrac18,-\tfrac5{32},-\tfrac{21}{128},\dots\); \(n\le60\)); it fails for \(K=4\) too (\(-\tfrac18,-\tfrac{17}{64},\dots\)). Selection KL 0.3: c_K for K >= 4, the asymptotic margin, and why two proof routes fail

Monotone approach of r(n,K,1/2) to c_K: theorem for K = 2, 3 (0.2); for
K >= 4 still no theorem, but the obstruction is now located. The overlap
profile w_m = F_n(m)(1 - F_n(m)) gives M_n(K) = sum_m P_K(w_m) with
2 P_K(u(1-u)) = 1 - u^K - (1-u)^K, so M_n(4) = 2 S_1 - S_2 with
S_j = sum_m w_m^j. S_2 has no de Moivre identity, the step ratio
M_{n+1}(4)/M_n(4) is not a rational function of n through degree 6, and
2^{4n+1} M_n(4) obeys an order-4, degree-8 recurrence with characteristic
polynomial (x-16)^2 (x+2)(x+4) (verified n <= 300), so the K = 2
telescoping has no analogue. The tie-mass bound of the second route is an
identity only at K = 2 and misses by exactly -(n/2) sum q_m^3 at K = 3.

The continuity-corrected Edgeworth expansion gives
n(rho_n - 1) -> c(K) = (E[M_K^3] - (5/2) E[M_K]) / (6 E[M_K]), M_K the
max of K standard normals: c(2) = c(3) = 0 exactly (reproducing the 1/(8n)
deficit of the K = 2 theorem), c(K) > 0 and increasing for K = 4..100
(c(4) = 0.020561), and Richardson extrapolation of the exact rho_n at
n = 399, 400 matches the quadrature to 4.5e-8 at K = 4. Exact sweeps:
a_n(K)^2 strictly increasing for K = 4..100, n <= 400, and for
K in {200, 500, 1000, 10^4}, n <= 60; the slimmest margin anywhere is
K = 4, n = 400 (rho = 1.0000516), approached from above.

Status: theorem for K = 2, 3; for every K >= 4 a finite verified example
plus a cited asymptotic with positive limit margin. 56 checks (was 42),
86 tests (was 68), receipt selection_kl_v0_3.

Selection KL 0.3: c_K for K >= 4, the asymptotic margin, and why two proof routes fail

Monotone approach of r(n,K,1/2) to c_K: theorem for K = 2, 3 (0.2); for
K >= 4 still no theorem, but the obstruction is now located. The overlap
profile w_m = F_n(m)(1 - F_n(m)) gives M_n(K) = sum_m P_K(w_m) with
2 P_K(u(1-u)) = 1 - u^K - (1-u)^K, so M_n(4) = 2 S_1 - S_2 with
S_j = sum_m w_m^j. S_2 has no de Moivre identity, the step ratio
M_{n+1}(4)/M_n(4) is not a rational function of n through degree 6, and
2^{4n+1} M_n(4) obeys an order-4, degree-8 recurrence with characteristic
polynomial (x-16)^2 (x+2)(x+4) (verified n <= 300), so the K = 2
telescoping has no analogue. The tie-mass bound of the second route is an
identity only at K = 2 and misses by exactly -(n/2) sum q_m^3 at K = 3.

The continuity-corrected Edgeworth expansion gives
n(rho_n - 1) -> c(K) = (E[M_K^3] - (5/2) E[M_K]) / (6 E[M_K]), M_K the
max of K standard normals: c(2) = c(3) = 0 exactly (reproducing the 1/(8n)
deficit of the K = 2 theorem), c(K) > 0 and increasing for K = 4..100
(c(4) = 0.020561), and Richardson extrapolation of the exact rho_n at
n = 399, 400 matches the quadrature to 4.5e-8 at K = 4. Exact sweeps:
a_n(K)^2 strictly increasing for K = 4..100, n <= 400, and for
K in {200, 500, 1000, 10^4}, n <= 60; the slimmest margin anywhere is
K = 4, n = 400 (rho = 1.0000516), approached from above.

Status: theorem for K = 2, 3; for every K >= 4 a finite verified example
plus a cited asymptotic with positive limit margin. 56 checks (was 42),
86 tests (was 68), receipt selection_kl_v0_3.

  `evaluation_selection_kl` (Theorems A-C: tie rules, KL(pi_K||p0) <= ln K - (K-1)/K for every finite law via jitter + Jensen, DV bound; sup of gap/bound = 1 via c_K -> 1, c_2 = 0.90775);
  `evaluation_gold_calibration` (three-rater Walsh identities, (1-2eta_1)^2 = kappa_12 kappa_1C / kappa_2C; sign convention is an assumption; constraint check vacuous at balanced prior; copy-grader false finding);
  multigen 0.3 (Prop 8: gate lowers the TRUE value in stochastic order for any threshold rule, proven; count dominance finite only, 972 cells; lowering a threshold is not monotone in general).
  Open now: structural description of the optimal patch policy (Lemma 9 only), count dominance proof, monotone approach to c_K, sampling distribution for eta-hat, Dawid-Skene asymmetric case.
- Round 3 (Patrick: "proceed, don't worry about Will"): a5ab4ff lattice 0.5 — Theorem 10: one-hit optimum is exactly min_c (n_c+1)/(F_c+1), best finisher, never switch; CORRECTION: the 0.2 claim "greedy by rate optimal at one hit" was wrong (exchange argument incomplete), fails at size 7 ({(2,1),(7,4)}: 8/5 vs 3/2); the grid's two regularities and the two-category single-switch pattern all refuted. 70f6f27 selection KL 0.2 — monotone approach to c_K proven for K=2 (a_n^2 step ratio 1+1/(4n(n+1))) and K=3 (M_n(3) = 3/2 M_n(2)), finite for K>=4. 0f583ee multigen 0.4 — Proposition 9: count dominance PROVEN for every threshold rule (first-passage indicators; L1 new-better-than-used, L2 count-monotone survival, L3 level-monotone, L4 window prefix-average; Q P^k <= P^{k+1}); naive optimal among threshold rules only (a one-step deviation beats it). Gold calibration 0.2 — sampling law of eta-hat exact and prior-free (4-category multinomial, to m=742), delta variance V=(49/90)^2 at the fixture, planning m=742 for s.e.<0.02; two-class Dawid-Skene with three raters solved explicitly (R^2 = k3^2 + 4 c12 c13 c23), just identified, NO independence test (absorbs a copying grader as asymmetry); asymmetric gold-noise inversion; agreement rate is invariant under any label-dependent flips. Round 3 complete and pushed 2026-10-13; suite 704.
  Open after round 3: structural description of the optimal patch policy for H>=2 (Theorem 10 covers H=1; DP otherwise); monotone approach to c_K for K>=4; count dominance for mixed gain laws; joint interval for (eta-hat, eps1-hat); a fourth rater for independence testing under asymmetry.
  Lesson: small exhaustive grids let two false "theorems" through (greedy at H=1; equal-rate larger-first); always stress a grid regularity at larger sizes before calling it a proof.

Context: Patrick's framing is whether Will Brown (@willccbb, Prime Intellect) overestimates the RL paradigm; the math locates where reported RL gains can be phantom (reuse, narrow reward channel, correlated judge) and what a ledger must publish. His posts of 2026-10-12 could not be read (see [[x-posts-access]]); the note cites his July 2026 sigmoid post and the Latent Space interview. Patrick never answered whether to paste them or allow Chrome.

**Why:** Spiral's remote is public ([[spiral-remote-is-public]]); the atlas names labs, so it went through a source check before the push.
**How to apply:** further work goes on this branch (create a worktree on it; the main checkout stays on rtg-0) and is pushed with `git push origin feedback-channel-and-rsi-atlas`. Open items: an index rule for the optimal adaptive policy, extreme-value asymptotic, correlated candidates, gate-vs-naive theorem under true gains, a measurement procedure for eps1, the topology side (RSITopology repo).

# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|

def mixed_window_sums(kernel, iterate, items) -> dict[tuple[int, int], list[Q]]:
    """``window_sums`` for a kernel with several landings per count: the
    prefix sums over ``J = c+1..n`` of ``sum_{y: count J} p(y) [f(y) -
    f(c, i)]`` with the kernel's own landing probabilities, so that the
    entry for ``a`` is ``(P f - Q f)(c, i)`` for the rule with ``a(c) = a``."""

    out = {}
    for (c, i), entries in kernel.items():
        by_count: dict[int, Q] = {}
        for y, p in entries[1:]:
            by_count[y[0]] = by_count.get(y[0], Q(0)) + p * (iterate[y] - iterate[(c, i)])
        running, sums = Q(0), []
        for J in range(c + 1, items + 1):
            running += by_count.get(J, Q(0))
            sums.append(running)
        out[(c, i)] = sums
    return out

def mixed_window_sums(kernel, iterate, items) -> dict[tuple[int, int], list[Q]]:
    """``window_sums`` for a kernel with several landings per count: the
    prefix sums over ``J = c+1..n`` of ``sum_{y: count J} p(y) [f(y) -
    f(c, i)]`` with the kernel's own landing probabilities, so that the
    entry for ``a`` is ``(P f - Q f)(c, i)`` for the rule with ``a(c) = a``."""

    out = {}
    for (c, i), entries in kernel.items():
        by_count: dict[int, Q] = {}
        for y, p in entries[1:]:
            by_count[y[0]] = by_count.get(y[0], Q(0)) + p * (iterate[y] - iterate[(c, i)])
        running, sums = Q(0), []
        for J in range(c + 1, items + 1):
            running += by_count.get(J, Q(0))
            sums.append(running)
        out[(c, i)] = sums
    return out

# Estimating the gold grader's error with a second grader

Draft 0.3 — 2026-10-13. Closes the boundary of [judge_shared_error_measurement.md](judge_shared_error_measurement.md) §5: Proposition 2 inverts
gold noise at a *known* flip rate \(\eta\); here \(\eta\) is estimated from a second independent grader, exactly. 0.2 added the sampling law of \(\hat\eta_1\) (§6) and the asymmetric
Dawid–Skene model (§7); 0.3 adds a fourth rater, which makes that model testable (§8), and a joint statement for \((\eta_1,\varepsilon_1)\) (§9). Files: `src/spiral_ln/evaluation_gold_calibration.py`,
`tests/test_evaluation_gold_calibration.py` (126 tests), `output/evaluation_gold_calibration/gold_v0_3.json` (58 checks, source hashes, exact fractions, floats under `headline`).
No model, judge or grader was called; every number is a `Fraction` (or an integer bound, §9); the judge module's tails and maps are reused.

```powershell
$env:PYTHONPATH = "src"; python scripts/verify_evaluation_gold_calibration.py --sampling-size 400 --sampling-size 742 --joint-size 4000 --workers 4 --output output/evaluation_gold_calibration/gold_v0_3.json
python -m pytest tests/test_evaluation_gold_calibration.py -q
```

## 1. Model

True label \(Y\in\{0,1\}\), \(\pi=\Pr[Y=1]\). Three raters report \(Y\) flipped independently given \(Y\), each with one symmetric error rate: the gold
grader \(G_1\) (\(\eta_1\)), a second grader \(G_2\) (\(\eta_2\)) and the controller's own answer \(X_C\) (error \(1-a\)). The judge is excluded: its verdict
implies a label that equals \(Y\) iff \(J=1\), and that label is conditionally independent of \(X_C\) given \(Y\) iff \(\varepsilon_0=\varepsilon\), i.e. iff
\(\varepsilon_1=\varepsilon\) — axiom A2, the hypothesis under test. Write \(\tau=1-2\pi\), \(d_i=1-2e_i\), and for \(S\subseteq\{1,2,3\}\) the Walsh
coefficient \(\hat p_S=E\prod_{i\in S}(-1)^{X_i}\).
......
## 8. Four raters: the asymmetric model becomes testable

Add a third grader \(G_3\), keep the controller \(C\) as rater 4; the cost is one more independent grading of the same sealed sample. Nine parameters \((\pi,\alpha_i,\beta_i)\) on
15 degrees of freedom (`four_rater_model`); write \(k_S=E\prod_{i\in S}(X_i-p_i)\), \(c_{ij}=k_{ij}\).
**Proposition 5.** \(k_S=\mu_{|S|}\prod_{i\in S}\delta_i\), \(\mu_2=u\), \(\mu_3=u(1-2\pi)\), \(\mu_4=u(1-3u)\). *Proof.* \(E[X_i-p_i\mid Y]=\delta_i(Y-\pi)\); conditional independence multiplies. \(\square\)
Hence six equalities (`four_rater_residuals`): tetrads \(c_{12}c_{34}=c_{13}c_{24}=c_{14}c_{23}\) (each \(u^2\prod\delta\)); ratios \(k_{123}c_{14}=k_{124}c_{13}\), \(k_{123}c_{14}=k_{134}c_{12}\), \(k_{123}c_{24}=k_{234}c_{12}\)
(both sides \(u^2(1-2\pi)\delta_p^2\prod_{q\ne p}\delta_q\), \(p\) the pivot); and \((k_{1234}-c_{12}c_{34})c_{12}=k_{123}k_{124}\), as \(\mu_4-u^2=u(1-2\pi)^2\). The other nine ratio relations follow (`ratio_relations`).
**Proposition 6 (exactly six).** (a) The \(16\times9\) parameter Jacobian has rank 9 wherever \(0<\pi<1\) and three \(\delta_i\ne0\): Proposition 4 on that triple with \(\delta_4=c_{14}/(u\delta_1)\),
\(1-\alpha_4=p_4+(1-\pi)\delta_4\), \(\beta_4=p_4-\pi\delta_4\) is a smooth left inverse. (b) The residuals' \(6\times15\) Jacobian in the centred moments (coordinates on the simplex) has rank 6
wherever \(c_{12}c_{13}\ne0\), model or not: on \((c_{24},c_{34},k_{124},k_{134},k_{234},k_{1234})\) the minor is lower triangular with determinant \(-c_{12}^4c_{13}^2\). So near an identified model
point the nine-dimensional image is the zero set of six independent functions. \(\square\) Both ranks are also computed exactly on 243 grid points; moments match the \(2^5\) latent
enumeration on 1024. **Test** (`four_rater_constraints`): with every \(c_{ij}\ne0\), a table is in the model iff the residuals vanish and the triple fits exist with all nine rates in
\([0,1]\) (triple \((1,2,3)\) fixes \(\pi\) and three raters, \(c_{14},p_4\) rater 4, the equalities the remaining six moments; the four fits must agree; exact fits are rebuilt cell by cell).
A chance rater keeps rank 9 but zeroes three covariances: the residuals degenerate (rank 4 with \(G_2\) at chance, 6 with \(C\)) and the test refuses; two chance raters lower the rank.
**Fixture.** \(\pi=\tfrac14\); \((\alpha,\beta)\): \(G_1\) \((\tfrac1{10},\tfrac15)\), \(G_2\) \((\tfrac15,\tfrac1{10})\), \(G_3\) \((\tfrac15,\tfrac25)\), \(C\) \((\tfrac1{10},\tfrac3{10})\); \(\delta=(\tfrac7{10},\tfrac7{10},\tfrac25,\tfrac35)\). Counts at \(m=10000\) (lexicographic
in \(x_1..x_4\)): 2269, 981, 1516, 684, 256, 144, 184, 216, 576, 324, 414, 486, 99, 351, 186, 1314. \(c_{12}c_{34}=\tfrac{1323}{320000}\), \(k_{123}=\tfrac{147}{8000}\), \(k_{1234}=\tfrac{3087}{320000}\);
residuals zero, ranks 6 and 9, all nine parameters recovered exactly on every triple (\(R=u|\delta_i\delta_j\delta_k|\) is rational). An anti-informative \(G_2\) needs `rater_1_informative`.
**Copying grader.** If \(G_2\) copies \(G_1\) with probability \(\rho\), \(\mathrm{Cov}(X_1,X_2\mid Y)=\rho\,\mathrm{Var}(X_1\mid Y)\): \(c_{12}=u\delta_1\tilde\delta_2+\rho V_1\), \(V_1=\pi\alpha_1(1-\alpha_1)+(1-\pi)\beta_1(1-\beta_1)\),
\(\tilde\delta_2=\rho\delta_1+(1-\rho)\delta_2\), the other covariances keep product form, so **\(c_{12}c_{34}-c_{13}c_{24}=\rho V_1c_{34}\)** and \(c_{13}c_{24}=c_{14}c_{23}\) (`copy_grader_tetrad_residual`; exact on
24 cells). Fixture: \(V_1=\tfrac{57}{400}\), \(c_{34}=\tfrac9{200}\), residual \(\tfrac{513}{80000}\rho\). Witness at \(\rho=1\), \(m=10000\): 2525, 1125, 1700, 900, eight zeros, 675, 675, 600, 1800; its triple
\((G_1,G_2,G_3)\) fits exactly and in range (\(\pi=\tfrac38\), two perfect graders: §7's absorption), four raters reject it (residual \(\tfrac{513}{80000}\), triple fits inconsistent). Any \(\rho>0\) is
detected when \(V_1>0\), \(0<\pi<1\), \(\delta_3\delta_4\ne0\), **at \(\pi=\tfrac12\) too**, where §3's check is vacuous. The odd product names the split \(\{1,2\mid3,4\}\), not the dependent side.
*Evidence status.* Propositions 5–6, the converse, the residual: *algebraic identities*, enumeration-checked; fixtures: *finite verified examples*. All are population identities:
on observed counts the residuals never vanish exactly, and their sampling law is not derived.

## 9. A joint statement for \((\eta_1,\varepsilon_1)\)

`joint_statement(record, alpha, grid)`, symmetric model, withheld when §3's check fails. (1) \(H\) = grid points \(\eta_0\) kept by (a) the disagreement bound at level \(\alpha/2\) (exact)
and (b) the two-sided test of the observed square at \(\alpha/2\): \(p(\eta_0)=\min(1,2\min(\Pr[\tilde S\le\hat s],\Pr[\tilde S\ge\hat s]))\) under §6's law at \((\eta_0,\hat\eta_2,1-\hat a)\), \(\tilde S\) putting
sign failures below every square and range failures above. (2) At each \(\eta_0\in H\): §4's inversion (clamped into the feasible range, flagged), the exact ceiling and independence
tests and the two-sided level-\(\alpha\) Clopper–Pearson bracket on the corrected counts. (3) **If \(\eta_1\) is a grid point, with probability \(\ge1-2\alpha\) (Bonferroni) \(\eta_1\in H\) and
\(\varepsilon_1\in\bigcup_H\mathrm{CP}(\eta_0)\)**: exactly for (1a), else under two plug-ins: (1b) fixes \(\eta_2,a\) at their estimates (their error is not propagated), (2) treats the corrected
counts as a binomial sample, as §4 does. The sampling law of \(\hat\varepsilon_1\) is not derived.
*Tails.* Given \(\mathrm{rest}=k_{12}+k_{13}\), \(d=m-2\,\mathrm{rest}\) is fixed and \(ab\le\hat s\,md\) is two tails in \(k_{12}\): `square_tail_law` sums prefix sums, \(O(m^2)\) big-integer products (about 270 s a
point at \(m=4000\)), equal to the label-table enumeration at \(m=16\). `square_tail_bracket` bounds the same tails in integers: the law factors into \(\mathrm{Bin}(m,q_{12}+q_{13})\), \(\mathrm{Bin}(m-\mathrm{rest},\cdot)\),
\(\mathrm{Bin}(\mathrm{rest},\cdot)\); each pmf is floored and ceiled at \(2^{-160}\) outward from its exact mode (ratios \(\le1\)), terms below \(2^{-128}\) are bounded in bulk. The bracket holds the exact law
on nine cases up to \(m=742\), is narrower than \(10^{-34}\), takes 3 s a point at \(m=4000\); one straddling the level would fall back to the exact law (never needed). *Counts.* Rounding the
\(N_{ij}\) separately can break the parity \(\sum N_{ij}\equiv m\) (at 742: 549, 549, 505, which no table has); `agreement_counts` rounds the four pattern counts by largest remainder: (549, 549, 504),
\(\hat s=\tfrac{31684}{49343}\approx0.6421\); at 4000 (2960, 2960, 2720), \(\hat s=\tfrac{16}{25}\). Grid \(k/100\), \(\alpha=\tfrac1{20}\), \(\varepsilon=\tfrac1{10}\) declared:

| \(m\) | \(H\) | independent judge: \(\varepsilon_1\in\) | shared judge: \(\varepsilon_1\in\) | ranges | tests, jointly |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 742 | 0.06–0.14 (9 points) | [0, 0.2970] | [0.2509, 0.6553] | overlap on [0.251, 0.297] | separate |
| 4000 | 0.09–0.12 (4 points) | [0.0030, 0.1629] | [0.3927, 0.5580] | disjoint | separate |

"Separate": at every \(\eta_0\in H\) the ceiling test rejects for the independent judge (\(p\le2.8\times10^{-13}\) at 742) and the independence test for the shared one (\(p\le1.7\times10^{-12}\)),
while neither is rejected under its own hypothesis everywhere (at 742: independence at 0.06–0.08, ceiling at 0.13–0.14). **At the planning size the judges separate jointly by the
tests but not by the \(\varepsilon_1\) ranges**; at 4000 by both. The overlap comes from the ends of \(H\) (\(\hat\varepsilon_1=\tfrac13\) for the shared judge at 0.14, 0.228 for the independent one
at 0.06). With the disagreement bound alone (\(\eta_0\le0.288\) at level \(\alpha\)) the set passes \(1-a'=0.26\), where the inversion implies a perfect controller: \(\varepsilon_1\) undetermined. §7's
asymmetric record is withheld. *Evidence status:* coverage is a theorem given the plug-ins; the sets, ranges and p-values are *finite verified examples*.

## 10. Not delivered

- No observed graders; binary labels only. Real counts give brackets, and §8's residuals never vanish on them: no level-\(\alpha\) test of the six equalities on \(m\) items.
- §6's law is conditional on the defined event. §9 holds given its plug-ins, on the grid, in the symmetric model; no sampling law for \(\hat\varepsilon_1\) or the three- or four-rater fits.
- A bracketed Dawid–Skene fit brackets \(\hat\varepsilon_1\) only if the inversion is monotone in \(R\) (not checked). The four-rater test refuses a chance rater though the model stays
  locally identified; three raters cannot test conditional independence; §3's check has no power at \(\pi=\tfrac12\).

cat > "$SP/commit20.txt" <<'EOF'
Gold calibration 0.3: a fourth rater makes the asymmetric model testable; a joint statement for (eta1, eps1)

Section 8. With a third grader beside the gold grader, the second grader
and the controller, the two-class latent model has nine parameters on 15
degrees of freedom. Proposition 5: k_S = mu_|S| prod delta_i with
mu_2 = u, mu_3 = u(1-2pi), mu_4 = u(1-3u). Hence six equalities: two
tetrads c12c34 = c13c24 = c14c23, three ratio relations, and
(k1234 - c12c34)c12 = k123k124. Proposition 6: exactly six, since the
parameter Jacobian has rank 9 where pi is interior and three delta_i are
nonzero, and the residuals' Jacobian has rank 6 wherever c12c13 != 0 (a
lower-triangular minor with determinant -c12^4 c13^2). A table is in the
model iff the residuals vanish and the fitted rates lie in [0, 1]. A
grader copying the gold grader with probability rho leaves the residual
rho V1 c34 on one tetrad: three raters absorb it as two perfect graders,
four reject it, and they detect it at pi = 1/2, where the three-rater
check has no power. Population identities only; no level-alpha test of
the residuals on observed counts is derived.

Section 9. joint_statement keeps the grid values of eta1 that pass the
disagreement bound and a two-sided test of the observed square, then
brackets eps1 by Clopper-Pearson at each. Coverage 1 - 2 alpha is a
theorem given two plug-ins and eta1 on the grid. At the planning size
m = 742 an independent and a shared judge are separated by the tests
but their eps1 ranges overlap; at m = 4000 they are disjoint.

The first agent on this ran out of usage credit after writing most of
the module; a second agent finished it and corrected six defects in the
first one's code (separately rounded agreement counts that no item table
can produce, a wrong chance-rater rank expectation, anti-informative
orientation, a joint statement not withheld when the check fails, a
false disjointness check at m = 742, an off-by-one in the tail law).

SP="/c/Users/patri/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/C--Users-patri-OneDrive-Documents-GitHub-Spiral/af5af8c1-0184-44ad-ab52-2aae8f4d54ac/scratchpad"
PY=/c/Users/patri/OneDrive/Documents/GitHub/Spiral/.venv/Scripts/python.exe
$PY -I - "$SP/checks/redaction_terms.local.json" <<'EOF'
import json, sys
from pathlib import Path
p = Path(sys.argv[1]); d = json.loads(p.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
if "ark-audit" not in d["dir_suffixes"]:
    d["dir_suffixes"].append("ark-audit")
extra = [
    # regex-escaped forms of the root names, as they appear when the terms file itself is shown in the transcript
    [r"\\+b(?:[redacted]|[redacted]|[redacted]|[redacted]|[redacted]|[redacted]|[redacted])(?:\\+s\*wallet)?\\+b", "[redacted]", "i"],
[withheld by redaction: this text named the private review terms]
    [r"[redacted]", "[redacted]", "i"],
    [r"[redacted]", "[redacted]", "i"],
[withheld by redaction: this text named the private review terms]
[withheld by redaction: this text named the private review terms]
    [r"[redacted]\(-tvc\)\?", "[redacted]", "i"],
]
have = {t[0] for t in d["tokens"]}
# put the escaped-form rules first so the plain word rules don't half-match them
d["tokens"] = [t for t in extra if t[0] not in have] + d["tokens"]
p.write_text(json.dumps(d, indent=2) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
print(len(d["tokens"]), "token rules;", d["dir_suffixes"])
EOF
P="/c/Users/patri/.claude/projects/C--Users-patri-OneDrive-Documents-GitHub-Spiral"; SID="af5af8c1-0184-44ad-ab52-2aae8f4d54ac"
S="$SP/export_full3"; rm -rf "$S" "$SP/export_redacted6"; mkdir -p "$S"
cp "$P/$SID.jsonl" "$S/transcript.jsonl"
cp -r "$P/$SID/subagents" "$P/$SID/tool-results" "$P/$SID/custom-title.json" "$S/"
cp "$SP/export/metadata.json" "$SP/export/local-session-state.json" "$S/"
sha256sum "$S/transcript.jsonl" | cut -c1-64 > "$SP/transcript_raw_sha.txt"; stat -c %s "$S/transcript.jsonl" >> "$SP/transcript_raw_sha.txt"; cat "$SP/transcript_raw_sha.txt"
$PY -I "$SP/checks/redact_export.py" "$S" "$SP/export_redacted6" "$SP/checks/redaction_terms.local.json" | head -1
